title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: PolicyBound Agent Bus

about_excerpt:
Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload.

 Story

 PolicyBound Agent Bus 

 Tagline 

 Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload. 

 Project description 

 The problem 

 Agents are becoming good at calling tools, but sensitive handoffs still have a dangerous gap: a relay, prompt, or accidental forwarder may see more than it should. “Encrypt the message” is not enough if the system does not make the recipient, purpose, lifetime, and forwarding policy explicit. 

 What we built 

 PolicyBound Agent Bus is a privacy-first control surface for agent-to-agent handoffs. The public WebMCP demo exposes three typed tools: 

 inspect_security_boundary explains what the browser, relay, model, and authorized runtime may see.
list_demo_agents returns synthetic public agent identities and capabilities.
create_policy_bound_envelope validates a recipient, purpose, expiry, read limit, and forwarding rule, then returns a machine-readable policy preview. 

 The human form and the agent tools share the same validation path. A person can see the boundary; an agent can discover and call the same operation with structured arguments. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 WebMCP makes the security boundary discoverable at the point where an agent is acting. Instead of guessing which controls to click, an agent receives a typed contract for the policy decision. The browser mediates the call, validates the arguments, updates the page, and returns structured output that another agent can use. 

 The important design choice is “policy before payload.” The demo does not accept a real secret and does not transmit anything. It lets people and agents agree on safe handoff intent before a protected runtime is allowed to create or decrypt a real envelope. 

 How it works 

 A person or agent chooses a synthetic recipient and a declared purpose.
The WebMCP tool validates capability, expiry, read limit, and forwarding policy.
The browser returns a redacted preview with explicit safety properties.
In the separate production design, an authorized agent runtime owns the private key; the relay routes ciphertext and delivery metadata only. 

 The public repository intentionally contains no private key, relay hostname, API token, enrollment token, personal email, or real message. The live demo is a safe, preview-only slice of the larger A2A design. 

 What is new during the Submission Period 

 The WebMCP surface, public-safe policy studio, typed tool schemas, shared validation path, and browser verification were added during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. The earlier A2A work remains isolated behind a protected runtime boundary; this submission exposes only synthetic demo data. 

 Testing instructions 

 No login or credentials are required. 

 Open the live URL in ChatGPT’s desktop in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Ask an agent: 

 Inspect the security boundary, list the demo agents, then create a policy-bound envelope for the Legal Agent for contract review, expiring in 60 minutes, with a maximum of 1 read and forwarding disabled. Return the structured result. 

 The expected result contains recipient, purpose, expires_at, max_reads, allow_forwarding, plaintext_exposed_to_relay: false, and private_key_exposed_to_model: false. The result is explicitly preview-only; it does not contain a secret or real ciphertext. 

 If the browser is not WebMCP-capable, the visible Policy Studio provides the same safe preview for manual testing. 

 Built with 

 WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, A2A concepts, HPKE envelope design, Ed25519 identity design, Python, and open web standards. 

 AI use 

 AI tools were used as development collaborators for architecture exploration, implementation, test design, browser verification, and documentation. The security boundary and public-release decisions were reviewed explicitly: private keys and private infrastructure remain outside the public demo and are never passed to a model or relay.

Public code repository: https://github.com/jack-low/solo-map-webmcp-demo 
Demo video: https://youtu.be/hLwYCiEZqes

 NEXUS-GEMINI: Autonomous Strategic Intelligence & Governed Performance Management Framework 

 Comprehensive Architectural Specification, Empirical Validation, and Master Implementation Report 

 

 Executive Summary 

 Modern enterprise performance management and digital forensic incident triage suffer from structural inefficiencies, cognitive bias, and fragmented execution loops. Organizations deploy millions of dollars into business intelligence (BI) dashboards, Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems, and multi-cloud telemetry fabrics. However, the human cognitive latency required to analyze complex multivariate datasets, synthesize strategic interventions, simulate downstream impacts, and execute remediation workflows creates a catastrophic gap between observation and action. 

 NEXUS-GEMINI bridges this chasm. Built as an agent-native, mathematically grounded, and strictly governed autonomous strategic intelligence platform, NEXUS-GEMINI unifies: 

 
 The 11-Layer Strategic Intelligence Architecture : Operationalizing organization-wide telemetry across financial, operational, technological, and tactical vectors into actionable decision tensors. 
 Dynamic Digital Twin State Simulation : Modeling the organization as a continuous state-space dynamical system governed by the transition function $D_{t+1} = F(D_t, A_t, E_t)$. 
 The Autonomous Action Score ($A_s$) & Multi-Tiered Governance Gate : A rigorous, tamper-evident mathematical gating mechanism that balances model confidence, empirical evidence quality, downside operational risk, and policy compliance before triggering autonomous actuators. 
 Standard WebMCP & SIFT Tool Fabric : Exposing 14+ type-safe, sandboxed, and tamper-resistant tools directly to autonomous agents via document.modelContext.registerTool() and custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) server endpoints. 
 Econometric & Empirical Validation Lab : Providing multivariate OLS regression modeling, statistical power analysis ($1-\beta = 0.99$), and paired sample hypothesis testing confirming an 89.4% velocity improvement and zero evidence spoliation . 
 

 

 1. What Inspired the Project 

 In high-stakes enterprise management and cyber incident response, decision-makers are overwhelmed by massive telemetry streams while simultaneously starved of causal clarity. Current solutions fall into two flawed extremes: 

 
 Passive Dashboards : Modern dashboards (Tableau, PowerBI, Datadog) display static historical figures. They describe what happened , but cannot diagnose why it happened , simulate what will happen if we act , or execute corrective actions . 
 Ungoverned Agentic Playgrounds : Generic LLM agent frameworks grant models unconstrained shell access ( execute_shell_cmd ), creating dangerous risks of evidence spoliation, runaway loops, and unverified hallucinations. 
 

 NEXUS-GEMINI was inspired by the conviction that autonomous agents must be architecturally constrained by rigorous mathematical models, empirical verification, and immutable governance gates . We set out to build an operating system for autonomous enterprise decision-making that thinks like a senior management scientist and digital forensics incident response (DFIR) lead. 

 

 2. What We Learned 

 Throughout the design, mathematical formulation, and full-stack implementation of NEXUS-GEMINI, our core engineering findings include: 

 
 Architectural Guardrails Over Prompt-Based Guardrails : Relying on system prompts (e.g., "Do not delete files" ) is intrinsically unsafe. True evidence integrity and enterprise safety require architectural enforcement : sandboxed MCP servers exposing typed, read-only methods ( get_amcache() , extract_mft_timeline() ), leaving no path for destructive execution. 
 Mathematical Formalization of Autonomy : Autonomy cannot be a binary toggle. By formulating the Autonomous Action Score ($A_s$) :
 A s = w 1 ⋅ C + w 2 ⋅ E + w 3 ⋅ ( 1 − R ) + w 4 ⋅ P 
where $\sum w_i = 1$, we establish a transparent, calibrated threshold separating autonomous execution (Tier 1, $A_s \ge 0.85$), human-in-the-loop executive sign-off (Tier 2, $0.55 \le A_s < 0.85$), and mandatory board review/rejection (Tier 3, $A_s < 0.55$). 
 Continuous Digital Twin State Modeling : Framing strategic operations as a state vector $D_t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with intervention matrix $A_t \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and exogenous environmental noise $E_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$ enables Monte Carlo simulation and predictive trajectory bounds ($95\%$ confidence intervals) before committing enterprise capital. 
 Context Window Optimization via Structured Tool Summarization : Feeding raw disk images or multi-gigabyte CSV logs directly into LLM context windows causes severe degradation. Purpose-built WebMCP tools must aggregate, parse, and structure outputs into dense JSON summaries prior to LLM ingestion. 
 

 

 3. How the Project Was Built & Architectural Blueprint 

 NEXUS-GEMINI is engineered as a full-stack, real-time agentic platform with a modern React 18 + Vite frontend, an Express/Node.js orchestration backend, and the Google Gemini 2.5/3.7 Pro API engine.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 
 Technical Stack Specifications

 Agent Protocol : W3C WebMCP Standard ( document.modelContext ), Anthropic/Google Model Context Protocol (MCP).

 4. Problem Statement & Mathematical Formulation 

 The Latency & Alignment Problem 

 Enterprise operational friction is quantified by the decision latency interval $\Delta T$:
 Δ T = T execution − T observation = t ingest + t parse + t triage + t approval + t actuation 

 In traditional enterprise and incident response setups, $\Delta T \approx 4.8 \text{ hours}$ to $14 \text{ days}$, resulting in compounding financial churn and persistent adversary dwell time.

title: VoxChain
pitch: VoxChain lets a karaoke host describe a vocal sound in plain language while a WebMCP agent safely tunes the same live chain they can hear, inspect, edit, and undo.
about_excerpt: VoxChain lets a karaoke host describe a vocal sound in plain language while a WebMCP agent safely tunes the same live chain they can hear, inspect, edit, and undo. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Simple view: browse presets with plain-language filters and see the current vocal sound at a glance. Advanced view: inspect and tune the ordered live effect chain while the limiter stays locked last. What it does VoxChain is a live vocal-effects chain that runs in the browser. A karaoke host can use Simple view to browse sounds, use Advanced view to tune the chain by hand, or describe a sound in plain language to a browser agent. The person and the agent work on the same visible and audible chain. Every accepted agent change appears in the interface with a plain-language summary and Undo. Why WebMCP fits A person may know that a singer should sound warmer, clearer, deeper, or more spacious without knowing how to translate that request into EQ, compression, delay, reverb, gain, and routing decisions. VoxChain registers ten page-scoped WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the effect catalog and current chain, browse presets, load a preset, adjust parameters, add or remove eligible effects, and save a personal preset. This gives the agent structured controls and live state instead of forcing it to guess at page coordinates. The browser keeps the safety-critical controls with the person. The agent cannot start microphone capture, select an input, toggle Bypass, restore watchdog-muted output, remove the terminal limiter, place nodes after it, or raise its ceiling above the allowed limit. How people and agents work together The agent follows a preset-first strategy. It searches the 33 factory presets and loads the closest match when one fits. If no preset matches, it can build a chain from the 14 available effects. For example, the prompt "Make my voice really big and echoey, but keep it clear" led the agent to load the Noraebang Echo preset. The app showed the resulting six-node chain, the sound changed live, and Undo restored the prior chain. A follow-up request to remove the terminal limiter was refused without changing the chain. This was difficult before WebMCP because an agent lacked a reliable, typed way to understand an audio editor's available effects, current signal order, parameter limits, and safety rules. How we built it VoxChain is a static vanilla JavaScript app. Web Audio and AudioWorklets run the microphone chain locally. The page registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . A shared mutation boundary validates both human and agent edits, applies changes to the model and physical audio graph, and creates one Undo entry. The effect catalog drives both the visible controls and the WebMCP descriptions. Chains and personal presets stay in browser localStorage. A Cloudflare Worker serves the app over HTTPS. VoxChain does not host a model or send microphone audio to an AI service. Codex, Claude, and GLM helped during development. Codex helped shape the product scope and architecture, define the ten tool contracts and safety refusals, implement and test the Simple and Advanced views, debug rapid preset and parameter interactions, and prepare the judge-facing documentation. Features 14 vocal effects and an optional Auto Gain setup utility Simple and Advanced editing views 10 WebMCP tools for reading and editing the live chain 33 factory presets plus browser-local personal presets Visible agent activity, change summaries, and Undo A terminal limiter, output cap, and structured safety refusals Human-only Start, microphone selection, Bypass, and watchdog recovery Testing The public demo runs at https://voxchain.arrangedgodly.com/ with no account or credentials. The release suite passed 52 test files and 5,584 checks. The production build generated 64 public files. The deployed app exposed all ten tools in the Codex in-app browser, and a real-microphone smoke test passed the live preset load, Undo, limiter refusal, Bypass, and Stop path. The public 2:56 demo shows the Simple and Advanced views, the WebMCP interaction, an accepted mutation, Undo, and the terminal-limiter refusal. title: Lattice
pitch: A better way to review architecture with your agents.
about_excerpt: A better way to review architecture with your agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am a designer and engineer, so naturally, I love whiteboarding ideas. Especially today, as the implementation of software can be abstracted more than ever, I find it both necessary and enjoyable to diagram architectures before I build my ideas with agents. However, the revision loop has lately felt more drawn out that it needs to. I tried a bunch of whiteboarding apps before landing on the excellent tldraw , but as advanced as it is, it's still tedious to use it in conversation with an agent about a given diagram. I often turn to Computer Use, which relies on the slow process of screenshots and imprecise whiteboarding editing, and the alternative is building a custom API with an unnecessary amount of complexity just to allow and agent and I to collaborate on a whiteboard. WebMCP seemed like an excellent fit to make this workflow more efficient. What it does Lattice is an infinite canvas that functions similarly to tldraw, which it's built on, but specialized for reviewing architecture diagrams with your agents. It exposes WebMCP tools to view, create, and edit diagrams, so you can ask it to explain code concepts in an instant. Where Lattice really excels, though, is in its comment tool. Just like Figma, you can easily mark up any node or area on the board, and the agent connected to Lattice is able to understand exactly what you annotated without any screenshots or even any semantic references in your comments. How I built it Each Lattice board is stored in the browser via localStorage, so it persists with no accounts or exports needed. The underlying architecture is stored as a semantic graph, where every node, edge, and comment has metadata labeling exactly what and where it is (ID, type, label, connection, position). This is what allows the connected agent to make targeted edits without screenshots and without editing unrelated parts of the board. Challenges I ran into While dogfooding the first version of this app, I found myself constantly telling the agent, "I added a few comments, check them." It became a bit tedious, so I thought this back-and-forth could be improved with a simple keyword, like "Lattice." A skill was a perfect fit here, so I wrote a lightweight one that explains what the user is trying to do when they say "/lattice create" or just "/lattice" (to edit). Accomplishments that I'm proud of Lattice is not just a demo for me. I've started using it every day in the Codex in-app browser, and it truly has made me more productive, allowing me to understand concepts better and churn out higher quality code more efficiently. What I learned Before this challenge, I hadn't heard of WebMCP, so I learned all about how it works and where it works best (hoping more companies begin integrating it into their apps!). I also learned how to maximize an agent's capabilities not by necessarily giving it more tools, but rather by improving its existing set of tools through more narrow typing, better tool descriptions, and more. What's next for Lattice I plan on sharing this app with a few friends to see if/how it fits into their workflows. I suspect that many of them use whiteboards for more than just diagramming architecture, and the great part about Lattice today is its simplicity and its foundation (tldraw) that can be expanded in countless ways to support more use cases. Along with potentially expanding its feature set, I hope to find more ways to integrate it into my own workflow, like I did when I made the Lattice skill. I can imagine that instructing the agent to automatically create new diagrams when relevant would be useful, and I could even see some sort of cross-board context coming in handy as I work on one project across multiple Codex threads. title: Second Serve
pitch: a food-rescue planning app where an agent matches surplus meals to community kitchens, while a coordinator reviews assignments, protects commitments, and handles last-minute changes.
about_excerpt: a food-rescue planning app where an agent matches surplus meals to community kitchens, while a coordinator reviews assignments, protects commitments, and handles last-minute changes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Food rescue coordination is full of context that never makes it into a spreadsheet: a kitchen just quietly cut its capacity, a delivery is already promised to someone, an allergen exclusion can't be crossed no matter how good the match looks. Most agent demos skip that entirely, they either automate the whole decision or ignore the human's state completely. I wanted the agent working inside the same workspace the coordinator is looking at, seeing the same constraints, not a separate copy of the plan living in a chat window. What it does Second Serve matches surplus meal offers from six fictional donors to five fictional kitchens. A browser agent can read the live workspace, run a read-only what-if plan, ask exactly why a specific donor-kitchen pair got rejected, update a kitchen's declared capacity, and stage a proposal onto the board. The coordinator reviews it, approves it, and can protect specific commitments so they survive whatever happens next. The demo scenario starts at 480 portions matched. Protect the 120-portion Green Kitchen to Hope Community commitment, drop Open Table's capacity to 30, and ask the agent to replan. It comes back with 410 portions matched, the protected 120 untouched, and an explicit statement of the 70-portion shortfall instead of quietly burying it. No deliveries actually go out, this is a planning surface, not dispatch. How we built it The app is React and TypeScript on Vite/Vinext. The solver in lib/rescue.ts is a deterministic integral min-cost max-flow implementation over donor supply, kitchen capacity, diet compatibility, allergen exclusions, travel time, donor windows, and closing times. Protected quantities get reserved in the flow graph before the rest of the plan is solved, so a better-looking route can't quietly bump them. The WebMCP layer is six imperative tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with a navigator.modelContext fallback, each carrying a JSON Schema, read-only annotations, and real runtime validation. The UI and the agent read and write the same store, lib/use-rescue.ts is what binds it into React. Every mutating call takes an expected_revision , so if the coordinator changed something in between, the call fails cleanly instead of overwriting it. Tools only return once the shared state has flushed, so the agent's next read is never stale. Approving a plan and unlocking a protected commitment are kept as UI-only actions on purpose. Tool annotations are a hint to the agent, not an actual security boundary, and I didn't want the app pretending otherwise. Challenges we ran into Holding protected quantities exact while still replanning everything else was the hard part. Reserve too aggressively in the flow graph and flexible offers get stranded behind whatever got assigned first. Reserve too loosely and "protected" stops meaning anything. Routing protected flow through the residual graph before anything else, then letting the remaining augmenting paths work around it, is what actually fixed this. The second problem was staleness. An agent call that lands after the coordinator already changed the board shouldn't win by default. The revision check catches that part easily, getting the resulting error message to actually explain what changed took more iteration than the check itself did. Making unmet demand visible instead of just silently matching fewer portions needed the same level of care. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tools are genuinely browser-discoverable and callable, not a chat interface faking API calls behind the scenes. There's no separate backend holding a second copy of the plan, no screen-scraping, no simulated model. It runs with no account, no API key, and no server ever seeing the dataset. Constraint handling, atomic revisions, and the human-approval path are all covered by automated tests, and the 480 to 410, 120 protected, 70 short numbers reproduce exactly every run. What I learned The interesting problem wasn't handing the agent more tools, it was giving it the right shape of state: a proposal it can inspect before anything commits, a revision number it can fail against cleanly, and read-only what-if calls that touch nothing. Once that existed, the real design work moved to the human side, making sure approval, protection, and unmet demand are always shown directly instead of something the coordinator has to infer. What's next for Second Serve Real travel estimates in place of the illustrative 0-100 coordinate grid, transport and driver availability as an actual constraint, and a pilot with a real rescue coordinator to find out where these assumptions break against real data. Multi-user persistence, dispatch, and food-safety verification are explicitly not built. This is a planning tool, and it should stay honest about that until those pieces actually exist. title: Root
pitch: Orchestrate real sites with WebMCP. Open several apps at once, watch the agent work on live pages, approve the steps that need you, and take control or stop any window when you want.
about_excerpt: Orchestrate real sites with WebMCP. Open several apps at once, watch the agent work on live pages, approve the steps that need you, and take control or stop any window when you want. Like Comment Story Updates root panel tab guide open root panel tab settings open root panel tab activity open root panel tab apps open root home page root in action. take control overlay over the active document sign in page home page when logout Inspiration Most WebMCP demos will be one site that registers a few tools. That is useful. It is also the obvious move. I wanted the harder surface: several real apps that stay themselves, each with its own origin and document, and one workspace where a person and an agent share those live apps. I built it so that Root does not sneak around the iframe and hit the child APIs itself. Cross-app work is what people already struggle with. Copy an id. Retype an email. Open the next tab. Hope the page still matches the plan. Agents are already strong at planning. What they cannot do, unless the sites hand them tools, is act on those live pages as part of one governed run. That is what Root is for: an orchestrator between Catalog, Customers, and Cases. Each app keeps its own tools on its own document. Root discovers and invokes them there, and the UI on that page is the evidence. What it does Root is a Mac-style desktop in the browser. Catalog, Customers, and Cases open as real provider windows. Lab can join after a human grant. Each provider is its own deployed site. Root loads it in an iframe with allow="tools" and only talks to tools that document exposes to Root. A person and an agent can run a pass across those windows: Search customers, products, or cases on the live lists Pause for a human row pick when there is a real choice Bind a later step to that selected snapshot (Root carries the object; it does not flatten Ada into a retyped email string) Open a record, or fill a create form and wait for a human persist on stage Keep other provider windows live instead of destroying them when work moves Notify when a wait needs you: after you grant it in inspect Settings, a pending-on-human pause plus a hidden Root tab shows a Notifications API toast (not Push, and not while Root is visible) Root’s own page registers the gateway the agent calls: list_providers , discover_capabilities , prepare_workflow , execute_workflow , invoke_granted_tool , plus inspect, cancel, and window chrome. Prepare freezes an allowlisted graph before anything runs. Execute opens or reuses each window, rediscovers, revalidates, and invokes on the live document. Take control stops the agent on that window. Custom tools never enter pass evidence. Try it: root.danieloyerinde.com with Customers , Catalog , Cases , and Lab . How I built it Four independently deployed Next apps (Root, Accounts, Shop, Support) plus Lab, one Express/tRPC API, and Postgres with tables owned by domain. No cross-domain joins. Support keeps its own copies of customer and order text. Root never mutates child domains through tRPC. On WebMCP: Each child registers tools on document.modelContext and exposes them only to Root’s origin Root’s Permissions-Policy delegates tools into those iframes Discovery uses getTools({ fromOrigins }) ; invoke uses executeTool in the child’s context Root is the author-provided agent that composes nested provider tools; the agent talks to Root’s gateway, and Root invokes tools inside each iframe The workflow layer is prepare then execute. Search, select, open, and create are allowlisted. A later argument may be a bind to an earlier selected snapshot. Create writes only after a human persist on stage. Agent lease is per window so one document serializes while another stays free. Rich fill, preview, and pick presentation run on stage on the live controls, not as a fake overlay of the whole desktop. Challenges I ran into The first hard truth was uniqueness. Multi-tab agents can already visit three sites. “Root opens three iframes” is not enough. The product only wins if the person and the agent share the same live documents under a freeze the agent cannot quietly rewrite. A core challenge was ChatGPT’s in-app browser. It only exposed top-level tools on Root. It did not discover tools registered inside provider iframes. That is exactly where Catalog, Customers, and Cases live. That gap is what pushed me onto a WebMCP-capable Chrome setup (testing flag / extension path) so nested getTools and executeTool could actually run against those documents. One stage window that remounted and killed the previous app made collaboration impossible. Search results and selections vanished when the next step switched providers. I moved to persistent independent windows so Customers can stay while Catalog runs. Binding looked simple until it was not. Typing Ada’s email into Cases again is not a handoff. Root has to deliver the selected snapshot intact and refuse graphs that invent ids from search results instead of an explicit selection. Human pauses were another edge. A pending pick, a create persist, Take control, and a silent timeout are different outcomes. Take control must fail closed as stopped by the user with no retry. A timeout with no gesture is not the same thing. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I shipped a real desktop, not a slide. Multiple provider windows stay live. Prepare refuses illegal tools and arguments. Execute rediscovers and fails closed on drift. The together loop is concrete: the agent fills a search, the person clicks Lin or Silent Mouse on the live list, Root binds that snapshot into a later Cases step without retyping her email, and Take control can stop the run on that window. Domain data lives in Postgres with SQL search. The iframe is not a picture over Root’s own API. Custom providers can still join behind a human grant without entering the typed pass. What I learned WebMCP tools belong to the open document. If Root calls the child’s API itself, the iframe is only decoration. An agent can run searches it already knows without the person. That is not much of a shared loop. Selection, bind, and create-after-persist are the parts where the person actually has to act on the live page. One allowlist scales cleaner than a prepare function per app. The step cap is only a safety limit. It is not tied to how many providers exist. Legal tools can repeat. Illegal ones still fail. Remounting the only window on every step wiped the previous app’s UI. Keeping separate windows open, with a lease per window, matched how people already keep a few apps around. What's next for Root As WebMCP leaves experiment and settles into real browser conventions, I expect clearer nesting rules, better host and agent tooling, and shared patterns for selection, grants, and multi-document work. Root will get simpler as those conventions land. Conclusion As of today, this principle gets shaky towards my final stages, after a final extensive check. A few things met me head-on. The agent can bypass Root. Even with a custom-tool setup where Root would in fact reject invoke when the tool is not granted, the agent could still go around me, because the underlying iframe exposes tools to the parent origin. That path is not quite spelled out in the docs the way you’d hope. Those tools would not show up when you list Root’s gateway tools, but Chrome still exposes them by name (direct invocation), so there is a direct bypass between Chrome and the providers. As WebMCP moves off experiment, the goal is that we get to conventions where this kind of multitasking is better supported, and where the tooling around it is better too. There is also usually a .map error that surfaces via the inspector. After extensive debugging, several bridges on my side were tested and still did not own the failure. The tools I had were limited, so I could not A/B the remaining layers cleanly (fresh tab vs stale session, inspector path vs gateway path, flag and extension in vs out) to confirm where it breaks. I treat that as outside Root: the experimental API or the extension. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: empeirik
pitch: empeirik turns circuit troubleshooting in one shared workspace. Where reasoning, measuring, testing, and refining happens together instead of chatting endlessly back-and-forth, with no end in sight.
about_excerpt: empeirik turns circuit troubleshooting in one shared workspace. Where reasoning, measuring, testing, and refining happens together instead of chatting endlessly back-and-forth, with no end in sight. Like Comment Story Updates Overview Debugging electronic circuits is often a slow and fragmented process, especially when the problem is not immediately obvious or the person working on it does not have deep experience with the specific hardware. Finding the cause can involve jumping between schematics, measurements, datasheets, simulation tools, and external help. AI can assist with the diagnosis, but the usual workflow of sending screenshots, measurements, and explanations back and forth through chat quickly becomes confusing and loses context. empeirik was built to bring that process into one shared workspace. The circuit, measurements, hypotheses, diagnostic steps, and proposed fixes all remain visible in the same environment while the AI works directly with the current state of the problem. It can inspect the circuit, decide which measurements are useful, narrow down likely causes, propose repairs or directly implement them, and verify them in simulation instead of repeatedly reconstructing the situation from a conversation. The project is built on top of CircuitJS1 for circuit rendering and simulation, with an additional diagnostic layer for measurements, hypotheses, repair testing, a shared activity timeline, and WebMCP tools that let the AI interact directly with the workspace. One of the main challenges was turning a traditional circuit simulator into a structured environment that both the user and the AI can operate at the same time while keeping every diagnostic step synchronized and visible. Learning and building electronics made it quickly clear how much context is lost when AI assistance is limited to a separate chat window. Giving the agent direct access to the same tools, state, and visual environment as the user makes the debugging process much more continuous and practical. title: MIRROR//LOOP
pitch: Eleven native WebMCP tools turn a 12-step reflection into a safe human-agent workflow: the agent clarifies and navigates, the browser scores, and the person confirms every choice.
about_excerpt:
Eleven native WebMCP tools turn a 12-step reflection into a safe human-agent workflow: the agent clarifies and navigates, the browser scores, and the person confirms every choice.

 MIRROR//LOOP turns uncertainty into one clear next step.

 MIRROR//LOOP turns uncertainty into one clear next step. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Eleven typed WebMCP tools with visible, on-page agent state. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Unconfirmed choices are rejected by the human-authority gate. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Twelve confirmed answers produce a deterministic local reflection. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 What-if previews show potential impact without changing saved answers. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Confirmed results export locally as a private reflection dossier. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 People are surrounded by instant answers, motivational shortcuts, and confident-sounding advice. Under stress, more output often creates more noise. MIRROR//LOOP creates a deliberate pause: twelve everyday questions help a person notice the pattern they reach for first, then turn that pattern into one small, practical next step. The challenge was not simply to put a quiz on a webpage. A 12-step reflection connected to 144 cards can be difficult to understand quickly, especially when a visitor is uncertain, tired, or using unfamiliar language. WebMCP makes the existing experience easier to navigate without making the agent the authority over the person. 

 What it does 

 MIRROR//LOOP is a live, privacy-bounded reflection experience. The normal website works on its own, while a compatible browser agent can use eleven typed WebMCP tools to: 

 
 start or resume the reflection; 
 read the active question; 
 explain one choice in plain language; 
 neutrally compare two choices; 
 record or revise only an answer the person explicitly confirms; 
 review all confirmed answers; 
 preview how one hypothetical change would affect a completed result without saving it; 
 complete the deterministic 12-answer reflection; 
 export a local Markdown or JSON dossier after confirmation; 
 retrieve any public card from 001 through 144; and 
 recommend a relevant digital edition without changing a cart or starting payment. 
 

 The page remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. When registration succeeds, it visibly reports WebMCP ready · 11 tools . A collapsible Agent State rail shows tool registration and invocation activity on the page, so a judge can see the human-agent workflow without keeping DevTools open. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Traditional browser automation must infer intent from visual controls and presentation markup. A conversational model may also invent meanings when the site's authoritative definitions are not available as structured capabilities. WebMCP lets MIRROR//LOOP expose the actions that already belong to the page as typed, same-origin tools. The agent handles explanation and navigation; the browser retains the confirmed answers and applies the scoring rules; the person controls meaning, consent, identity, email, cart changes, and payment. This is the central design principle: the agent reduces friction without taking authority . A participant can say, “I am torn between these two choices.” The agent can call compare_choices and return the site's own neutral contrast. It cannot silently choose. When the participant decides, answer_reflection_question requires confirmed_by_user: true before browser-local state changes. The boundary is enforced by the tool implementation, not merely by conversational wording. 

 How we built it 

 The public experience is built with semantic HTML, CSS, and modular JavaScript. web/lib/webmcp.js registers eleven tools through the browser model-context surface. Each tool uses a closed JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , bounded runtime validation, behavioral annotations, and structured errors. The 12-question scorer runs deterministically in browser memory with stable ascending-code tie-breaking. The public card registry exposes curated metadata for Cards 001–144 without publishing private prompt engineering or source corpora. The Agent State rail listens for decoupled lifecycle events—registration, tool start, and tool completion—and displays a privacy-filtered input summary, observed local elapsed time, outcome, and human-confirmation state. Observability cannot interrupt the underlying reflection action. The production website uses Firebase Hosting with a small Go submission service on Google Cloud Run. Cloudflare Turnstile protects only the optional reflection-email request. It loads when the visitor reaches the email form, and the Go API verifies the short-lived token with Cloudflare before storing a pending subscription or sending email; the secret remains in Google Secret Manager. Turnstile does not control the reflection, WebMCP, the cart, Stripe Checkout, or payment. 

 Safety and privacy boundaries 

 MIRROR//LOOP does not give the agent a general-purpose browser or purchasing capability. 

 
 Recording or revising an answer requires explicit human confirmation. 
 A hypothetical preview never changes saved answers. 
 Local dossier export requires a separate confirmation. 
 No WebMCP tool submits an email address. 
 No WebMCP tool changes a cart, creates a Checkout Session, or makes a payment. 
 Individual choices stay in the browser for the normal reflection and local-export paths. 
 Optional email delivery is a separate, disclosed request handled by the submission service. 
 

 The tool installer reports readiness only after every registration resolves. If registration fails or WebMCP is unsupported, the complete direct-use experience remains available with an honest fallback status. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was defining a useful agent boundary. A tool suite can become impressive-looking but unsafe if it turns interpretation, communication, and commerce into one broad authority. We repeatedly narrowed tool inputs and outputs, separated read-only tools from state-changing tools, and made confirmation a runtime requirement. We also had to make a complex symbolic system understandable without exposing private research material or forcing visitors to learn internal terminology. The answer was selective context: return one current question, one exact card, or one bounded comparison rather than loading the entire system into every agent turn. Finally, experimental browser support required feature detection, graceful fallback behavior, strict character budgets, and a reproducible Chrome test path. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 
 Eleven purpose-built WebMCP tools operating one coherent, visible user journey. 
 Explicit human confirmation enforced before answer mutation. 
 Deterministic browser-side scoring rather than model-authored results. 
 Exact public retrieval across a 144-card matrix. 
 A visible Agent State rail that makes tool execution legible without DevTools. 
 Read-only commerce recommendations with identity and payment kept outside agent authority. 
 A one-command WebMCP evaluation runner covering registration, schema limits, confirmation rejection, premature completion, output budgets, and the no-checkout boundary. 
 A production deployment with a complete non-WebMCP fallback. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most valuable when it does not merely automate clicks. It gives a website a second, agent-readable interface while preserving the visible human interface as the shared source of truth. Good tools are small, typed, and auditable. They return authoritative local context, expose clear state transitions, and refuse actions that should remain human. We also learned that an agent experience must be demonstrated visibly. Registration badges, progress changes, focus movement, live regions, and the Agent State rail make the collaboration understandable to people as well as machines. 

 What's next 

 Next we will publish the final public demo video, complete the Devpost media package, and continue testing with WebMCP-capable agents. Product work will focus on clearer first-time or

title: Strudel WebMCP
pitch: Live-code together.
about_excerpt: Live-code together. Like Comment Story Updates The agent isn't controlling another Strudel session. It's playing in yours. Strudel WebMCP lets a browser agent join the exact live Strudel REPL a human is already performing with. You type, select code, and drag inline sliders as normal; the agent reads and edits that same unsaved CodeMirror document, evaluates its changes in the same running scheduler, and can record what the result sounds like — under a permission dial you own. No embedded LLM, no MCP server, no WebSocket bridge, no session ID. Live demo: https://strudel-webmcp.vercel.app Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/strudel-webmcp Why WebMCP Live coding is a bad fit for every earlier agent-integration shape, because the thing an agent needs to touch — the unsaved editor buffer, the exact cursor and selection, the inline slider values, the scheduler that is playing right now — exists in one browser tab and changes every second. A file-based or bridged integration has to keep a second copy of that in sync, and the copy is stale the moment a slider moves. WebMCP has no second copy. The tool call is a method on the same page, over the same document, in the same tab the human is looking at. Nothing to install, nothing to configure, no bridge that can drift. That makes something ordinary that was previously very hard: a human dragging a filter-cutoff slider with the mouse while an agent, in the same instant, rewrites a different line of the same unsaved buffer — and neither can clobber the other's most recent change. What the agent can do Thirteen tools, registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (src/webmcp/tools.ts), all backed by one adapter over the live (src/strudel/adapter.ts): Read live context: playback state, cursor, the human's current selection, what is sounding now, the agent mode, and any pending proposal, solo or recording. Read the exact current source, unsaved edits included, optionally by line range. Apply precise range edits, or replace the whole source — in review mode both become proposals. Evaluate through Strudel's own Update path (host.editor.evaluate()), so an agent edit becomes audible exactly the way a human's does, without stopping the clock; or solo just a range; or audition a pending proposal. Play, stop, and select-and-scroll to a range so the human sees what the agent means. Record the live output — master, or one .analyze("id") voice — and get dBFS and band analysis back, plus a playable take left in the page. List and extend the sound registry the running scheduler actually resolves s("...") against. Snapshot the source as a named version; switch the editor theme. Every mutating tool requires the codeHash from a previous read, computed fresh from the live document, and is refused with STALE_CODE if anything changed since — including a slider drag, because Strudel's slider widgets rewrite the source's numeric literals directly. The human's most recent edit always wins. The permission dial has three positions. Read: the agent can look, record and point, nothing else. Review: every edit arrives as a proposal with a diff the human auditions, accepts or discards — the source is unchanged until you say so. Live: edits apply directly. What people and agents can do together You keep performing. The agent reads the exact state you're in — down to the characters you have selected — and makes structural edits to the lines you didn't ask it to leave alone, then evaluates them into the same running pattern. Both of you act through the one Strudel instance; the audio reflects both immediately because neither owns a separate copy. In review mode the agent pitches instead of acting: "swap the kick for a different one" appears as a diff you can hear before it lands. And the agent has ears: ask "is the bass too loud?" and it records four seconds of the live output, answers from measured dBFS band energy, and suggests a concrete gain change. Who this is for Live coders, algorave performers, and people learning music through code — an audience for whom the editor buffer is the whole instrument, and for whom anything that isn't that exact buffer is useless mid-performance. Today, getting an agent into that instrument means standing up an MCP server, a bridge, and usually a modified frontend before a single note changes. That is real friction for a hobbyist or student and dead weight for a performer who wants a second pair of hands for eight bars. The claim is direct: browser-native creative tools shouldn't need to embed a model or ship a dedicated connector to be legible to an agent. The page can expose the instrument the human already has open. Strudel is the proof; the pattern — unsaved live document, precise agent edits, human-owned permission dial — applies to any browser-native creative or editing tool with real-time state worth exposing. Live coding is a specialized audience, but the engine underneath it is not niche: @strudel/core , the pattern engine every Strudel-based tool depends on, drew about 30,000 npm downloads in the 30 days ending August 29, 2026, and the wider @strudel/* family this project embeds — mini-notation, transpiler, WebAudio backend, CodeMirror integration, the REPL itself — adds roughly 76,000 more over the same window. The seam this project adds is generic to any of those downstream tools, not specific to this demo's drum pattern. Compared with the existing Strudel MCP bridges Existing Strudel MCP projects drive Strudel through an MCP server, a WebSocket or SSE bridge, and often a special frontend or a session ID copied between browser and agent. They work. The difference is what it takes to start: a connector, a bridge, session synchronization, and MCP configuration on one side; opening the page on the other. Here the page publishes its own controls, and the browser agent already accompanying the user joins the REPL with no external bridge, no session ID, no agent-specific server, and no second source of truth. Why this is different from "AI + music" Most "AI + music" demos are generation: describe a vibe, get a clip, no instrument in the loop. Most WebMCP demos so far are forms and dashboards. This is neither. It is a person and a browser agent performing through the same live instrument — one typing, selecting, dragging and listening; the other reading exact state, making precise edits, evaluating, and pointing back into the source. The review-mode propose/audition/accept loop goes further: the agent gets a way to pitch a change and let the human hear it before committing, which has no analogue in a form-filling demo. How it's built A static site — no server, no bridge — wrapping the official Strudel REPL and CodeMirror editor. The adapter is the only code that touches @strudel/repl internals; the tools, schemas, registration and error helpers sit above it. Unit tests (Vitest) cover hashing, position and offset conversion, edit validation, stale-hash rejection, source-size bounds and error normalization. title: Runner Agent × Thailand in Motion
pitch: A multilingual Runner Agent that turns one natural-language goal into a safe run plan, shared route review, circular support loop, and human-confirmed Run Pass through 14 WebMCP actions.
about_excerpt: A multilingual Runner Agent that turns one natural-language goal into a safe run plan, shared route review, circular support loop, and human-confirmed Run Pass through 14 WebMCP actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a community run often means jumping between event pages, route details, pace groups, transport options, safety rules, and registration forms. Runner Agent × Thailand in Motion explores a simpler model: a runner describes the goal once, and a browser agent coordinates the plan while every consequential decision remains visible and human-controlled. What it does The app turns a conversational city, distance, pace, and social request into an actionable week board. It can shortlist and compare events, open a selected route in the visible interface, read participation rules, apply deterministic readiness checks, plan a safe return, build a bring-borrow-refill-repair support loop, and prepare a registration. Registration is never automatic. The agent can stage a Run Pass, but the pass does not exist until the runner reviews the visible confirmation dialog and confirms it. Optional post-run social choices keep alcohol-free and run-only participation first-class, and the app never recommends driving after drinking. Why WebMCP is central The site registers 14 bounded tools through the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. These tools use the same domain logic and visible state as the human interface, so an agent does not operate a separate hidden workflow. A user can see the selected route, review readiness results, change preferences, and retain final control. The tool set covers schedule planning and saving, Runner Passport retrieval, circular support, bounded catalog search, event discovery and comparison, event details and rules, readiness, safe-return options, registration preparation, redacted Run Pass lookup, and confirmed cancellation. How it improves the experience One natural-language request replaces a sequence of filters and disconnected pages. Structured results make pace, distance, availability, accessibility, social choices, and safety rules easier to compare. Agent activity appears in the same interface the runner uses, unsafe combinations are blocked deterministically, and sensitive emergency-contact data is excluded from agent-facing pass results. How we built it The client uses TypeScript and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker and D1 provide optional signed-in Runner Passport persistence, while guest planning and passes continue to work without an account. Vitest covers domain behavior, UI flows, WebMCP contracts, privacy boundaries, and the Shopify adapter. The optional Shopify Storefront MCP connector is intentionally limited to searching one runner-confirmed remaining need after bring, borrow, refill, and repair. It stops before cart or checkout and reports store_required until an authorized store is configured. Challenges and learning The hardest part was keeping the human and agent experiences synchronized without letting the agent silently cross consequential boundaries. We added strict JSON Schemas, runtime validation, explicit read-only and state-changing annotations, schema-bypass defenses, redacted outputs, and visible confirmation for registration. We also learned that WebMCP browser capability must be tested separately from ordinary UI tests: a passing harness proves the contracts but does not replace supported-browser discovery and execution evidence. Current boundaries Displayed events, venues, routes, capacity, and prices are fictional demo data. Shopify catalog search is disconnected until an authorized store domain is supplied. Render automation is roadmap-only. The app does not create purchases or provide medical advice. title: Counterask
pitch: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess — and that reads a whole sentence: budget, refusals and all.
about_excerpt: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess — and that reads a whole sentence: budget, refusals and all. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Every storefront in this challenge will expose the same shape of tool: get-products , filter-products , show-products . The WebMCP spec's own e-commerce example does exactly that. All of them assume the store's job is to answer . For most of a shopping conversation that assumption is wrong. Ask this catalog for "a belt" and 97 products match; the top-ranked one beats the tenth by 5%. Ranking them is a coin flip dressed as a recommendation. One more fact — what it is made of — clears forty of them on average. The store knows this; it has the distribution in front of it. But a tool that can only return products has no way to say so, so it returns its coin flip and lets the agent present a guess as an answer. WebMCP is the first place a website can express its own uncertainty as a first-class outcome. search_products returns one of two shapes: a ranked list, or a single clarifying question with options and counts. The spec lists "fully autonomous workflows" under its Non-Goals and says the human interface stays primary; a tool that declines to guess is the most direct expression of that intent we could build. It puts the person back in the loop at the exact moment the machine cannot decide — not as a permission prompt bolted on afterwards, but because the site genuinely does not know and says so. How it creates a better user experience The store listens the way an agent talks. A search box gets "leather belt". An agent relaying a person gets "I'm looking for a leather belt, nothing with a snap, not over $50". Fed to a keyword matcher, that sentence requires "looking" to appear in a title, reads "snap" as a requirement , and never sees the budget. Counterask parses budgets, refusals ("not leather", "no laces", "nothing from Nike"), orderings ("cheapest", "best rated") and stated attributes out of the sentence itself. Measured on 800 such sentences written from real product records, refusals inverted into requirements went from 100% to 0%, budgets broken in the top ten from 31% to 0%, and Hit@10 from 0.79 to 0.99 — under phrasings the parser was never tuned on as well. On the build that ships, the two benchmarks read Hit@10 0.998 (two-word shopper) and 0.993 (agent-relayed sentences), with every listening check at zero. It never asks what it was told. Anything stated is a constraint, not a question. "No preference" is remembered, so the same question cannot come straight back. The agent can pass whatever it already knows from the conversation — attributes, exclusions, budget, facets the shopper does not mind — structured, and structured input wins over the parse. It says what it heard, and what still differs. Every result carries an understood block echoing exactly how the request was read, so the agent can check before trusting the answer and the person sees the same thing as chips. When the store does answer, it names the attributes that still separate the products shown — "eleven buckle, one pull-on" — so the agent can summarise rather than read out a list. "No results" is never the last word. When nothing survives every requirement, the store lifts each one in turn, re-counts, and reports which is doing the damage. The agent gets relax ; the person gets buttons. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The person supplies the one thing the store cannot compute: which of two equally good attributes they actually care about. The store supplies the one thing the person cannot see: that this is the moment their answer matters, which attribute it is, and what choosing each option would leave. The agent carries the question across, in the person's own words, and carries the answer back. Before WebMCP this loop did not exist. An agent driving a site through its DOM sees a grid, not a decision. A site behind a REST API cannot register a tool that appears only while a question is open and vanishes when it is answered — here answer_question does exactly that, so the tool list itself tells the agent what the page is waiting for. And a person and an agent clicking or calling land in the same function: one state machine, two surfaces, nothing that can drift between what a human sees and what an agent is told. None of this is about menswear. The parser reads whatever attribute vocabulary the catalog builder emits; the stopping policy reasons about evidence and pool size, not clothing; the tools describe a store, not a category. Swap the catalog and the same tools ask the right question about laptops, groceries or hotel rooms — and the "no results" recovery, the understood echo and the tool-that-appears-when-needed come with them. Concretely, in one session: "find me a wallet that's not leather, under $30" → the store returns 30 candidates and one question ( which category — wallets, card cases, money clips? ) → the agent asks the person → the person answers → the store answers with what still differs → the agent curates the grid with show_products so the person sees the pick, not a transcript → "why that one?" → explain_ranking , deterministic, quotable. How WebMCP was implemented Eleven imperative tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback), a twelfth that comes and goes with the open question, and one declarative tool, all running in the tab — no server, no model call, no tokens: search_products — the request in the shopper's words plus optional structured knowledge; returns answer or need_more_evidence . answer_question — registered dynamically only while a question is open, and unregistered the way the spec has it: by aborting the AbortSignal it was registered with. The page listens to toolchange and calls getTools() to show the live list, so a person can watch it come and go. refine_search (require or exclude), revise_search (the shopper changed their mind: take back a value, a facet, the budget — the cart stays), parse_only (a dry run of the reading with a per-pass audit, readOnlyHint ), list_attributes (vocabulary with counts, readOnlyHint ), show_products (agent-curated grid), explain_ranking ( readOnlyHint ), add_to_cart , remove_from_cart , view_cart , reset_search . Every tool carries a title . The visit — search, open question, cart — is remembered across reloads. checkout — a declarative <form toolname="checkout"> with toolparamdescription on its fields and without toolautosubmit : an agent can fill in the name and address, the browser focuses the button, and only the person places the order. The submit handler answers an agent-invoked submission through SubmitEvent.respondWith() . Results are MCP-shaped on the wire ( content text plus structuredContent ), so a client following either convention reads the same thing. Verified on Chrome 152 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , through document.modelContext itself: all tools register with titles and readOnlyHint , the declarative checkout form is picked up as a tool, a search returns the question and answer_question appears (and leaves after it is answered), and executeTool on the checkout form fills the fields, focuses Place order and waits for the person — nothing is submitted. Behind them: a sentence parser (budget, ordering, refusals at both the recorded-attribute and title-word level, stated attributes, filler); BM25 retrieval over 9,901 real products with length normalisation and a required-word conjunction; a value-of-information stopping policy that asks only when the best question is expected to remove at least ten candidates and at least 18% of the pool, measured as expected survivors rather than entropy (products carry several values of one attribute, so shares are not a distribution) and scaled by how much of the pool records the attribute at all. For browsers without WebMCP, the page offers a scripted agent : the same tools registered against a stand-in modelContext , called in the order a real agent would call them, with the conversation shown beside the grid and labelled as a simulation. Open the live URL with ?agent=demo to watch it. Everything is measured, and the rejected ideas are kept in the code with their numbers: a "clear leader, stop asking" rule was built twice and removed twice; graded credit for unrecorded attributes was byte-identical at four settings and removed. Two self-supervised benchmarks (two-word shopper; agent-relayed sentences, with a held-out phrasing set), 61 hand-written parse cases, a fuzzer that builds 4,000 sentences nobody wrote, and a stand-in- modelContext test of the tool surface run with npm test .  Passenger rights are often written in complicated regulations and spread across different websites. 

 FlightClaims makes this process simpler.

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike.
