title: OpenMemoz
pitch: A personal content library where AI agents are the writers and you're the editor. 35 WebMCP tools let any AI curate news from open & allowed sources, lives in your browser, no backend needed.
about_excerpt: A personal content library where AI agents are the writers and you're the editor. 35 WebMCP tools let any AI curate news from open & allowed sources, lives in your browser, no backend needed. Like Comment Story Updates 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 Inspiration Content discovery is fragmented. The same story surfaces across multiple apps, each optimizing for engagement rather than what the reader actually wants. Long-form content on YouTube has incredible depth, but finding the right video takes longer than watching it. And none of these platforms are agent-native. The vision was a consolidated personal content library where AI agents curate open sources and the reader decides what to read. Not another algorithmic feed, but a place where agents search the web, summarize videos, discover discussions on Bluesky and Mastodon, and organize it all into a newspaper the reader can actually use. WebMCP made it possible. Chrome 150 shipped document.modelContext.registerTool() , which lets a web page expose structured tools to any AI agent visiting it. No extensions, no API keys. The browser becomes a User-Agent Generated Content (UAGC) platform — users direct, agents curate. What it does OpenMemoz exposes 36 WebMCP tools to any visiting AI agent. The agent reads the current edition, searches stories, discovers content from YouTube, Bluesky, and Mastodon, writes original articles, embeds videos, manages reader preferences, and reshapes the newspaper layout. Everything happens through the browser's native tool-calling protocol. The reader experience is a newspaper: a hero story with an embedded YouTube video, a sidebar with text stories, a mid-row section, a video feature row, and a below-fold masonry grid. Thirteen color palettes, four visual styles (flat, glass, neumorphic, paper), two layout modes. The agent experience is a structured workflow. Here is what a typical interaction looks like: User tells ChatGPT: "Discover trending YouTube videos, read the transcript of the best one, write a summary, and add it as my hero story." Agent calls discover_youtube_content to find trending videos Agent calls get_youtube_video to read the full transcript of the top result Agent writes an original summary from the transcript, calls add_story with pinAsHero: true The newspaper layout recalculates instantly: new hero with embedded video, sidebar adjusts, masonry reflows The page is the interface. The agent is the editor. The reader stays in control. How we built it The entire system runs client-side as a Next.js PWA. There is no backend for content curation. The AI agents visiting the page are the backend. Server-side API routes exist only as thin CORS proxies for YouTube, Bluesky, and Mastodon. The flow above shows one real interaction: the user asks for trending content → the agent discovers document.modelContext and its 36 tools → calls discover_youtube_content → picks the best video → calls get_youtube_video to read the full transcript → writes an original summary → calls add_story → source validation checks the allowlist (~90 approved) and banned list (~280 blocked) → edition data updates in localStorage → the layout rule engine rescores and reflows → the page updates instantly, live. The agent can also use its own web search to find content from any source and call add_story directly — the discover tools are convenience shortcuts, not the only path. Personalized interests via AI conversation Tell the agent what you want to learn — "This week I want to learn about LLMs and quantum computing" — and it sets your topic interests via set_user_interests . The interests persist in localStorage and influence what the agent curates next. The agent can search anywhere on the web, write original articles in its own words, and add them via add_story . WebMCP tools Every tool is registered through the browser's document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The registration function runs on page load and registers all 36 tools in parallel: // src/lib/webmcp.ts const modelContext = document.modelContext ?? (navigator as any).modelContext; // Chrome 146-149 compat if (typeof modelContext?.registerTool !== "function") return; modelContext.registerTool({ name: "openmemoz.add_story", description: "Add a new story. Page updates IMMEDIATELY.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { headline: { type: "string" }, excerpt: { type: "string" }, section: { type: "string" }, sourceName: { type: "string" }, youtubeVideoId: { type: "string" }, pinAsHero: { type: "boolean" }, }, required: ["headline", "excerpt", "section", "sourceName"], }, execute: (args) => { /* validate source, create story, update edition */ }, }, { signal: abortSignal }); Tool descriptions do double duty as agent instructions. When search_stories returns zero results, its description guides the agent to discover tools. When discover_youtube_content finds a video, its description tells the agent to read the transcript with get_youtube_video and write an original summary before adding. The descriptions chain tools into workflows — they need the same care as system prompts. Source validation OpenMemoz only accepts content from approved sources. Every add_story call validates the source URL against two lists before the story is accepted: // src/lib/curatedSources.ts export const APPROVED_SOURCES = [ { domain: "nasa.gov", licenceBasis: "public-domain-usgov" }, { domain: "youtube.com", licenceBasis: "youtube-embed-tos" }, // ~90 total across government, CC, open API, video, social ]; export const BANNED_DOMAINS = ["nytimes.com", "wsj.com", /* ~280 total */]; Layer Sources Legal basis Government SEC, Fed, NASA, NOAA, BLS, NIH, CDC Public domain (17 USC 105) Creative Commons The Conversation, Global Voices, VOA, Wikipedia CC licence terms Open APIs Hacker News, YouTube, Bluesky, Mastodon Permissive API / embed ToS Provenance tiers Every story carries a provenanceTier in its data schema. Tier 1 means the text comes directly from the source (a government press release, a CC-licensed article). Tier 2 means the AI synthesized the summary. The agent knows the difference. // src/lib/types.ts export interface Story { storyIdentifier: string; headline: string; excerpt: string; section: string; provenanceTier: 1 | 2; // 1 = source text (quotable), 2 = AI-synthesized sourceName: string; sourceUrl: string; licenceBasis: string; // legal basis for redistribution youtubeVideoId?: string; isHeroPinned?: boolean; } Layout rule engine The layout engine assigns stories to slots the way a newspaper editor would. No empty space, no mixed-height rows. The hero is scored automatically based on visual impact: // src/lib/layoutRuleEngine.ts function scoreHeroCandidate(story: Story, index: number): number { if (story.isHeroPinned) return 100; let score = 0; if (story.youtubeVideoId) score += 5; if (story.imageUrl) score += 3; if (story.provenanceTier === 1) score += 2; return score; } The engine produces a structured layout: hero + sidebar, then a uniform mid-row (all-thumbnail or all-text to avoid dead space), then brief strips in full rows of 4, a video feature row, and a below-fold masonry grid packed with a greedy shortest-column algorithm. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new and barely documented. Chrome 150 shipped document.modelContext.registerTool() with no tutorials and few examples. We discovered edge cases through trial: tools fail silently when descriptions are too long, agents call tools in unexpected orders, and Chrome 146 through 149 used navigator.modelContext instead of document.modelContext . Our code handles both entry points. AI agents are unpredictable editors. The first time we asked ChatGPT to "add some tech stories," it added 47 stories in a row, all in the Tech section, most from banned domains. We built guardrails layer by layer: source validation against ~90 approved and ~280 banned domains, duplicate detection by headline slug, and rate guidance baked into tool descriptions. The agent still needs coaching, but it cannot publish from the New York Times. Newspaper layout is harder than it looks. Our first layout was a 3-column masonry grid. It looked like a Pinterest board, not a newspaper. Real newspapers have hierarchy: the hero is visually dominant, sidebar stories complement it, mid-row stories are uniform height, and the below-fold grid fills every pixel. We built a rule engine that enforces these constraints automatically. YouTube video verification is a rabbit hole. We curate static editions with YouTube video embeds. Matching video IDs to story topics turned out to be fragile. A story about the Federal Reserve was showing a Linkin Park music video. The fix was YouTube oembed API verification and strict video-to-topic matching. Accomplishments that we're proud of 36 WebMCP tools under the openmemoz.* namespace, making this one of the most comprehensive WebMCP implementations built so far Zero backend for content curation. AI agents visiting the page are the editorial team Personalized int

Like Comment Story Updates paining complete Inspiration MythWeaver asks: what if painting with an AI felt like pair programming? Instead of prompting for a finished image, people and agents create together on one shared canvas. What it does A person and ChatGPT take turns coloring predefined sections. The agent reads named objects, chooses colors with visual judgment, explains each choice, and paints live. Nine semantic tools expose the canvas, regions, colors, turns, presence, undo, and story actions. Tokenized rooms synchronize people and agents across browser sessions. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making agent participation real and visible. We built explicit joining, presence heartbeats, conflict-safe state, server-enforced turns, protected human work, and an authenticated fallback when direct WebMCP is unavailable. Accomplishments that we're proud of MythWeaver is a complete shared experience, not a scripted demo. People can see who is painting, where the agent is working, why it chose a color, and when the brush changes hands. What we learned Agents work better when websites expose meaning, not coordinates. “Color the river” is more reliable than “click here.” Visible rules, authorship, explanations, and reversible actions also make collaboration more trustworthy. title: FigureFoundry
pitch: Publication-ready figures, graphs, and charts in less than a minute. Powered by Webmcp for safe and efficient collaboration with AI-agents.
about_excerpt: Publication-ready figures, graphs, and charts in less than a minute. Powered by Webmcp for safe and efficient collaboration with AI-agents. Like Comment Story Updates Showcase Why FigureFoundry Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Scientific figure editors are exactly the kind of dense, form-heavy applications where agents currently struggle. Agents are often forced to navigate these interfaces by clicking through an unfamiliar DOM, while researchers spend excessive amounts of time manually performing tasks that an agent could draft in seconds. FigureFoundry addresses this directly. It registers seven document.modelContext tools: inspect_dataset_catalog inspect_dataset_fields inspect_figure_workspace analyze_dataset analyze_group_comparison propose_figure_revision apply_figure_revision This allows an agent to inspect the actual dataset schema and current figure state rather than guessing at the interface structure. The agent can then propose a structured revision that FigureFoundry itself validates. How It Creates a Better User Experience A researcher can request something as simple as: "Compare body mass by species, colored by island." Instead of blindly interacting with the editor, the agent inspects the bound dataset's actual fields, runs a deterministic analysis, and stages a typed Figure Spec diff against the relevant panel. Nothing immediately changes on the canvas. Every proposal is presented as a preview, and applying it requires explicit user confirmation showing both the target panel and the revision being applied. The result is an agent that assists with the tedious work without taking scientific control away from the researcher. What's Newly Possible Previously, turning a request such as "compare these groups" into a correct, publication-ready panel required manual field mapping, chart-type selection, and statistical setup. With WebMCP, the agent can perform the data inspection and analysis steps first. The researcher remains responsible for the scientific judgment: approving, discarding, or editing the proposed revision. Every applied change is also recorded in an append-only provenance ledger, including the revision it was based on. This keeps the figure's history reproducible even when an agent contributes to its construction. How We Implemented It The tools are schema-bound to the active dataset, meaning an agent cannot propose a field that does not actually exist. apply_figure_revision uses optimistic concurrency control through basedOnRevision and rejects proposals that are stale, unapproved, or target an invalid panel. This makes the agent integration operational rather than cosmetic: the model is given structured access to the application's actual state, while the application remains responsible for validation and state changes. Why FigureFoundry There is no doubt that FigureFoundry is a straightforward concept. That is precisely why I chose to build it. Its value is not in being a flashy novelty application. The efficiency implications are the point. Scientific figure editing contains exactly the kind of repetitive, structured interaction where WebMCP can have a meaningful impact: the agent can understand the data and application state, prepare the work, and explain what it intends to change, while the researcher retains control over the final scientific decision. That is where I believe WebMCP has the greatest potential: not replacing the user, but removing the friction between what the user wants to accomplish and the interface they currently have to operate manually. title: Counterfactual
pitch: See your future before you choose it. Name a big decision, watch it branch into possible paths, protect what matters, and decide with an agent by your side.
about_excerpt: See your future before you choose it. Name a big decision, watch it branch into possible paths, protect what matters, and decide with an agent by your side. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dynamic paths Home page Flight Recorder for tool calls Decisions, assumptions, and goals Testing with WebMCP tools Chrome extension Tutorial mode Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of taking actions across the web, but users do not always get a clear picture of the consequences before those actions happen. A decision like buying a car can affect several competing goals at once, yet most financial tools reduce that complexity to a single static calculation. I built Counterfactual around a simple question: what if an agent could show you several possible futures before asking you to commit to one? Instead of immediately executing an action, Counterfactual gives the agent and user a shared space to explore alternatives, revise assumptions, understand tradeoffs, and decide together which future—if any—should become real. What it does Counterfactual is a WebMCP-powered decision simulator and permission layer for the agentic web. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can discover structured tools exposed by Counterfactual, read the user's financial assumptions, create alternative scenarios, simulate their outcomes, and compare them. Counterfactual turns those scenarios into explorable futures with dynamic visualizations that show how each decision affects the user's finances and protected goals. Users can change an assumption at any time and immediately see every future recalculate. A built-in WebMCP Flight Recorder makes the agent's behavior visible by recording each tool it discovers and invokes, along with its arguments, risk level, origin, status, and results. Rather than receiving only the agent's final recommendation, users can inspect the actual sequence of actions that produced it. Most importantly, Counterfactual distinguishes between exploring a future and making it real . Read-only and simulation tools can run freely, but when an agent attempts a consequential action, Counterfactual pauses execution and requires explicit human approval. The result is a simple principle: agents can explore autonomously, but humans retain control over commitment. How I built it I built Counterfactual with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and client-side state . Its scenario engine uses deterministic calculations so the agent's conclusions and the visual interface always operate from the same source of truth. Counterfactual exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These include tools for reading financial state, defining a decision, protecting goals, creating scenarios, comparing outcomes, simulating purchases, and committing to a selected scenario. Each tool has a natural-language description, JSON Schema input definition, validation, and metadata describing its behavior and risk. To support browsers that do not yet implement WebMCP natively, Counterfactual uses the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill package. A thin compatibility layer detects the available context—native, polyfilled, legacy, or fallback—and registers the same tool surface against it. Every invocation, whether initiated manually or by an external agent, passes through the same execution and logging pipeline. Calls are timestamped and risk-tagged before appearing in the Flight Recorder. Consequential actions go through an additional policy and approval layer before they can modify committed state. The approval is tied to that specific proposed action, preventing an agent from silently turning a simulation into a real commitment. I also tested the WebMCP integration end-to-end using Google's webmcp-evals CLI. That testing uncovered an issue that was invisible through Counterfactual's own UI but appeared when a tool was invoked through the actual WebMCP path. Fixing it helped ensure the project works through the protocol itself rather than only through a scripted demo. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was building against an experimental standard whose API and browser support are still evolving. Counterfactual needed to target the current document.modelContext API while remaining usable in browsers and agents relying on earlier or unsupported implementations. Another challenge was maintaining a single source of truth across the agent, editable controls, scenario calculations, visual branches, and Flight Recorder. A tool call could not simply generate an answer—it had to operate on the same live state the user was seeing and immediately update the rest of the experience. The final challenge was designing meaningful human oversight without making the agent feel unnecessarily constrained. Requiring approval for every tool call would defeat much of the value of an agent, while allowing every action to execute automatically would remove meaningful user control. Counterfactual therefore treats risk as a gradient: agents can read, simulate, fork, and compare independently, while actions that create real commitments stop at the point where human judgment matters most. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that Counterfactual uses WebMCP as a core interaction model , rather than adding it as a superficial integration. The agent does not simply fill out a form or operate a scripted demo—it collaborates with the user inside a shared decision environment. I also built a complete flow from tool discovery → simulation → comparison → recommendation → approval . Users can see what the agent is doing, inspect how it reached its recommendation, modify the assumptions themselves, explore alternative futures, and ultimately reject or approve the proposed action. Most importantly, Counterfactual turns an abstract AI safety problem into something tangible: consequential agent actions become forkable futures that people can inspect before making them real. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is more than a reliable way for agents to interact with websites. It can enable entirely new forms of human-agent collaboration . Structured tools allow an agent and an interface to share the same capabilities and application state without relying on fragile DOM interpretation or browser automation. I also learned that confirmation alone is not enough to provide meaningful user control. Before approving an action, people need to understand what they are approving, which goals may be affected, what alternatives exist, and whether the action can be reversed. Building Counterfactual showed me how structured tool schemas, deterministic application logic, risk classification, and visual design can work together to make agent behavior more transparent, understandable, and trustworthy. Why my use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Many agent experiences focus on reading the web: searching, summarizing, and answering questions. Counterfactual focuses on the harder problem— what happens when an agent can act on something that matters? That is where WebMCP becomes especially valuable. Counterfactual's decision process maps naturally onto a set of well-defined tools such as get_financial_state , define_decision , set_protected_goal , fork_scenario , compare_scenarios , and commit_scenario . Those tools also span a genuine risk gradient. Reading financial state is fundamentally different from simulating a hypothetical decision, and both are fundamentally different from committing to one. Counterfactual uses that distinction to determine when an agent can proceed independently and when control must return to the user. Instead of bolting permissions onto a chat interface after the fact, the application's capabilities, schemas, risk levels, and guardrails are part of the same structured tool environment the agent discovers and uses. How it creates a better user experience Instead of interacting with a black box that eventually reports, "I looked into it and think you should wait," Counterfactual lets the user see what the agent actually explored. Each hypothetical future becomes a visible branch with its own projected balance, goal impact, and explanation. The Flight Recorder shows the sequence of tool calls that produced those futures, including their arguments, risk levels, and results. That makes questions like "Why did the agent recommend this?" answerable by inspecting what actually happened rather than trusting a secondhand explanation. Counterfactual also includes a Manual Tool Console that lets users invoke the same tools themselves through the same schemas and Flight Recorder pipeline. The human and the agent are therefore operating the same system rather than two separate interfaces. And when an action would turn a hypothetical future into a real commitment, execution stops. Counterfactual shows the consequences and requires explicit approval before anything changes. The user sees the future before they inherit its consequences. title: SAVS: Visual Proof for WebMCP Agents
pitch: A successful tool call is not a visual verdict. SAVS gives WebMCP agents revision-bound evidence for the interface humans actually see.
about_excerpt: A successful tool call is not a visual verdict. SAVS gives WebMCP agents revision-bound evidence for the interface humans actually see. Like Comment Story Updates 1 · Fresh R1 is blocked. The action succeeded. The rendered revision did not. 3 · Fresh R2 passes. Only a fresh audit of the repaired revision returns PASS. 2 · Four native WebMCP tools. State, action, audit, and repair are page-registered. 4 · Old evidence remains blocked. Visual evidence belongs to the exact revision it inspected. Inspiration WebMCP makes website actions explicit and reliable, but successful execution does not prove that the human-visible result is correct. An agent can invoke the right tool and still leave clipped text, a shifted baseline, an overflow, or another visual regression behind. People experience the rendered page; agents usually receive a structured action result. We built SAVS to connect those two meanings of success. What it does SAVS is an agent-native visual verification workbench for WebMCP. The workbench begins at approved reference revision R0. An agent invokes a valid compact-layout tool, which succeeds and creates immutable revision R1. R1 contains a small but visible two-CSS-pixel baseline defect in the metric strip. The agent then audits R1. SAVS rerenders the approved reference and requested revision, compares their pixels, and returns a fresh BLOCK verdict with visual evidence. A constrained alignment repair creates successor revision R2. The earlier R1 result cannot approve R2 because its evidence is bound to R1 and is now stale. Only a fresh audit of R2 returns PASS . Four native page tools expose this flow: get_visual_state reads the current immutable revision and audit state. apply_compact_layout performs the valid action that creates R1. run_visual_audit audits an explicitly requested revision and reports whether its evidence is fresh. apply_alignment_repair creates a successor revision using an allowlisted repair and an expected-revision precondition. The tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . They are semantic capabilities, not wrappers around screen coordinates. The visible controls use the same application endpoints, so the person and agent share one state, history, evidence surface, and set of verdicts. How we built it The reference app is self-contained. A Node.js server maintains isolated sessions, immutable revisions, idempotency receipts, and audit records. The browser renders the current revision and evidence while registering the four WebMCP tools. A controlled renderer produces approved-reference and candidate PNGs. The verifier checks exact pixel differences, protects a stable control region, limits accepted changes to the intended target, and binds every audit to its requested revision. The same R0 → R1 → R2 behavior is exercised through native WebMCP discovery and invocation in Google Chrome and through an independent verifier against the public Render deployment. The live app requires no account or credentials. The public repository contains the standalone source, tests, instructions, MIT license, and Challenge-period provenance. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not detecting that pixels changed. It was making the result trustworthy across time. An audit that was valid for R1 must not become approval for R2, and a repair must not overwrite the history that explains the failure. That led us to immutable revisions, freshness-aware verdicts, expected-revision checks, and idempotent action receipts. The demo also exposed a more human problem: a two-pixel baseline defect can be obvious to a viewer while looking harmless in code or DOM geometry. We made the rendered pixels—not styling intent—the final evidence boundary. Accomplishments that we are proud of Four real page-registered WebMCP tools form one coherent workflow. A technically successful action produces a visible defect and a structured fresh BLOCK verdict. Stale evidence remains blocked after the page advances to a new revision. A constrained repair creates R2 without erasing R1. A fresh R2 audit returns PASS with zero changed pixels. The same behavioral chain has passed against the public Render origin. The accepted 2:37 demo uses real native WebMCP calls, audible narration, and burned-in English captions. What we learned Structured tools solve action ambiguity, but agents also need structured evidence about outcomes. Visual approval is not a timeless property of a page; it belongs to a particular rendered revision. That small change in the contract makes failure, repair, and approval understandable to both the agent and the person supervising it. What's next This Challenge workbench proves the smallest complete loop. The longer-term direction is to generalize the same revision-bound visual contract across real applications, responsive states, and richer human-approved visual intent while keeping the evidence inspectable by both people and agents. Challenge-period provenance SAVS began as pre-existing visual-verification research. During the Challenge period, we built this self-contained WebMCP reference implementation: a new page-registered four-tool interface, immutable revision workflow, freshness-bound visual verdicts, constrained repair path, native WebMCP browser verification, public deployment, and Challenge demo. This repository does not import the private SAVS research runtime. title: Knot Your Table
pitch: Wedding seating, without the social Tetris. Say what everyone needs. We’ll make it fit!
about_excerpt:
Wedding seating, without the social Tetris. Say what everyone needs. We’ll make it fit!

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Knot Your Table came from 2 problems I ran into recently. 

 At work, while building an ERD tool with an infinite canvas, I realized how awkward large canvases are for agents. Once something is outside the viewport, the agent has very little idea what is out there or which direction to explore. I even had to build extra navigation UI just to help humans find far-away objects. For AI bulk editing, the usual approach was a dedicated LLM call through something like OpenRouter: package up some context, ask for one transformation, apply the response. It works, but it is still basically an isolated LLM call, not an agent continuously working with the live app state. 

 Recently, my best friend has been planning a wedding with 80+ guests and kept complaining about seating. The painful part was not dragging names onto tables. It was keeping all the invisible rules in her head: these people are vegetarian, these friends should sit together, these 2 people should not sit together, and then something changes at the last minute and you have to reshuffle everything again. 

 That felt like a very natural problem to explore with a canvas app + WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 Knot Your Table is a visual wedding seating planner where the human gets a clean, playful canvas and the agent gets access to the structured data underneath it. 

 A user can say: 

 
 “Keep the vegetarians mostly together, keep my college friends together if possible, and family tables should be closest to the stage.” 
 

 The agent can reason across the whole wedding, including guests and tables that are completely offscreen, make coordinated changes, validate the result, and summarize what changed. 

 The key idea is that the user should not have to see every relationship, dietary preference, constraint, table capacity, or room coordinate at once. That information is useful for the agent, but overwhelming for the human. The user gets to focus on visual arrangement, judgment calls, and checking whether the result feels right, while the agent handles the grunt work. 

 How I built it 

 I built Knot Your Table as a client-side visual planner with a shared application state that both the canvas and WebMCP tools use. 

 I registered a set of WebMCP tools that let the agent: 

 
 understand the seating plan 
 manage planning rules 
 modify guests and seating 
 verify and present seating changes 
 

 The agent is not clicking pixels or dragging from one coordinate to another. It is operating on the actual data underneath the UI in verifiable ways. 

 Human edits and agent edits also stay in sync. If I manually move someone because I prefer where they are, the agent immediately sees that new state and can work around it without me having to explain what I just changed. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the hardest parts was deciding what not to expose. 

 It would have been easy to create dozens of tiny overlapping WebMCP tools, but that not only increases the initial build complexity, it also gives the agent too many similar choices to make. A larger, overlapping toolbox introduces more variance into the agent’s decisions, which can make the same user request behave differently over time and ultimately make the product feel less predictable and trustworthy. The challenge was finding a small set of semantic actions that were broad enough to handle different requests while still being clear and predictable. 

 The other challenge was visual design. I do not have an art background, and I wanted the app to feel more like a fun wedding-decorating experience than an AI dashboard. Getting the canvas to feel playful, readable, and still functional took a lot of iteration. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The human and agent are actually working on the same live plan. A person can manipulate the room visually, while the agent can reason over information that may be hidden or far outside the current viewport. That makes the interaction feel much more natural than either manually doing everything in the canvas or sending a one-off LLM request and trying to merge the result back into the app afterward or filling out and managing complex forms of rules. 

 I am also happy with how much complexity we were able to keep out of the visible interface. The product can support fairly rich operations without turning into a wall of filters, rule builders, and bulk-edit controls. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP can change how we think about web interfaces. 

 A functionally rich app does not need to expose every operation visually. The visible UI can be the tip of the iceberg: the human sees the part that is useful and enjoyable, while the agent handles much of the operational complexity underneath. 

 That creates a cleaner division of labor. The human focuses on judgment, visual thinking, and verification. The agent handles the tedious coordination needed to make the whole plan work. 

 What's next for Knot Your Table 

 Next, I want to share Knot Your Table more broadly as a free tool and see how real couples actually use it. I’m especially interested in which seating problems come up repeatedly, where the agent is genuinely useful, and where the interaction still feels confusing or unpredictable. 

 From there, I’d like to gradually expand it beyond seating into a fuller wedding planning suite, while keeping the same idea: let the human focus on the visual, social, and creative decisions they care about, and let the agent handle the repetitive coordination underneath.

title: DevPilot WebMCP
pitch: An agent-native DevOps platform where AI agents diagnose failures, investigate incidents, and collaborate with developers through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native DevOps platform where AI agents diagnose failures, investigate incidents, and collaborate with developers through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Inspiration 

 Modern DevOps teams have powerful monitoring tools, dashboards, CI/CD systems, cloud consoles, logs, and AI assistants, yet incident recovery is still fragmented. 

 When production fails, engineers jump between alerts, logs, GitHub, Kubernetes, deployment dashboards, runbooks, and communication tools while downtime continues. 

 DevPilot AI was originally built to compress this workflow into a human-approved AI incident recovery platform. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave me the opportunity to take the next step: make DevPilot not only usable by humans, but directly understandable and operable by AI agents. 

 Instead of forcing an agent to visually navigate a complex DevOps dashboard, DevPilot WebMCP exposes structured tools that clearly describe what an agent can inspect and what actions it can request. 

 The goal is a web application where the developer and their AI agent can investigate and resolve production incidents together. 

 What it does 

 DevPilot WebMCP is an agent-native DevOps control plane for detecting, diagnosing, and recovering from production incidents. 

 The existing DevPilot platform already brings together infrastructure alerts, deployment failures, logs, incident memory, AI diagnosis, remediation planning, GitHub workflows, and human-approved recovery actions. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, DevPilot is being extended with structured WebMCP tools for agent interaction. 

 The WebMCP interface is designed around capabilities such as: 

 
 Analyze application and infrastructure incidents 
 Inspect service and deployment health 
 Diagnose likely root causes 
 Retrieve incident context and historical information 
 Generate structured remediation plans 
 Explain why a deployment failed 
 Prepare recovery actions 
 Verify system health after remediation 
 

 This means a developer can work with an AI agent through natural language while the agent interacts with DevPilot through explicit structured tools instead of guessing how to click through the interface. 

 A workflow can look like: 

 
 A production problem is detected. 
 The developer asks their AI agent to investigate it. 
 The agent discovers DevPilot's available WebMCP tools. 
 DevPilot returns structured incident and infrastructure context. 
 The agent requests a diagnosis and remediation plan. 
 DevPilot presents the proposed action to the human. 
 The human reviews or approves the action. 
 DevPilot verifies recovery and records the result. 
 

 The human remains responsible for high-impact actions while the agent handles investigation, information gathering, and repetitive operational work. 

 Why WebMCP 

 DevOps applications are an especially strong fit for WebMCP because their interfaces can contain dozens of dashboards, tables, alerts, logs, buttons, and operational workflows. 

 A traditional browser agent has to interpret these visual interfaces and infer what each element means. 

 WebMCP lets DevPilot expose the underlying capabilities directly. 

 Instead of an agent searching the screen for an incident and guessing which controls to use, it can discover a structured tool such as an incident-analysis or service-health capability with a defined schema. 

 This makes agent interactions more reliable, explainable, and efficient. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP allows the human-facing application and the agent-facing interface to exist together. 

 Humans keep the rich visual operations cockpit. 

 Agents receive precise structured tools. 

 Together they can perform workflows that would otherwise require engineers to manually gather information from many different systems. 

 How I built it 

 DevPilot is a full-stack AI DevOps platform. 

 The frontend is built with Next.js and React and provides the operations cockpit used by developers. 

 The backend is built with Python and FastAPI and handles incident workflows, AI analysis, authentication, persistence, and external integrations. 

 Neon PostgreSQL provides persistent storage. 

 OpenAI is used for AI-assisted diagnosis and remediation workflows. 

 GitHub integration supports development and remediation workflows, while the platform also contains production monitoring, CI/CD checks, Docker support, and infrastructure-oriented recovery capabilities. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I am extending the web application using the WebMCP API so the browser can register DevPilot capabilities as structured agent tools. 

 Each WebMCP tool is designed with: 

 
 A clear tool name 
 A precise description 
 Structured input schemas 
 Restricted operational scope 
 Predictable outputs 
 Human approval for sensitive actions 
 

 The challenge-specific implementation is being developed after the WebMCP Challenge start date and documented separately in the repository and commit history. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 DevPilot is intentionally not designed to remove engineers from incident response. 

 The agent handles tasks that are expensive for humans but safe to automate: 

 
 Gathering context 
 Reading health information 
 Correlating incident signals 
 Identifying likely root causes 
 Retrieving previous incident knowledge 
 Preparing remediation plans 
 

 The human remains in control of consequential infrastructure actions. 

 This creates a workflow where the AI agent acts like an extremely fast operations investigator while the engineer acts as the decision maker. 

 WebMCP is the bridge that makes this collaboration reliable. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the biggest design challenges is deciding what should become an agent tool and what should remain a human-controlled action. 

 DevOps systems can affect real infrastructure, so simply giving an agent unrestricted operational access would be unsafe. 

 The WebMCP layer therefore needs narrowly scoped tools, explicit schemas, predictable responses, and approval boundaries. 

 Another challenge is converting information that was originally optimized for visual dashboards into structured results that agents can reason about reliably. 

 The final challenge is preserving the existing human experience while introducing a second, agent-native interaction layer without duplicating the entire application. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that DevPilot already functions as more than a chatbot. 

 It is a working DevOps control plane connecting incident signals, AI diagnosis, remediation planning, monitoring, deployment workflows, and human approval. 

 The WebMCP extension evolves that architecture further by allowing AI agents to interact with the same operational capabilities through a purpose-built machine interface. 

 Rather than redesigning the application only for AI, the project explores a web where humans and agents have interfaces designed specifically for each of them while sharing the same underlying application. 

 What I learned 

 Building DevPilot has taught me that useful AI systems need more than model responses. 

 They need structured context, predictable tools, observability, permissions, validation, and clear human control. 

 WebMCP introduces another important principle: websites should not require AI agents to reverse-engineer their interfaces. 

 If applications can explicitly describe what agents are allowed to do, agent interactions can become significantly more reliable. 

 What's next for DevPilot WebMCP 

 The next step is expanding DevPilot's WebMCP interface into a complete agent-native operations API for the browser. 

 Future capabilities could include: 

 
 Repository and CI/CD investigation 
 Kubernetes health analysis 
 Deployment rollback planning 
 Infrastructure drift investigation 
 Security incident triage 
 Cost anomaly analysis 
 Multi-agent incident collaboration 
 Persistent incident memory 
 Organization-level policy and approval controls 
 

 The long-term vision is for DevPilot to become an operations environment where engineers and AI agents continuously collaborate to keep software reliable.

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. about_excerpt: The agent finds the show and lights the dates. You tap Book. Like Comment Story Updates Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This is the live tickadoo storefront. A person still taps Book. Buying theatre tickets is a page you already trust, not a hackathon toy. Dates, seats, and price only make sense on the live product page. Remote MCP can search a catalog. It cannot move the calendar you are looking at, or stop an agent from inventing a checkout. WebMCP lets ChatGPT and Chrome call the same search and availability tools on www.tickadoo.com , then write the result back into the page the person can see. How it creates a better user experience You stay on tickadoo. Ask for West End tonight, or for dates on a specific show. The listing updates, or the calendar highlights real available nights. You still press Book. There is no pay tool. Cart, checkout, and account URLs are blocked from agent navigation. The agent does the hunting. The person does the money. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Before: an agent either guessed through the UI or quoted a catalog card in another window, while you tried to match that to the real page. After: the agent and the page share one session. search_events refreshes the visible search or London listing. whats_on_tonight opens /london/today. get_availability highlights dates on the show calendar when that UI is on screen. You confirm. That is a shared buyer path, not a scrape. How we implemented WebMCP www.tickadoo.com already ran on Cloudflare Workers (TanStack Start, apps/www in tickadoo/frontend). During the submission window we registered tools with document.modelContext.registerTool in the existing client bundle (apps/www/src/lib/webmcp.ts, wired from entry-client.tsx). Tools call the live catalog at https://mcp.tickadoo.com/mcp (search_experiences, availability, details). Page language and city come from the URL. A small live-page bridge updates search, /london/today, and calendar highlights without replacing checkout. tickadoo_open_product can open product, search, city, and booking-date URLs only. This is an existing-app extension, not a greenfield demo. Prior WebMCP on www (before 25 Aug 2026) exposed a thin 3-tool proxy. Challenge work is frontend#2935, merged to main as c8a0fa0 on 27 Aug 2026: search_events, get_availability, get_experience_details, whats_on_tonight, locale context, in-page actuation, and a hard block on checkout/cart/account. Judges should score the PR, not the older proxy. Optional Chrome Origin-Trial header is wired (WEBMCP_ORIGIN_TRIAL_TOKEN) and currently empty. Prefer ChatGPTs in-app browser, which supports WebMCP without the token. Chrome 149+ works with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. How judges should test Open ChatGPT desktop → in-app browser (preferred). Or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Go to https://www.tickadoo.com/london/the-lion-king-tickets Ask: Find West End shows I can see tonight. You should land on or see /london/today. On that show page, ask: Which dates are available next month? The calendar should highlight real nights. Do not ask it to pay. Click Book yourself. Stop on the human checkout. Confirm tools exist in the page bundle: search_events, get_availability, whats_on_tonight. No login. No API key. Do not complete a paid booking. title: Fluent Notebook
pitch: A browser-based Python workspace powered by WebMCP, where AI agents act as active research partners to fetch datasets, fix bugs, and execute analysis code directly alongside you.
about_excerpt: A browser-based Python workspace powered by WebMCP, where AI agents act as active research partners to fetch datasets, fix bugs, and execute analysis code directly alongside you. Like 4 Comment Story Updates Product WebMCP Inspiration During my time working heavily in quantitative research and portfolio construction, I kept hitting the same friction: context switching. Jupyter is the industry standard for index research and data analytics, but jumping between the notebook to write boilerplate, browser tabs to hunt for dataset documentation, and terminal windows to manage environments breaks the analytical flow. I wanted an environment that respects deep work. By combining WebMCP with a strict, distraction-free UI, the goal was to turn the static notebook into an active research partner. What it does Fluent Notebook is a Jupyter-style Python notebook that runs entirely in the browser. Python executes in Pyodide (WebAssembly) with pandas, NumPy, matplotlib and %pip install via micropip, so there is no kernel server and no data leaves the machine. Around that kernel sits a Fluent UI workspace: a code editor with IntelliSense and Jupyter command mode, an Explorer with Python, Markdown, CSV and JSON files, a Problems panel fed by pyflakes, a Data Wrangler for DataFrames and CSVs, a Variables panel, interactive charts, and a Python terminal. The page registers 49 WebMCP tools , so a browser agent (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) can read and edit cells and files, insert cells between cells, run cells and .py files, install packages, inspect kernel variables, find bugs, open a DataFrame in Data Wrangler, restyle and explain charts, write per-cell summaries, import notebooks from .ipynb JSON, rename, move and delete files, restart the kernel, and save or load the user's cloud workspace. Every tool returns real notebook state; nothing is mocked. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A notebook is not a page you can scrape. It is a live kernel, an editor, a file tree and a set of outputs. Screenshot-and-click agents cannot reliably "run cell 2" or "read the table under cell 3". WebMCP lets the notebook hand the agent the same levers a person has, each with a JSON schema, read-only and untrusted-content hints, and a structured result the agent can chain: add_python_cell → run_python_cell → get_cell_table . Because Python runs in the tab, the person and the agent share one kernel, one file tree and one problem list, with no server round trip. How it creates a better experience Ask "how expensive is the S&P 500 versus its own history?" and the agent writes the pandas cell, downloads Shiller's monthly data inside the kernel, drops the months with no valuation data, runs it, charts CAPE against its long-run average, and reports the answer, while you watch it happen in the notebook. That is the demo video, recorded live in the ChatGPT app. Ask "find bugs in analysis.py" and the agent runs static analysis, reads the Problems panel, edits the file with a find-and-replace, and re-checks. Ask "summarize each cell" and the agent pins its own two-line summaries under every cell and in the Outline. Every agent edit is badged with the tool that made it ( Agent · add_python_cell ) and keeps a one-click Revert until you edit the cell yourself. The WebMCP panel lists every call, linked to the cell it touched. What people and agents can do together now The person keeps the editor, the keyboard and the judgement; the agent gets the same kernel, files and problem list. Debugging, data cleaning and documentation become a shared loop inside one tab instead of a copy-paste relay between a chat window and a notebook. Cell and file tools resolve only once the change is on screen, so the agent can chain calls without racing the UI, and the person can step in at any moment: rerun, edit, revert, or keep going by hand. How I implemented WebMCP Each of the 49 tools is declared once and registered with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute }) . The page falls back to navigator.modelContext for Chrome's flag and keeps checking briefly for hosts that inject the context after load. execute calls the same functions the toolbar buttons use (insert cell, run cell, find bugs, rename, restart kernel), then awaits the React state flush, so results describe what is actually on screen. Results are structured JSON: cell ids, table summaries, chart specs, problems, file paths. Tools carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations and support abort signals. A tracking wrapper records every call for the status chip and the WebMCP panel, and tags cells the agent touched so the UI can show the badge and the Revert button. Tech stack React 19 in a Next.js-style app on Vite (vinext), Microsoft Fluent UI v9, Recharts for interactive charts, a custom code editor with Python IntelliSense; Pyodide with pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, micropip and pyflakes; static export hosted on Azure Static Web Apps (Free tier) with a managed Azure Functions API that stores each signed-in user's workspace in Azure Blob Storage behind optional GitHub or Microsoft sign-in. Challenges I ran into Running Python entirely in the browser brings sandboxing limits: no git clone , and CORS blocks many dataset hosts. I turned that into a showcase for tool use: the agent fetches what the page cannot and passes it in through import_notebook_from_json or create_project_file , or downloads inside the kernel with pyodide.http.open_url . The other hard part was timing: tool calls have to wait for React state to land, or a chained run_python_cell runs a cell that does not exist yet. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The human-agent loop feels fluid. Python IntelliSense sits alongside the agent's edits, so manual changes to a generated pandas DataFrame or chart script are smooth, and the agent can read a traceback from the Problems pane and inject the fix without the user leaving the keyboard. In the demo, ChatGPT completes a full market-valuation analysis with seven tool calls. What I learned Structured tool access beats open-ended prompting. Giving an agent specific, well-defined tools, such as converting a GitHub URL to raw .ipynb JSON and parsing the cells, produces faster and more deterministic help than letting it guess its way through a UI. What's next for Fluent Notebook Expanding the WebMCP tool set for data pipelines: tools for zero-copy business-intelligence queries, so the agent can explore large remote databases and stream aggregated results into the local browser session for visualization. Available robots, tiles, mats and instruction packs determine grouping and rotation. The shared canvas turns accepted context into a structured mission across all four learning-cycle stages. Learner supports and extension challenges are reviewed separately from the core mission. WebMCP proposals stay pending until the teacher accepts, edits or rejects each operation. Deterministic validation reports 13 checks. Ready for teacher review is not approval. Accepted lesson content becomes a printable Teacher Guide preview. The printable Observation Checklist supports observation without inventing evidence. Inspiration Primary teachers who want to teach computational thinking through physical, screen-light activities face a complicated planning task. A usable lesson has to connect the curriculum goal, class size, lesson duration, available robots and tiles, learner differences, group participation and observable assessment evidence. A conventional AI chatbot can generate a lesson plan, but it normally works outside the teacher’s planning interface. It does not automatically share the application’s accepted class context, may rewrite too much when only one section needs changing, can overlook physical equipment limits, or present generated text without a clear human review boundary. We created Tangible Coding Studio: Mission Builder to explore a different relationship: a primary teacher and an AI agent working on the same structured lesson canvas through WebMCP. The agent can understand the available actions and propose precise changes, while the teacher remains the authority over every accepted lesson decision. What it does Mission Builder supports a seven-step teacher workflow covering: Class context Tangible resources and grouping Mission design Learner support and extension The tangible learning cycle Proposal review Deterministic validation The production application registers exactly five WebMCP tools: set_class_context select_tangible_resources build_tangible_mission adapt_for_learners validate_and_prepare_lesson The first four tools do not directly overwrite accepted lesson content. They create section-scoped pending proposals. The teacher can inspect each operation and then accept it, edit and accept it, or reject it. The fifth tool runs the same deterministic validator available in the visible interface. Validation can mark a lesson Ready for teacher review , but it cannot approve the lesson. Teacher approval and prepared-file generation are intentionally not implemented in this challenge prototype. The Preview workspace derives three browser views from currently accepted content only: Teacher Guide Pupil Mission Card Observation Checklist Pending and rejected proposal content is excluded. Native printing can print the currently selected browser preview, but no PDF-generation or prepared-output service is claimed. Why WebMCP fits this use case WebMCP changes the collaboration from “copy text out of a chatbot” into structured work on a live web application. The key shift is that the agent moves from outside the teacher’s workflow to operating through typed tools against the same structured lesson state. The browser exposes a small, purpose-built set of tools with typed schemas and meaningful descriptions. The agent can select the correct action, return a portable structured proposal and operate against the lesson’s current accepted context. The teacher can see exactly what is proposed inside the product before anything becomes authoritative. This makes several things possible together that are difficult in an ordinary chatbot workflow: The agent works with the application’s real class, equipment and lesson structure. Changes are section-scoped rather than uncontrolled full-document rewrites. Accepted content and proposed content remain separate. Context fingerprints detect stale downstream proposals. Every accepted contribution retains teacher/AI provenance. Validation checks the accepted lesson rather than the agent’s unreviewed draft. The manual workflow remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. WebMCP is therefore not an add-on chat box. It is the collaboration boundary between a browser agent and a teacher-controlled lesson state. Demonstration scenario For our public demonstration, we use The Lost Story Path, a fictional P4 literacy lesson designed for 24 pupils and a 45-minute session. The class has three robots, nine tile sets, three activity mats, three instruction-card packs and 24 role cards. Working in groups, pupils plan a route through a story, arrange the instructions in sequence and test their route using either a robot or a tile-only walkthrough. When they find the mixed-up instruction, they explain what went wrong and how their change repairs the story. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can suggest learner supports and extension activities using the lesson’s actual class context and resources. These suggestions never enter the lesson automatically: the teacher reviews each proposed change and decides whether to accept, edit or reject it. Once the accepted lesson is complete, it passes all 13 validation checks with no errors or warnings. Its status becomes Ready for teacher review, and the teacher can preview a Teacher Guide, Pupil Mission Card and Observation Checklist based only on accepted content. How we built it The application is a browser-local Vite, React and TypeScript prototype. Zod validates WebMCP inputs and portable proposal packages. The accepted lesson, proposal history, validation result and provenance are stored in browser localStorage for the exact origin. The proposal model supports operation-level review and atomic acceptance. Downstream proposal packages can bind to a SHA-256 fingerprint of copied accepted context so stale packages are rejected instead of silently applied to a changed lesson. The same domain validation logic is used by both the visible Validate workspace and the WebMCP validation tool. The Preview workspace reads accepted lesson state only and does not create a second output state. The public application is deployed on Vercel and the complete challenge source is available in a public MIT-licensed GitHub repository. Tangible Coding Ltd’s trademarks, commercial curriculum, hardware designs and other excluded commercial materials are outside the challenge repository’s licence scope. Challenges we faced Preserving human authority The hardest design decision was ensuring that a successful agent call never meant that lesson content had already been accepted. Tool execution may create pending proposal state, but only an explicit teacher action can move a proposed operation into accepted lesson content. Moving context safely between agent and teacher browsers Browser-local storage is intentionally origin- and profile-specific. We created portable proposal packages and accepted-context packages so the teacher controls what moves between contexts. Versioned packages, structural “before” values and context fingerprints protect against stale imports. Recovering a lesson without bypassing review During testing we restored a lesson from portable proposal evidence. The mission operations and learner adaptations were imported as pending changes and accepted individually. This demonstrated that recovery could preserve the teacher-review boundary instead of importing an authoritative lesson snapshot. Keeping readiness separate from approval The validator can determine that required planning information is present, durations match and resource/grouping conditions are feasible. It still reports Ready for teacher review rather than “approved.” This distinction is visible across Validate, Preview and the WebMCP result. Verified production result On 31 August 2026, we tested the complete workflow in production using a WebMCP-capable browser agent. The agent discovered and successfully used all five registered WebMCP tools. Across the session, the teacher reviewed and individually accepted 13 proposed changes. The completed lesson then passed all 13 validation checks with no errors or warnings, and all three accepted-content previews rendered correctly. We also refreshed the application to confirm that the lesson, resources, proposal history, authorship information and validation result were retained. The lesson remained Ready for teacher review, not approved. This is an important part of the design: the agent can help create and improve the lesson, but the teacher remains responsible for every accepted decision. NetaWatch is an evidence-first civic research platform. With WebMCP, AI agents can discover, verify, and compare political data through natural-language queries.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Although political and parliamentary information is available to the public it is generally spread out among various sources and hard to research efficiently. That is why we decided to make civic research more accessible by bringing key public records together on a single, structured platform. 

 AI agents are at the same time turning into a new means of interacting with software, and we wanted to find out what would occur if an AI could go beyond drawing on its own knowledge to directly interact with a civic data platform. 

 That was the result of NetaWatch WebMCP . 

 What We Built 

 NetaWatch is a civic research platform guided by evidence which arranges information on politicians into structured research dossiers. It combines data on parliamentary activity, public statements, election affidavits, assets, legal records and other publicly available information. 

 We then included WebMCP features so that AI agents will be able to interact directly with NetaWatch. 

 Instead of manually navigating through the website, a user can ask an AI agent to perform tasks such as: 

 
 Find a politician's dossier 
 Retrieve specific civic or parliamentary information 
 Answer research questions using NetaWatch data 
 Compare politicians across important metrics 
 

 For instance, in the demo we request that ChatGPT finds Rahul Gandhi's dossier using NetaWatch; the agent identifies and makes use of the exposed features, retrieves the relevant information, and then makes it available in the conversation. 

 The workflow becomes: 

 ASK → DISCOVER → VERIFY → COMPARE 

 How We Built It 

 We created NetaWatch as a structured civic research platform, including politician-specific dossiers and organized datasets; the WebMCP layer makes available certain NetaWatch features so that compatible AI agents are able to discover and call them. 

 The key idea is to separate the system into two parts: 

 NetaWatch is the source of the structured evidence. 

 The interface offered by WebMCP enables AI agents to interact with it. 

 It turns natural-language requests into real interactions with the application rather than just chatbot responses. 

 Challenges 

 A major difficulty was working out how to make useful application capabilities available to an AI agent without ending up with an interface that consisted of too generally worded tools. 

 We also had to give careful consideration to structured data, reliable retrieval, and making it easy for the user to understand the agent's interactions. In order for a workflow to be a success it had to be not only technically functional but also easy to demonstrate. 

 A further difficulty was giving users complex civic information without it being overwhelming. To deal with this we grouped the information into targeted dossiers and important metrics. 

 What We Learned 

 We discovered that attaching AI to an application is fundamentally different from just attaching AI to a database, the agent having to have clear and well-defined capabilities which correspond naturally to user intent. 

 We also found that structured civic data becomes considerably more useful when it can be queried using natural language and still keeps the underlying evidence and context. 

 Most importantly, this project demonstrated to us how WebMCP is able to convert a conventional website into something that an AI agent can actively use, thus establishing a new kind of interaction model between users, AI, and web applications. 

 What's Next 

 We would like to enhance NetaWatch WebMCP by adding more research capabilities, incorporating a wider range of civic datasets, providing richer comparisons, and including further agent actions. 

 We want evidence-based civic research to be just as easy as posing a question—yet at the same time we want the basic information to remain structured, transparent, and verifiable.
