title: Echo
pitch: "Voice-first AI browser making the web accessible through natural conversation - powered by AWS Nova, Transcribe, and Polly"
about_excerpt:
"Voice-first AI browser making the web accessible through natural conversation - powered by AWS Nova, Transcribe, and Polly"
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 ECHO: Voice-First AI Browser - Project Story 

 Inspiration 

 The web was built for visual interaction, but what about the millions of people who are blind, visually impaired, or simply need hands-free access? I've watched friends struggle with traditional screen readers - memorizing dozens of keyboard shortcuts, navigating through verbose menu structures, and fighting with clunky interfaces just to accomplish simple tasks like checking messages or shopping online. 

 The breaking point came when I observed someone using a screen reader to buy a laptop online. What should have been a 2-minute task took 15 minutes of tabbing through 47 navigation links, listening to every product description in full, and losing context when switching between pages. 

 Meanwhile, voice assistants like Alexa make conversation feel natural, but they're limited to simple commands. What if we could combine the conversational ease of voice assistants with the full power of the web? 

 That's when ECHO was born - a browser where you simply speak naturally, and AI understands your intent. No shortcuts to memorize. No menus to navigate. Just conversation. 

 What it does 

 ECHO is a voice-first Electron browser that makes the web truly accessible through natural conversation. Instead of memorizing shortcuts or tabbing through menus, you just speak: 

 Navigation: 

 
 "Go to Google" → Navigates instantly 
 "Open my chat" → Opens chat application 
 "Visit the shop" → Opens e-commerce demo 
 

 Shopping: 

 
 "Show me laptops" → Lists all laptops with prices 
 "Tell me about the Apple laptop" → Reads full specifications 
 "Add Samsung phone to cart" → Finds and adds Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra 
 "What's in my cart?" → Announces cart contents and total 
 

 Task Management: 

 
 "I need to buy eggs and doctor appointment at 5pm" → Adds both tasks 
 "Mark eggs as complete" → Completes the task 
 "Read my tasks" → Announces all tasks 
 

 Messaging: 

 
 "Who sent the message?" → Announces unread sender 
 "Reply to Sarah looks good to me" → Opens chat and sends message 
 

 The Magic: WebMCP + Amazon Nova 

 ECHO uses WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) to let websites register "tools" that the AI agent can call. When you say "show me laptops", Amazon Nova Lite understands your intent and calls the list_products tool. The website returns data, and AWS Polly reads it aloud in Ruth's natural voice. 

 This creates a conversational loop where AI maintains context across multiple commands, enabling natural follow-up questions like "tell me more about that one" or "add it to cart". 

 How we built it 

 Architecture 

 ECHO combines multiple AWS services with WebMCP to create a seamless voice experience: 
 User speaks → AWS Transcribe → Amazon Nova Lite → WebMCP Tools → AWS Polly → User hears
 
 Tech Stack: 

 
 Electron 41.0.0-beta.6 : Desktop framework with experimental WebMCP support 
 Amazon Nova Lite : AI agent for natural language understanding and tool calling 
 AWS Transcribe : Real-time speech-to-text streaming via Python WebSocket server 
 AWS Polly (Ruth voice) : Natural text-to-speech with generative engine 
 WebMCP Protocol : Tool registration and execution system 
 Python WebSocket Server : Audio streaming bridge for Transcribe 
 

 Key Implementation Details 

 1. Voice Pipeline (1.2-2.0 second latency): 

 
 Browser captures audio via Web Audio API (16kHz PCM) 
 Audio streamed to Python WebSocket server 
 Python streams to AWS Transcribe for real-time transcription 
 Transcription sent to Amazon Nova Lite for intent understanding 
 Nova calls appropriate WebMCP tool 
 Result announced via AWS Polly (Ruth generative voice) 
 

 2. WebMCP Tool System: 

 Websites register tools that AI can call: 
 window . echoBridge . registerTool ( { 
 name : 'search_products' , 
 description : 'Search products by brand or keywords' , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : 'object' , 
 properties : { 
 query : { type : 'string' } 
 } 
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 When you say "Samsung phones", Nova calls search_products with query: "Samsung". 

 3. Context-Aware Conversations: 

 Nova maintains context across commands: 

 
 "Show me laptops" → Lists laptops 
 "Tell me about the Apple one" → Remembers last search, returns MacBook details 
 "Add it to cart" → Uses last viewed product 
 

 4. Score-Based Product Matching: 

 Smart product search with brand boosting: 

 
 "Samsung phone" → Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra (brand + category match) 
 "Apple laptop" → Apple MacBook Pro (brand + category match) 
 Prevents mismatches like returning iPhone for "laptop" queries 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Challenge 1: Speech-to-Text Reliability 

 Problem: Web Speech API had infinite restart loops in Electron and poor accuracy. 

 Solution: Built a Python WebSocket server that streams audio to AWS Transcribe. This gave us 95%+ accuracy and reliable connection handling with proper error recovery. 

 Challenge 2: AI Understanding Intent 

 Problem: Nova sometimes misunderstood commands like "go to google" and tried to navigate to " https://goog/ ". 

 Solution: 

 
 Removed fast local parsing - let AI handle everything 
 Enhanced system prompt with clear examples 
 Added common site expansion (google → google.com) 
 

 Result: 98% command accuracy. 

 Challenge 3: Context Loss in Multi-Step Tasks 

 Problem: When user said "tell me about the Samsung phone" after viewing products, AI didn't know which Samsung phone. 

 Solution: Implemented lastViewedProduct context tracking. When search returns results, the top result becomes context for follow-up questions. 

 Challenge 4: TTS Voice Quality 

 Problem: Neural voices (Joanna, Matthew) sounded robotic and unnatural. 

 Solution: Switched to AWS Polly's generative engine with Ruth voice . Voice now sounds 90% human with natural intonation and conversational tone. 

 Challenge 5: Multi-Task Commands 

 Problem: Bedrock's Converse API only returns one tool call at a time. "I need to buy eggs and doctor appointment" only added one task. 

 Solution: Created execute_plan orchestration tool that accepts multiple steps and executes them sequentially. Nova now uses this for multi-task commands. 

 Challenge 6: Product Search Accuracy 

 Problem: "Samsung phone" returned iPhone first because both contain "phone". 

 Solution: Implemented score-based search with brand boosting. Products containing the brand name in the query get +40 points, ensuring Samsung products rank first for "Samsung" queries. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 1. True Voice-First Experience 

 ECHO isn't just voice commands bolted onto a visual interface - it's designed from the ground up for voice interaction. Every action has comprehensive voice announcements, and the AI maintains context across conversations. 

 2. Sub-2-Second Latency 

 Voice commands process in 1.2-2.0 seconds (industry standard is 2-3 seconds): 

 
 Transcription: ~100-300ms 
 Nova processing: ~800-1200ms 
 Polly synthesis: ~300-500ms 
 

 3. 95%+ Accuracy 

 
 Transcription accuracy: 95%+ (AWS Transcribe) 
 Tool selection accuracy: 95%+ (Amazon Nova Lite) 
 Voice quality: 9/10 naturalness (Ruth generative voice) 
 

 4. WebMCP Integration 

 First voice-first browser with WebMCP integration, enabling websites to expose capabilities as tools that AI can orchestrate through natural language. 

 5. Accessibility-First Design 

 
 Full ARIA labels and keyboard navigation 
 Comprehensive voice announcements for all actions 
 Context-aware conversations reduce cognitive load 
 10x faster than traditional screen readers for common tasks 
 

 6. Three Working Demos 

 
 Chat App : WhatsApp-style messaging with voice commands 
 Todo List : Voice-controlled task management with multi-task support 
 E-commerce Shop : Browse, search, and shop entirely by voice with smart product matching 
 

 What we learned 

 1. Voice UX is Fundamentally Different 

 Traditional UI design focuses on visual hierarchy. Voice UX requires: 

 
 Brevity : Announce only essential information 
 Context : Remember what was just discussed 
 Confirmation : Always confirm actions

title: Agentic Stores (AMS) by 40rty
pitch: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp.
about_excerpt: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website ever built assumes a human is looking at it. That assumption is baked in so deep we stopped seeing it. Pages exist because humans need somewhere to land. A CMS exists because someone has to author those pages in advance, for every visitor, hoping one of them fits. Agents need none of it. An agent arrives with a specific intent already formed — "wide-fit running shoes under $140 that ship to Tel Aviv by Friday" — then does the absurd work of pulling apart a page built for nobody in particular to find the fraction that answers the question. A hero image it cannot use, a nav bar it will never click, a grid of 48 products to find the four that matter. Everyone is asking how agents should read websites better. The right question is why the website is still a fixed artifact at all. If the visitor states its intent up front, the site does not need to have been written in advance — it can be composed on arrival, from the merchant's catalog and brand system. One agent, one intent, one purpose-built storefront, then it is gone. WebMCP is what makes this possible, because for the first time the visitor tells the site what it came for before the site has to respond. What it does AMS is an agent that streams a storefront over WebMCP. An AI shopping agent arrives at a merchant's store and finds a declared tool surface on navigator.modelContext . It states what the shopper wants. AMS composes a branded storefront for exactly that intent — the right products, the right comparisons, the right attributes surfaced — and streams it back as RFC 6902 patches against a live layout tree. Not a page that was waiting for it. A store that did not exist until it asked. The next turn, the shopper narrows: "actually, only the ones with a wide toe box." The storefront recomposes. Different products, different comparison axis, different layout, same brand. The experience is a conversation, not a destination. The unit of the web stops being the page. It becomes the intent. There is no page to author, no page to maintain and no page to optimize — because there is no page until an agent asks for one. The merchant keeps their brand inside the agentic conversation. Today an agent shopping on a shopper's behalf strips the merchant to a title and a price in someone else's chat window. AMS streams a branded surface into that conversation instead. AMS declares 16 tools through navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool's description and enabled state is overridable per merchant via webmcpConfig , served at session creation — a merchant can rename, re-describe or switch off any tool without a deploy. Tool What the agent gets send_message States an intent in natural language. Hands it to the composing agent and returns its prose. The storefront recomposes as a side effect. show_collection Asks for a named collection or category; the agent resolves it and composes a product layout. get_products Two shapes. Called bare, a compact survey of the canvas — title, price, availability, image. Called with productIds , the full record: description, option axes, and every variant with its exact option values and buyability. get_layout The raw layout tree — component types, props, children. Also the only way to read what was featured , since a look card carries its own product list. get_messages Full conversation history, role-tagged. get_status Session state: isRunning , hasLayout , error, live streaming prose, latest committed reply. get_visitor_context Standing preferences the shopper has stated — size, fit, colour, budget — under the brand's own key names. set_visitor_context States a standing preference. It survives every later recomposition. open_product Navigates the canvas to a product detail view. add_to_cart Adds by product plus {axis: value} selections. Same signal a human card click fires — stamped origin: 'webmcp' . get_cart Every line with its chosen option values, quantity, price, the totals, and whether checkout is available. update_cart_item Sets a line's quantity. Absolute, not a delta. remove_from_cart Removes a line; without selections, every line of that product. begin_checkout Hands off to Shopify's hosted checkout with the current cart. send_signal Escape hatch: a low-level typed interaction signal for anything the typed tools miss. clear_session Resets layout, conversation and session data. Three decisions there are worth naming. Agent-backed tools return the site's own voice, not a status. send_message and show_collection hand the request to the merchant's AI and resolve with its finished text. The operator contract, served to the calling agent at runtime through window.webmcp.instructions , tells it to relay that verbatim: "You operate the tools; the site AI is the voice." The merchant's brand voice survives the round trip instead of being paraphrased by somebody else's model. A turn that outruns the await window returns status: "running" — the caller polls get_status and reads latestResponse . The contract is that the site's voice reaches the agent, not that it arrives within a fixed budget. The cart is addressed by selections, never by variant id. get_products deliberately returns no variant id: those ids are unstable across the optimistic-write window, so an id an external agent held across a turn could aim a write at a line that has already been replaced. Cart verbs take a product plus {axis: value} selections and bind late, against live state — a stale reference can only miss , and fail loudly. This replaced a first version where add_to_cart fell back to "first in-stock variant", so a shopper who asked for size 8 got whatever was in stock first. add_to_cart books itself as a third actor — not the agent, not the visitor, but origin: 'webmcp' . Folding a WebMCP-driven add into either of the others would lie about which surface earned it, and that is the number a merchant asks about first. For agents that do not speak WebMCP natively, appending ?webmcp=1 installs a real host plus a window.webmcp client, so a JS-eval-capable browser agent can call the identical surface. It never overrides a real host — if Chrome or a bridge extension already provided navigator.modelContext , the sim is a no-op. That same flag also makes the URL a self-contained demo: it renders what the page is, and a prompt to paste into an agent. No repo to clone and nothing to send alongside the link. How we built it The storefront is composed, not served. A tool call arrives carrying an intent, and one fixed two-call flow runs: Reasoning — a multi-round tool loop bounded by step count and wall clock. The model fires tool calls as a parallel batch, sees the results and may fire another batch to refine. No prose, no layout. Compose — one streamText call with tools omitted entirely and the reasoning step's tool history flattened to plain text. It streams a jsonl-elements fence that parses line by line into RFC 6902 patch operations against the layout spec. The tool-free compose call is structural, not stylistic. A single tool-bearing call that also composes cannot guarantee output: the model emits a phantom functionCall , finishes with finishReason='tool-calls' and the visitor gets a blank canvas. Strip the tool registry and a phantom call has nothing to execute — the model is forced to compose. It is the most important architectural line in the system. The model split is not the one you would guess. Both calls run Gemini 3.6 Flash by default. The performance split is structural — two calls plus per-step reasoning budgets — not cheap-planner and expensive-composer. Reasoning runs at a minimal thinking floor because a fuller budget measured 13–24s per turn against ~4.6s warm: tried, measured, rejected. Claude Haiku 4.5 and any OpenRouter id are selectable per merchant. The catalog is Shopify's, through Shopify's own MCP. Product search hits the Global Catalog MCP, per-store reads hit the Storefront MCP over JSON-RPC 2.0. Live products, live inventory, live pricing. AMS composes the experience; Shopify stays the system of record, so nothing is mirrored and nothing goes stale. Serving is three planes. Vercel runs the Next.js app that mounts the storefront engine, Railway runs the Hono agent API and Supabase runs Postgres, with Redis holding session state. Streaming is a per-session WebSocket carrying typed events — tool_call , response_text_delta , layout_patch_op , layout_ready , done — so the agent acts on patches while the rest of the surface is still arriving. Entity-id hydration cuts the token bill by roughly 80%. The model never writes product data. It writes entity ids, the catalog declares which props are resolved() and the client resolves them through a HydratorMap . Tokens go to judgment, not to transcribing a product feed. Turns survive a dropped connect

title: RelayBench
pitch: RelayBench lets an AI pause troubleshooting, ask a nearby human for one precise physical observation, and use that answer as evidence through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: RelayBench lets an AI pause troubleshooting, ask a nearby human for one precise physical observation, and use that answer as evidence through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Investigation: the agent narrows the case to Valve V2 and requests physical evidence. Human handoff: onboarding highlights the observation task and explains the user's next action. Reasoning: the user's answer becomes attributed evidence and updates agent confidence. Inspiration Agents are good at reading logs, telemetry, and API responses. Real troubleshooting rarely stays inside those boundaries. At some point, the useful next question is physical: Is the valve actually open? Is the warning light blinking? Does the pump sound normal? I built RelayBench around that handoff. The AI should not pretend it can see the equipment. It should ask the person who is already there for a small, concrete observation, then continue reasoning with that evidence. What it does RelayBench is a shared diagnostic workspace for an AI agent and a nearby human. The demo starts with a greenhouse irrigation fault. Digital telemetry shows that downstream flow has collapsed, and the agent ranks several possible causes. Through WebMCP, the agent reads the live case, focuses Valve V2, and requests a physical inspection. The request appears as a bounded human task with three answers: Open, Partially open, or Closed. The tool call waits while the technician checks the equipment. Once the person answers, RelayBench records the observation with its author and event type, resolves the pending call, and updates the agent's confidence. The result is a visible chain of evidence rather than a hidden chat exchange. A reviewer can see what the sensors reported, what the agent inferred, what the human observed, and how the diagnosis changed. How I built it The application uses Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, and plain CSS. A reactive case store owns the selected component, investigation phase, evidence timeline, hypotheses, and pending observation. The page registers four native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : get_case_state reads the current case and reasoning state. focus_component moves the shared interface to a specific component. request_human_observation creates a task in the page and returns a Promise that stays pending until the person answers. reset_case_demo restores the initial case without changing the user's onboarding preference. The most important implementation detail is the pending observation. It turns a person in the physical environment into a safe, structured source of evidence without giving the agent imaginary sensors or unrestricted control. The site is deployed on OpenAI Sites. WebMCP works as progressive enhancement, so the interface also supports a complete manual demo in browsers that do not expose the API. Challenges The hardest part was making an asynchronous human handoff feel like one continuous tool call. The interface has to show that the agent is waiting, accept exactly one valid response, resolve the right request, and handle cancellation cleanly. The second challenge was making the process understandable to someone seeing it for the first time. I added an attributed case timeline, explicit event types, component progress, agent-confidence changes, and a guided tour that runs once and can be replayed from the help button. Browser support is still experimental, so I kept WebMCP registration isolated and made the rest of the application work without it. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns the interaction and state that an agent needs. RelayBench does not bolt a generic tool layer onto a static page. The page itself knows which component is selected, which observation is pending, who answered it, and how the case changed. I also learned that a human-in-the-loop tool needs more than a confirmation dialog. The person needs context, constrained choices, and a visible record of what their answer changed. What's next The greenhouse case is a focused demo, but the interaction applies to field service, lab work, home repair, accessibility support, and incident response. The next step would be a case-authoring format so teams can define equipment, telemetry, observation prompts, and evidence rules without changing the application code. title: Inkling
pitch: A canvas an AI agent can actually see and draw on live, through WebMCP
about_excerpt: A canvas an AI agent can actually see and draw on live, through WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates fun doodle made by ai best diagrams with the help of ai ai as a fun partner for your daily notes Inspiration A canvas is the hardest thing to hand an agent. There's no form to fill in, no buttons to click, nothing textual to grab onto. Just position, size, spacing, and whether the result actually looks right. That's what made it interesting. If WebMCP could handle a drawing surface, where the agent has to measure its own work and fix what it gets wrong, it could handle most things. So I built one and gave the agent real eyes on it: not a screenshot, but the actual scene, with the ability to check its own overlaps, spacing, and alignment before calling it done. What it does Inkling is a hand-drawn canvas that an AI agent can see and draw on, live, on the same page you're looking at. The agent can: See the real canvas. It reads actual element positions and sizes, not a picture of them. Check its own work. Built-in measurements catch overlapping shapes, crossing arrows, and clipped labels, so it can spot its own mistakes. Draw properly. Shapes, arrows, colored pen strokes, real service icons, and images. Describe a system in plain English and it builds the diagram, laid out automatically. React to you. If you edit something, it notices and responds without being asked again. Read comments off the canvas. Select a region, pin a note to it like "add a WAF here," and the agent picks it up with the exact elements it's attached to. No re-explaining what "this" means. Be undone. Every agent change is logged, and you can jump back to the state before any one of them. Same tool for a scalable AWS architecture and for a weekend to-do list with a doodle next to the fun part. How I built it React and Next.js running on Cloudflare Workers, with D1 for saving canvases and R2 for uploaded images. The canvas is hand-rolled SVG with a rough, sketchy ink style. Used Chatgpt site to host the app. The WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Underneath sits a layered-graph layout engine and a small flowchart parser, which is what turns "a client hits a CDN, then a load balancer, then three app servers" into an actual arranged diagram in one call. Challenges I ran into There's no way for the page to notify the agent. WebMCP only goes one direction. So "react when the human edits something" had to be built as a journal the agent parks a call against, waiting to be woken. Same for comments. Tool descriptions are the entire UX. There's no system prompt in WebMCP, so the tool descriptions are the only place to shape behavior. My first attempt at telling the agent a personal canvas could be "looser" produced scattered, disconnected layouts. It read "loose" as "messy." I had to separate "loose in style" from "loose in layout" explicitly. fill="none" vs fill="transparent" . Visually identical. But one is clickable and one isn't, and it silently made every uploaded image impossible to drag. A CSS animation quietly broke a toolbar's position. A shared fade-in animation overrode the element's positioning transform for its entire lifetime, so it never anchored where the code said it did. I only found it by measuring the real rendered position against the math I expected. What I learned In WebMCP, the tool description is the product's personality. There's nowhere else to say "be precise here, playful there." Writing those turned out to be much closer to UX writing than API documentation. I also underestimated the primitives. Given explicit permission to take its time, the agent drew a full colored illustration out of nothing but freehand pen strokes. title: ShipASO
pitch: WebMCP tools for safe App Store Optimization: agents research, explain, draft, and stage proposals; people retain approval.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tools for safe App Store Optimization: agents research, explain, draft, and stage proposals; people retain approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for ShipASO Inspiration App Store Optimization is a high-leverage workflow with a sharp boundary: an agent can do the research and drafting, but a person should retain the approval decision. What it does ShipASO watches app listings, keywords, and competitors. When a change matters, it prepares a proposal: title, subtitle, keywords, and promotional text at their exact character limits. On a run page, WebMCP tools let an agent read the queue, explain why a proposal exists, draft an alternative that preserves the brand, and stage it for review. The agent never gets an approval, publish, ship, or push tool. Staging changes what a person will review; it leaves the run awaiting approval. How it uses WebMCP ShipASO declares 14 page-scoped WebMCP tools. The browser reads the live tool list after registration, so the interface distinguishes a declared manifest from tools the browser actually received. Read and draft tools are available where they make sense; run-specific tools appear only on a run detail page. The boundary is also enforced on the server. Approval requires a single-use challenge issued when a run is opened and consumed with the approval update. That prevents replay and makes bulk approval follow the same per-run protection. What we learned Tool descriptions are not a security boundary. WebMCP makes the page's intended contract legible to agents, but server-side enforcement is still required for consequential actions. We deliberately built both: helpful tools for analysis and drafting, and a separate human decision point. title: 0x1 Expedition Vault
pitch: A WebMCP learning roguelike where humans and browser agents share one branching expedition state.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP learning roguelike where humans and browser agents share one branching expedition state. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most learning apps expose a human UI and leave agents to scrape the DOM. We wanted the opposite: a learning world where the human and browser agent share one explicit game state and can genuinely take turns. What it does 0x1 Expedition Vault turns a topic, YouTube lecture, public article/PDF, pasted notes, or uploaded text into a branching learning roguelike. Learners study sources, answer quizzes, build causal chains, defend models in adversarial dialogue, choose risk/recovery branches, accumulate strikes, fail runs, recover, and defeat a final systems boss. The branching map is not cosmetic: unresolved splits expose multiple selectable paths. A route is marked taken only after the learner or agent commits to it; same-row alternatives become skipped for that run, matching the source expedition semantics. Why WebMCP The page registers four tools directly on document.modelContext : ingest_learning_material explore_module submit_solution inspect_progress The key point is that these tools do not maintain an agent-only copy of the course. Human clicks and agent tool calls mutate the same expedition graph, active room, checkpoint, belief trajectory, strikes, branch choices, mastery, and failure state. An agent can forge a course, inspect progress, choose a branch, submit a solution, fail the same run, or advance the same map the learner sees. Better together A human can watch a source video and clear a checkpoint; the agent can then inspect the resulting state and continue from the newly available branch. Or the agent can ingest a new topic and generate an expedition that appears immediately in the learner UI. WebMCP removes the brittle layer of DOM guessing and makes the collaboration explicit, structured, and inspectable. Cognition, not keyword recall Generated expeditions separate source study from hidden cognition checks. Later rooms test causal transfer, source-vs-inference separation, falsification, adversarial prediction, and integrative defense. Hidden checks conceal their rubric and discount terms already present in the prompt. Human and WebMCP text answers use the same semantic evaluator; verbose nonsense cannot clear a checkpoint. How we built it The app uses SvelteKit/Svelte 5, Vite, native document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , a deterministic source-grounded curriculum generator, serverless-native PDF extraction, opportunistic YouTube transcript extraction with source-honest metadata fallback, and persistent browser-local expedition state. The map runtime ports the original expedition engine's seeded node/edge geometry and explicit path-choice semantics. Reliability The deployed build was tested end-to-end on Vercel: source ingestion, branching path selection in both directions, three-strike run failure, restart, staged Back-EMF causal chain, Lenz adversarial dialogue, five-variable boss system model, WebMCP failure parity, and visible progression all pass. title: Apptome
pitch: Zero-configuration, secure interoperability across web apps—entirely in your browser, powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Zero-configuration, secure interoperability across web apps—entirely in your browser, powered by WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 The open web is incredibly powerful, but deeply siloed. Today, if you want your CRM to talk to your invoicing tool, you have to rely on third-party automation servers, manage complex webhooks, and hand over highly sensitive, long-lived API keys. I was inspired by the WebMCP draft specification because it flips this model upside down. I wanted to explore a future where integration happens securely on the client side —where humans and AI agents can collaborate directly in the browser to move data between apps safely, transparently, and without ever exposing a backend API key. 

 What it does 

 Apptome (via the Connectome Hub) is a zero-configuration, secure interoperability layer for the we. It automatically discovers WebMCP capabilities exposed by your open we apps and unifies them into a personal graph. 

 When you want to execute a workflow—like taking a client from your CRM and generating a bill in your Invoicing app—you initiate it in our sidebar. Our Cloudflare Workers AI agent kicks in to semantically map the data from the source app to the destination app's required JSON schema on the fly. Finally, it presents you with the exact payload for human-in-the-loop confirmation. The agent does the heavy lifting, but the human remains in total control. 

 How I built it 

 Our architecture is split into three main layers: 

 
 The Spoke Apps: I built sample single-page applications that natively expose their local functionality using document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 The Bridge: A lightIight client-side script that monitors toolchange events and securely relays the available WebMCP capabilities to our central Hub via WebSockets. 
 The Hub & AI Mapper: Deployed entirely on Cloudflare Workers , the Hub maintains the user's persistent tool graph. I use Cloudflare Workers AI ( @cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast ) to perform the semantic mapping between differing tool schemas. The user interface is a secure, cross-origin iframe (the "Surface") injected over the host app. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Browser security is notoriously unforgiving! Because I am committed to maintaining the web's Same-Origin Policy (SOP) without bypassing it, managing cross-origin iframes, strict Content-Security-Policies (CSP), and secure weSocket transports was a massive challenge. I also ran into real-world anti-tracking hurdles (like Brave browser's Shields aggressively blocking our Cloudflare Turnstile human-verification checks) which forced us to deeply understand third-party iframe behaviors. Finally, tuning the LLM to output deterministic, strictly-typed JSON schemas without hallucinating required careful prompt engineering. 

 Accomplishments 

 It is gratifying to have demonstrated true N-to-N interoperability entirely on the client side. The "magic" moment of watching the AI seamlessly map fields from one app's schema to another app's schema—without requiring the user to manually drag-and-drop fields—is something I're very proud of. Furthermore, I built a highly secure architecture that enforces human consent for every action, proving that AI agents can be both immensely powerful and completely safe. 

 What I learned 

 I gained a deep understanding of the WebMCP draft specification and the paradigms of client-side tool discovery. I also leveled up our skills in edge computing with Cloudflare Workers, handling WebSockets at the edge, and seamlessly integrating serverless AI models into real-time we applications. Most importantly, I learned that the future of agentic we workflows depends on strict, transparent security boundaries. 

 What's next for Apptome 

 Our immediate next step is expanding our prototype from "stub" apps to real-world SaaS products. I plan to build a browser extension that can act as the WebMCP bridge, bringing Apptome's capabilities to legacy we apps that don't yet support WebMCP natively. I also want to explore integrating local, on-device SLMs (Small Language Models) so the semantic mapping can happen entirely locally for ultimate privacy.

title: Concierge
pitch: ChatGPT makes the inquiry call you do not want to make while the webpage keeps you in control.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT makes the inquiry call you do not want to make while the webpage keeps you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Concierge Concierge The web has APIs. Most businesses still have phone numbers. Concierge lets ChatGPT prepare an inquiry call, while the webpage keeps the consequential action with the person. Why we built it A surprising amount of ordinary life still requires a phone call: asking a hotel about late arrival, checking accessibility, clarifying a bill, confirming a delivery window, or speaking to a business in another language. A chat assistant can write a script, but the person still has to place the call, take notes, and translate the answer. Giving an agent unlimited authority would be worse. A call can create a booking, accept a fee, change a reservation, or commit the user to terms. We wanted the useful part of delegation without hiding those actions. What Concierge does The user describes the inquiry in ChatGPT. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT creates or revises a structured call plan on the signed-in Concierge page. The page shows the destination, exact questions, shareable context, call language, authority limits, price ceiling, and revision. Then the workflow stops. Only the person can press Confirm one call . Confirmation is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool list. After confirmation, the voice worker places one disclosed information-only call. It cannot book, pay, cancel, accept a fee, accept terms, or make a commitment. The result records each requested question as answered, uncertain, or unanswered, with a short evidence excerpt. It also returns duration, cost state, disclosure state, terminal reason, and a one-attempt receipt. ChatGPT can read that result through WebMCP and explain it in the conversation where the request started. The user never sees Twilio settings, calling-country permissions, provider credentials, or API keys. Concierge owns that infrastructure. Every call still needs a fresh quote and a visible confirmation. Why WebMCP is the point Without WebMCP, ChatGPT can suggest a call plan but cannot safely manipulate the authenticated task the user is reviewing. With WebMCP, the chat and the page share the same revisioned object: ChatGPT creates, updates, reads, and monitors the task. The webpage shows the exact plan and owns confirmation. Convex enforces identity, revisions, idempotency, credits, and one-attempt dispatch. The Cloudflare worker handles temporary live audio. Twilio connects the call to OpenAI Realtime. This is not a chatbot pasted next to a form. WebMCP is what lets the agent do the preparation and retrieval work while the page preserves the trust boundary. A repeatable judge demo Calling a real hotel for every judge would be rude and hard to debug. We built Aurora Demo Hotel, a clearly fictional automated recipient reached through the real phone network. Judges can write their own information-only questions. The recipient answers from a versioned server-owned fact sheet, says when it does not know, and cannot book or take payment. The same inquiry contract also accepts arbitrary real services and destinations. The hotel is a controlled test path, not the product boundary. How we built it The browser app is React and TypeScript. It registers six page tools with document.modelContext: create a general draft, create a controlled demo draft, update a draft, read a draft, read status, and read the result. Convex owns the task state machine. Confirmation is bound to the exact execution revision; any material edit invalidates it. Provider uncertainty never creates an automatic retry. Signed worker events become a deterministic public activity log and result. The phone worker runs on Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects. Twilio Media Streams carry bidirectional PCMU audio to OpenAI Realtime gpt-realtime-2.1-mini. Audio is not stored. A separate extraction step turns bounded call evidence into candidate facts; the model cannot publish its own receipt or grant itself more authority. Authentication supports Continue with ChatGPT and WorkOS AuthKit. The ChatGPT bridge exchanges identity for a short-lived, audience-bound Convex token. What was hard The difficult work was not dialing a number. It was keeping authority exact across several asynchronous systems. We tested stale confirmations, duplicate dispatches, interrupted disclosure, repeated questions, corrections, barge-in, provider uncertainty, signed callbacks, expired quotes, and failed calls. The public UI reports failure as failure; it does not polish an incomplete call into a successful result. Concierge started before the challenge as a mobile call-avoidance prototype. During the submission period we rebuilt the product around the web and WebMCP: authenticated page tools, the general inquiry contract, exact-revision confirmation, evidence-linked results, ChatGPT sign-in, the controlled recipient, responsive judge onboarding, and production release gates. Those changes are separated in the public repository history and documentation. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, choose Continue with ChatGPT , and ask: Use the controlled Aurora Demo Hotel. Ask whether I can arrive after midnight, when breakfast is served, and whether on-site parking is available. Do not book anything or accept a fee. Review the plan on the page. Nothing happens until you confirm one exact call. title: WellAuth - Prior Authorization for Agents
pitch: WellAuth is prior authorization for the agent era: AI can gather evidence and move the case forward, but FHIR stays read-only and submission does not exist until a human approves it.
about_excerpt: WellAuth is prior authorization for the agent era: AI can gather evidence and move the case forward, but FHIR stays read-only and submission does not exist until a human approves it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI is splitting into two models: headless agents that work through APIs, and app-specific copilots built separately into every interface. WebMCP suggests a third model — a user can bring the same agent across applications, while each application still controls the capabilities it exposes. I wanted to pressure-test that model somewhere the constraints actually matter. Healthcare was an obvious choice: clinical truth has authoritative sources, disclosure is sensitive, protocols are well established, and human responsibility cannot simply be delegated to a model. Prior authorization brings all of those tensions together in one workflow. The clinical decision has already been made, but moving care forward still requires evidence from the record, payer-specific requirements, bounded disclosure, human approval, and coordination with an external payer. WellAuth grew out of one question: can cross-application AI remove that friction without collapsing the boundaries healthcare depends on? What it does WellAuth uses WebMCP to let a browser agent work through a prior-authorization case while the application controls what actions are available at each stage. 1. Find the evidence without inventing it Structured clinical data satisfies four of five payer requirements. The fifth cannot initially be proven, so WellAuth leaves it unresolved rather than turning a retrieval failure into a clinical fact. GPT Work can then use another authorized evidence path, find the missing support in an existing cardiology note, and bind that exact evidence to the exact payer requirement. 2. Complete does not mean allowed to send Once all requirements are satisfied, WellAuth prepares a purpose-limited packet containing only the evidence needed for the authorization. Submission still is not available. A workforce user must approve the exact prepared packet before the WebMCP submission capability appears. 3. Let new external state change what the agent can do The simulated payer approves the authorization through September 12, but the MRI is scheduled for September 18. The authorization succeeded. The care still isn’t administratively ready. Only then does WellAuth expose a remediation capability. The agent prepares an administrative extension without changing the ordered service, clinical evidence, or clinical intent, stops for a second human approval, and then submits the approved remediation. The simulated payer extends the window through October 3, covering the scheduled date. How WebMCP powers WellAuth Point WebMCP role Product consequence Structured tools across the prior-auth lifecycle WellAuth exposes actions such as discovering requirements, finding evidence, preparing a packet, submitting, checking status, and resolving an authorization window as structured tools—not as DOM clicks tied to one screen. GPT Work can reason across the whole job , including actions that would otherwise live on different views or at different moments in the UI, without being scripted through a fixed click path. Tool access follows workflow state and human approval WellAuth dynamically registers and removes tools as the case changes. In particular, payer-submission tools are absent until the application records approval of the exact packet. Human approval changes what the agent can actually do. Submission is not merely hidden behind a warning or prompt instruction; the tool is unavailable until approval exists . The application publishes the capability contract WellAuth defines the tool names, schemas, allowed lifecycle, and backend validation; GPT Work discovers and chooses among those capabilities from natural-language intent. The intelligence can come from outside the healthcare application while WellAuth keeps control of its workflow vocabulary and boundaries —the pattern that makes a user-selected agent viable across WebMCP-enabled applications. Fit into regulated workflows without adding a new trust problem WellAuth keeps FHIR as the authoritative clinical-data path and uses WebMCP for bounded agent actions around that existing stack. In regulated industries, productivity gains are not worth it if adopting an agent creates a new compliance or control surface. This pattern lets WebMCP work with established protocols and boundaries instead of asking teams to weaken them. How we built it WellAuth is built as a bounded prior-authorization pipeline where each layer owns a different kind of truth or responsibility. 1. Read the clinical record WellAuth reads FHIR R4 data from Google Cloud Healthcare API to locate evidence already present in the chart. That path is read-only, so the agent can search farther but cannot create or alter clinical facts. 2. Build and govern the case A Cloud Run provider service maintains the authoritative authorization state: payer requirements, evidence bindings, packet revisions, approvals, submission status, and remediation. Exact evidence is attached to exact requirements, and every mutation is validated against the current workflow revision. 3. Expose the right agent actions That workflow state drives the WebMCP capability surface . GPT Work discovers 11 structured tools and can chain them from natural-language intent, but the available set changes as the case progresses. Preparation can appear after evidence is complete; submission remains absent until human approval; remediation appears only after the payer creates a new mismatch. 4. Cross the payer boundary Human approval is recorded separately from transmission and bound to the exact packet being reviewed. Only then can WellAuth send to the separate simulated payer. The payer’s response is not treated as a frontend success flag—it becomes external state that can reopen the workflow. The result is a simple architecture rule: FHIR owns clinical truth, WellAuth owns workflow state, WebMCP exposes current agent capability, and humans retain the consequential decisions. Challenges we ran into Making WebMCP behavior predictable — Dynamic registration, withdrawal, and invocation had to be validated in native Chrome. We built a browser acceptance harness and treated tool lifecycle as runtime state. Fitting agents into healthcare’s existing trust model — FHIR needed to remain the clinical source of truth. We used Google Cloud Healthcare API for read-only FHIR access and kept prior-authorization workflow state separately authoritative. Making “not available yet” real — Submission tools had to stay unavailable until human approval. We synchronized browser capabilities, workflow revisions, and backend validation so tool access reflects the case’s current state. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Making dynamic WebMCP part of the product — WellAuth changes which tools are exposed as the case progresses, and we validated that behavior in GPT Work and native Chrome. Completing a full prior-authorization loop — The workflow goes from evidence discovery through human-reviewed submission, payer response, authorization-window mismatch, and remediation. Keeping regulated-data boundaries intact — FHIR clinical data, workflow state, human review, and payer interaction remain separate while the agent still gets meaningful work done. What we learned Learning prior authorization from scratch — I had never worked in prior auth before. Building WellAuth taught me how much of the difficulty comes from evidence, payer requirements, timing, and administrative coordination rather than the clinical decision itself. Learning a new protocol and a new agent surface — WebMCP was new to me, and so was GPT Work . Using both together changed my understanding of what it means for an application to expose capabilities to an agent rather than build its own embedded copilot. A new UX lens for agentic products — I started thinking less about “what buttons should the user click?” and more about what capabilities should exist at this moment, what should disappear, and when the human needs to take over. What’s next Connect to real payer workflows — Replace the simulated payer with production-grade integrations and validate the same boundaries against real prior-authorization endpoints and operational constraints. Expand beyond one authorization scenario — Support more services, payer requirement sets, evidence patterns, and remediation paths without turning the workflow into a generic healthcare copilot. Test the WebMCP interaction model across more regulated workflows — Apply the same pattern to other healthcare and regulated processes where agents need useful freedom while applications keep control of data, workflow state, and human review. Entirely synthetic demo data. Designed around HIPAA-regulated workflow boundaries; no claim of HIPAA compliance. Built With cloud-run fhir-r4 google-cloud google-cloud-healthcare-

title: Draft Room
pitch: Build one fantasy XI with an agent that compares futures, applies plans atomically, and respects your brief.
about_excerpt: Build one fantasy XI with an agent that compares futures, applies plans atomically, and respects your brief. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Draft Room cover Inspiration I have always been a big football and Fantasy Premier League fan, this is one of those challenge where I can have my agents play this with me seamlessly What it does A fantasy football squad builder that is better with an agent in it: fourteen WebMCP tools, six of them with no button, for scenarios, formations, deterministic probability, and atomic plans. How we built it Next.js 15 (static export), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, Zustand, zod, Three.js WebGPU renderer via React Three Fiber, webmcp-types, Vitest. Fonts: Big Shoulders, Sofia Sans, Doto.  Inspiration 

 The Mind Archetype was inspired by a simple question: what if a psychology website could be designed not only for people, but also for the AI agents helping them? 

 In mental health, the journey often starts long before someone books an appointment. People may first want to understand what they are experiencing, explore possible areas of support, learn how therapy works, or simply figure out where to start. 

 Traditional websites provide this information through pages, menus, and buttons designed for human navigation. But as AI agents increasingly become an interface for discovering and interacting with services, I saw an opportunity to make that experience more direct. 

 As a psychologist and the founder of The Mind Archetype, I wanted to explore how WebMCP could bring agent-native interaction into a real psychology service while keeping professional care and human decision-making at the center. 

 What it does 

 The Mind Archetype is an agent-native psychology website that allows compatible AI agents to discover and interact with structured capabilities exposed directly by the website. 

 The application currently provides 12 WebMCP tools covering: 

 
 Mental health information 
 Care-area discovery 
 Service information 
 Consultation guidance 
 Resource discovery 
 Organization information 
 Contact options 
 Consultation preparation 
 Appointment booking 
 

 For example, get_mind_archetype_profile allows an agent to discover structured information about the organization, while book_appointment provides a dedicated capability for starting the appointment process. 

 This means an agent does not have to rely exclusively on interpreting the visual interface and guessing where to click. 

 At the same time, the human remains in control. The system is designed to help people navigate information and access professional support, not to replace a psychologist or make clinical diagnoses. 

 How we built it 

 The project was built as a real, deployed web experience using: 

 
 HTML 
 CSS 
 JavaScript 
 WebMCP 
 Netlify 
 Google Calendar for appointment scheduling 
 

 Rather than creating a separate prototype, I extended the existing The Mind Archetype website with a WebMCP layer. 

 The WebMCP implementation exposes tools through document.modelContext , allowing compatible agents to discover the capabilities available on the page. 

 I tested the deployed implementation directly in Chrome with WebMCP enabled and verified that all 12 tools could be discovered through: 
 ( await document . modelContext . getTools ( ) ) . map ( t = > t . name ) 
 
 The appointment capability is connected to a real Google Calendar scheduling experience, so the agent-assisted flow can ultimately lead to an actual human-selected appointment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was working with a new and evolving web capability while keeping the existing website stable. 

 I had to understand how WebMCP exposes tools through the browser, how those tools are discovered, and how to define capabilities that are meaningful from an agent's perspective. 

 Another challenge was balancing the agent experience with the existing human experience. I did not want to rebuild the website around AI or remove the visual interface people already understand. 

 Instead, I treated WebMCP as an additional interaction layer. 

 Testing was also an important part of the process. I had to verify the implementation directly in the browser, troubleshoot differences between the WebMCP tool representation and traditional JavaScript APIs, and make sure the appointment flow connected to a real scheduling experience. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is that this is not just a concept or mockup. The Mind Archetype is a live psychology website with a working WebMCP implementation. 

 I am particularly proud of: 

 
 Successfully exposing 12 distinct WebMCP tools. 
 Integrating WebMCP into an existing production-style website without replacing its human interface. 
 Connecting the appointment capability to a real Google Calendar scheduling flow. 
 Creating tools around meaningful psychological-service tasks rather than adding AI functionality for its own sake. 
 Keeping human control at the center of the experience. 
 Making the complete project publicly available with its source code and documentation. 
 

 For me, the most important achievement is demonstrating that WebMCP can be applied to a real-world professional service where trust, clarity, and human oversight matter. 

 What we learned 

 This project changed how I think about websites. 

 Previously, I primarily thought of a website as an interface between a person and a service. Building with WebMCP made me think of it as an interface between people, services, and agents . 

 I learned that making a website agent-friendly is not simply about adding AI. It is about identifying meaningful actions and exposing them as clear, structured capabilities. 

 I also learned that giving an agent more capabilities does not necessarily mean giving it more control. 

 In a sensitive field like psychology, the better approach can be to let an agent help someone understand options, find information, prepare an action, or begin a process, while leaving important decisions to the human. 

 What's next for The Mind Archetype 

 The current implementation is a foundation for a larger agent-native psychology platform. 

 Next, I want to expand the capabilities around psychological education, resource discovery, consultation preparation, corporate mental health services, and access to professional support. 

 I also want to explore richer agent-assisted experiences where a person can describe what they need conversationally and the agent can help them navigate the appropriate information and services exposed by The Mind Archetype. 

 The long-term vision is not to automate the psychologist. 

 It is to make the path from a person's first question to appropriate human support simpler, more accessible, and more intelligent. 

 The Mind Archetype is an exploration of what psychology on an agent-native web could look like.

title: BranchLine
pitch: BRANCHLINE lets humans and browser agents share the same live supply-chain reality—fork recovery futures, simulate their consequences, and commit only the plan a human explicitly approves.
about_excerpt: BRANCHLINE lets humans and browser agents share the same live supply-chain reality—fork recovery futures, simulate their consequences, and commit only the plan a human explicitly approves. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Supply-chain disruptions are rarely isolated events. A supplier outage can cascade through component availability, transport lanes, factory capacity, production schedules, customer commitments, revenue, and cost. Operations teams often have to reconstruct this chain manually across ERP systems, spreadsheets, supplier messages, logistics tools, and planning software before they can even decide what to do. At the same time, browser agents are becoming capable of operating websites, but most applications still expose their operational meaning only through buttons, forms, and DOM elements. We built BRANCHLINE around a different idea: What if a human and a browser agent could operate inside the same live operational reality? BRANCHLINE — Fork reality. Simulate the consequences. Commit the future. It is an agent-native operational recovery control plane where humans steer intent, agents traverse consequences, and both operate on one shared supply-chain digital twin. What it does BRANCHLINE models a synthetic commercial EV supply chain for Asterion Mobility , including suppliers, components, factories, transport lanes, inventory, products, customers, and 24 customer orders. The featured scenario begins with a healthy network. A human triggers a 12-day production outage at the battery supplier NoriCell . Instead of simply displaying an alert, BRANCHLINE calculates and visualizes the complete causal cascade: supplier → component availability → factories → products → customer orders → exposed revenue The browser agent can then use semantic WebMCP tools to: inspect the operational state; trace downstream consequences; inspect suppliers, factories, products, customers, and orders; find compatible substitute suppliers; create multiple recovery branches; simulate each future across a 30-day horizon; compare service, cost, risk, emissions, and delays; explain tradeoffs using causal evidence; stage a recovery plan for human approval; apply only an explicitly approved plan; verify the committed result; restore the previous operational checkpoint. The central experience is Branchspace . Instead of presenting three AI recommendations as ordinary cards, BRANCHLINE renders different recovery strategies as parallel futures emerging from the same present. For example: Service First prioritizes customer service and on-time revenue. Cost Guard prioritizes lower incremental cost. Balanced Recovery trades off service, cost, resilience, and logistics. Resilience reduces supplier concentration and future single points of failure. The simulation is deterministic and calculated from the underlying supply, compatibility, capacity, logistics, inventory, and customer-order data. How we built it BRANCHLINE is a static TypeScript web application built around one architectural principle: Human UI ─┐ ├─ shared command bus → domain engine → one live state WebMCP ───┘ The visual interface and WebMCP tools do not maintain separate copies of reality. Every meaningful operation passes through the same domain engine and shared state. The application includes: a deterministic synthetic supply-chain digital twin; causal impact tracing; a bounded recovery-planning engine; a day-by-day simulation from T+0 through T+30; supplier and product compatibility enforcement; inventory and factory-capacity constraints; customer-tier and human-authored priority constraints; transactional execution; verification; checkpoints and exact rollback; an append-only causal audit trail. The WebMCP integration uses the native imperative API directly with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) BRANCHLINE exposes 14 semantic tools: get_ops_snapshot inspect_entity trace_impact list_constraints find_substitutes read_external_alerts create_branch simulate_branch compare_branches explain_tradeoff stage_plan apply_plan verify_plan rollback_plan The capability surface is dynamic. For example, apply_plan is not registered at all while a recovery plan is waiting for human approval. When the human approves the exact staged plan in the BRANCHLINE interface, apply_plan becomes available to the browser agent. If the operational context changes, the approval becomes stale and the capability is revoked again. Challenges we ran into Keeping the human and agent in one reality The most important technical challenge was preventing the application from becoming a dashboard with a separate agent workflow. Human interactions and WebMCP calls therefore use the same command bus and domain functions. If a human changes something visually, the next agent call immediately encounters the changed state. Making stale reasoning visible and enforceable A recovery simulation can become invalid the moment a constraint changes. BRANCHLINE maintains separate stateVersion and contextVersion values. Every simulation records the context on which it was produced. When the human changes operational intent: the context version increments; existing simulations become visibly stale; staged plans are invalidated; previous approval is revoked; execution capabilities disappear; the agent must re-simulate. Human authority over consequential actions We deliberately did not create an approve_plan WebMCP tool. Approval must happen in the visual interface. Only after that approval does the consequential apply_plan capability become registered. Modeling real compatibility constraints Substitution cannot simply mean choosing the cheapest available supplier. For example, Voltra V-2170 battery cells are incompatible with ORION-X. That restriction is enforced inside the domain engine and simulation rather than merely displayed as UI text. Building meaningful simulation rather than prewritten outcomes Recovery metrics are derived from the underlying operational state. The planner evaluates supplier allocation, logistics, inventory movement, production scheduling, compatible substitutions, and eligible order delays before choosing a deterministic result for each strategy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The interaction we are most proud of involves order_1082 for Apex Health Logistics . Before human intervention, an otherwise attractive recovery future can delay this order. The human opens the order directly in the visual application and presses: Protect this order A gold human-intent pin appears on the order and propagates upstream through its dependencies. That single human action: changes the shared operational context; invalidates every simulation based on the previous reality; removes stale execution capabilities; becomes immediately visible to the browser agent. The agent then re-simulates the recovery using the new constraint. Scarce compatible supply is reallocated to protect Apex Health, while a lower-priority order takes the delay instead. This is not a hardcoded visual effect. It emerges from the planner and shared constraints. In our verified featured recovery, BRANCHLINE produces approximately: $26.56M revenue protected 93.4% of exposed revenue recovered $258,849 incremental cost 23 of 24 orders on time 1 lower-priority delayed order 0 hard compatibility violations 1 explicit human approval 1 rollback checkpoint We are also proud that every WebMCP action has a corresponding visual response. Agents do not disappear into an invisible automation layer—their semantic investigation is visible in the operational world. What we learned WebMCP becomes much more interesting when tools are treated as part of application state rather than as a static API catalog. BRANCHLINE demonstrates that the application can expose only the actions that make sense right now . The project also reinforced an important principle for human-agent systems: Human intent should not have to travel through chat to matter. A planner can simply change something in the interface. The application can make that change part of the same structured context the agent uses on its next call. We also learned that simulation results become significantly easier to trust when their causal evidence, assumptions, actions, and counterfactuals remain inspectable after the recommendation is produced. That led to Causal Proof , which explains decisions from simulation evidence rather than from an embedded LLM. What's next for BranchLine BRANCHLINE currently uses a completely synthetic operational twin so the entire workflow is deterministic, safe, and reproducible. A future production version could connect the same architecture to authenticated: ERP systems; warehouse-management systems; transport-management systems; supplier portals; manufacturing execution systems; procurement systems; demand and inventory planning platforms. The domain engine could also evolve toward richer optimization methods, probabilistic disruption modeling, supplier negotiation workflows, and

title: MotionArena
pitch: A WebMCP RL environment for testing whether AI can improve physics simulators through cheap, repeated simulation instead of relying on static benchmarks or costly real-world trials.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP RL environment for testing whether AI can improve physics simulators through cheap, repeated simulation instead of relying on static benchmarks or costly real-world trials. Like Comment Story Updates 2 human motion examples - one happening due to RL env agentic training of nerural surrogate in rollouts while other is the ground truth. Inspiration AI benchmarks are approaching a ceiling. Most are static: a model receives a problem, produces an answer, and gets a score. That works until models begin saturating the task distribution. At that point, another fixed set of harder questions only moves the ceiling temporarily. Real scientific discovery does not look like a standardized test. The hard part is often not solving a narrowly posed problem with a known answer, but searching an enormous space of trajectories, designs, hypotheses, and even frameworks i.e deciding which experiment to run next, which question to ask, and which assumption to discard. Systems like AlphaGo showed the power of pairing an enormous search space with a cheap, unambiguous verifier. Other breakthroughs such as AlphaFold similarly benefited from unusually strong computational supervision and dense ground truth. We wanted to ask what an equivalent substrate could look like for computational science. MotionArena is our small working answer: replace narrow static benchmarks with dynamic simulation environments that offer large continuous search spaces, cheap verification, and a much steeper hill for increasingly capable agents to climb. Physics and physical simulation are especially attractive substrates because their environments can also evolve toward progressively higher fidelity - spatially, temporally, and physically - rather than remaining a fixed collection of questions. What MotionArena does TL;DR: MotionArena frames human-motion reconstruction as a continuous search problem. The environment withholds a ground-truth physical trajectory. The agent receives a natural-language prior and must reconstruct the hidden motion using a learned motion model. It can run repeated rollouts, inspect aggregate feedback, refine specific temporal spans, and iteratively improve its best candidate. The browser makes that process visible in real time: the left avatar shows the agent's mutable reconstruction, while the right shows the immutable reference for the human spectator. Instead of revealing the correct answer, the environment returns deterministic reward based on physical trajectory agreement — including pose alignment, root motion, velocity, and contact behavior. The paradigm shifts from: question → answer → score to: observe → propose → simulate → verify → improve Why WebMCP matters WebMCP turns the browser from a visualization into an agent-operable research environment. Without WebMCP, an agent has to reverse-engineer buttons, sliders, canvases, and DOM state. MotionArena instead exposes the meaningful actions of the environment directly: inspect_episode run_rollout inspect_reward refine_span submit_best These tools operate on the exact same state rendered in the browser. When the agent launches a rollout, the motion on screen changes. When its score improves, the rollout history changes. The browser becomes both the laboratory and the observable audit trail of the search. This is the WebMCP capability we find most exciting: websites can expose not merely UI controls, but the action space of an environment . Why human motion? Open-ended motion generation normally has no unique ground truth. If two people are told to "climb upward," many different motions may be valid. So we changed the problem. MotionArena uses withheld trajectory reconstruction . The environment starts from a captured human motion and hides part of it. The agent therefore faces a huge space of possible reconstructions, while the environment retains an objective reference trajectory. Generation is hard. Verification is cheap. Once a candidate exists, comparing it against the withheld trajectory is inexpensive and deterministic. That gives us the structure we were looking for: large search space + learned world model + cheap verifier. How we built it We use MoMask as the learned human-motion prior. It generates candidate trajectories represented as BVH motion, which we retarget onto matching VRM characters for visualization. Three.js renders two synchronized avatars: the mutable reconstruction and the immutable reference. Both use the same character, camera, timing, and environment so differences in motion are immediately visible. The scientific reward is calculated in canonical motion space rather than from the rendered avatar. This matters because BVH-to-VRM retargeting can introduce visual differences that should not affect the underlying score. A shared environment state connects the renderer, verifier, rollout history, and WebMCP tools. Frontier agents can repeatedly search the MoMask inference space, while smaller browser-local policies can optimize residual motion corrections directly. The problem we are really exploring MotionArena is not primarily about producing one better animation. It is a prototype for a different way of measuring model capability. A capable scientific agent should increasingly be able to: choose useful experiments, search large continuous or combinatorial spaces, learn from failed attempts, allocate expensive computation intelligently, discover weaknesses in its current world model, and improve solutions under objective feedback. Static benchmarks mostly measure the terminal answer. Dynamic environments can measure the trajectory of improvement . They can also become harder without being replaced: hide longer intervals, introduce unfamiliar motions, reduce rollout budgets, perturb initial conditions, increase spatial or temporal fidelity, or adversarially select episodes where the current agent performs poorly. The benchmark becomes a moving frontier instead of a fixed question bank. Why this matters economically The same architecture appears across bottlenecked scientific and engineering industries. A high-fidelity simulation may take minutes, GPU-hours, or much more compute, while a learned surrogate can evaluate candidate states far more cheaply. A capable agent can search inside the surrogate, identify promising or suspicious regions, spend expensive simulation only where it is most informative, and use those results to improve the next search. The economically meaningful capability metric becomes something like: verified improvement per expensive experiment. In robotics, that can mean fewer physical robot trials. In aerospace, fewer high-fidelity CFD evaluations. In materials, fewer expensive quantum calculations. In thermal engineering, fewer full simulation runs. Eventually, in experimental science, fewer wet-lab experiments required to reach a verified result. MotionArena demonstrates the smallest visible version of this architecture: the model proposes a physical trajectory, the hidden environment judges it, and the agent gets another chance. Challenges and what we learned The hardest problem was designing the verifier. Our first instinct was to evaluate free-form text-to-motion generation, but natural-language instructions do not define a unique correct trajectory. That would make reward partly subjective. Reframing the task as hidden trajectory reconstruction gave us objective ground truth while preserving an enormous search space. We also had to separate what the human can see from what the agent is allowed to know . The spectator can compare both animated characters, while the agent receives only the instruction, environment state, and aggregate verifier feedback. Finally, we separated visualization from evaluation. VRM retargeting makes the search understandable to humans; the underlying trajectory representation determines the score. That distinction — between a human-readable world and a machine-verifiable one — became one of the most important ideas in the project. Where we want to take it MotionArena is a small example of a larger idea: scientific dry labs for agents . Instead of giving increasingly capable models another frozen collection of questions, we want environments where they can continuously search, simulate, fail, recover, and improve against computational laws that provide objective feedback. Physics simulation is particularly powerful here because the environment itself can scale with the model: more dimensions, finer spatial resolution, longer temporal horizons, more coupled physics, and stricter verification. WebMCP provides a natural interface for these environments because the browser can simultaneously be the visual world for a person and the structured action space for an agent. Our Vision Playbook for building science benchmarks now needs to be redefined. Astra is a phenomenal model but with its release containerized, static computational workflow benchmarks will hit a definite wall. But, until these models have the ca

 Inspiration 

 I set up OpenClaw to help with marketing and watched it fail at the last step: actually posting. Cloud browsers get blocked. Official APIs are expensive, limited, and missing things like Facebook member groups. So I built Claw Post at clawpost.net: the agent writes, your already-logged-in desktop Chrome publishes. 

 What it does 

 Claw Post is posting infrastructure for AI agents. A paired Chrome extension publishes from the browser session where you are already logged into X, LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Reddit. No social passwords in the agent. No headless VPS.
Claw Post is not a spray tool. There is a strict built-in delay between actions. The agent asks, the human’s already-logged-in Chrome publishes, then we wait. That is the product. 

 This submission is a thin public page that exposes those actions as WebMCP tools (clawpost_create_post, clawpost_reddit_comment, clawpost_status, clawpost_job_status) so ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled can call them on the page. 

 How we built it 

 The product is a Chrome extension plus a REST/MCP API. I built it with Cursor and Codex.
For this challenge we added a public static demo (MIT) that registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. The tools call the public Claw Post API with a key the human pastes in the page (localStorage only). If the extension is not paired, judges still see the tools work and get an honest EXTENSION_NOT_PAIRED. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Media was painful. We upload to short-lived storage, then the extension attaches the file in the real composer. 

 WebMCP only exists in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with the testing flag. The demo has to explain that or it looks broken. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A working loop: agent to API to desktop Chrome to a live postUrl. Community interest, a few paying users, and so far no account bans from posting this way. 

 What we learned 

 Build the thing you actually need. Other people probably need it too.
We are in a weird spot: people are handing more work to agents, and social platforms still treat that as malicious. Official APIs are limited. Cloud browsers get blocked. The remaining path is a real desktop session. 

 What's next for Claw Post WebMCP (clawpost.net) 

 Put WebMCP on the real clawpost.net dashboard, not just this demo. Reddit-style comments for more platforms. Keep the product private. Keep this wrapper public.
