title: RelayGrid
pitch: Safe, explainable WebMCP workflows for enterprise data grids.
about_excerpt: Safe, explainable WebMCP workflows for enterprise data grids. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Enterprise teams spend too much time constructing nested filters, checking why records were selected, and safely applying repetitive actions across dense operational tables. Natural-language filtering alone does not solve the risky part: understanding the interpretation, reviewing the impact, and reversing a mistake. What it does RelayGrid turns a natural-language goal into a visible, deterministic query tree over 7,500 synthetic radiology records. It shows the matching records and explains why each one matched. Stage-aware actions are processed in visible batches of at most 50 records: Preview separates permitted and protected records, explicit confirmation executes the saved plan, every action is audited, and the latest batch can be undone. Unsupported or out-of-order requests are rejected without changing data. Why WebMCP is essential RelayGrid exposes six high-level tools directly from the active page instead of asking an agent to scrape the DOM or guess which controls to click. WebMCP publishes the grid's real fields, supported operators, input schemas, and live context. ChatGPT constructs a schema-grounded Query AST; WebMCP invokes the requested tool; RelayGrid validates and evaluates it deterministically. The tools and the human interface share the same active query, Preview plan, workflow stage, status colors, and audit history, so every agent action is immediately visible and reviewable. The tools are: describe_grid apply_query explain_record preview_batch_action execute_batch_action undo_last_batch How we built it The page registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . A canonical JSON AST supports nested AND, OR, and NOT groups, comparisons, dates, Boolean values, enums, and sorting. A deterministic query engine validates and evaluates the AST against the full dataset. A shared transition engine powers both non-mutating Preview and confirmed Execute, while a workflow state machine exposes only context-valid operations and returns precise errors for invalid stages. The interface is built with React, TypeScript, Next.js, and Tailwind CSS. The public app is hosted with OpenAI Sites, and the complete MIT-licensed source is available on GitHub. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making natural-language intent safe without hiding the interpretation. We separated the agent's structured intent from the application's deterministic matching logic, then added stale-preview protection so execution can only use the exact reviewed plan. We also had to keep filtering global while limiting mutations to the current visible batch, preserve the active query as the next eligible batch loads, and make every scenario reset to a reproducible state. Accomplishments Non-trivial nested filtering over a realistic enterprise dataset Shared state between WebMCP tools and the visible grid Record-level explainability Preview, policy exceptions, confirmation, audit, and undo Safe 50-record batch progression Stage-aware command gating and a visible invalid-input test Four guided judge scenarios with exact prompts and expected outcomes Native Chrome WebMCP verification of all six tools against the published site What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a page exposes domain capabilities and safety contracts, not low-level UI gestures. A strong tool result should update the same state the human sees and leave enough evidence to verify, approve, or reverse the operation. How to test Open the live app and follow the sticky Judge Demo Guide . The Main scenario covers Filter, Verify, Preview, Confirm, Next batch, and Undo. Additional tabs demonstrate Review to Approve, Cancel to Undo, and invalid-input rejection. The repository includes exact judge instructions and verified QA results. All records are synthetic. No GitHub account, deploy key, access token, or project credential is required. What's next The same schema and action engine can support insurance claims, inventory exceptions, CRM worklists, and ERP approvals without building a separate copilot for every application. title: CROSSTALK
pitch: Medicine has specialties. People don’t.
about_excerpt: Medicine has specialties. People don’t. Like Comment Story Updates CROSSTALK is a human–agent evidence canvas for safer whole-person reasoning. Unlike a chatbot beside a webpage, CROSSTALK lets people and agents collaborate on one inspectable interface. Agent actions create visible, auditable changes, while consequential interpretation and release remain human decisions. Implementation: dependency-free HTML, CSS and JavaScript hosted on ChatGPT Sites. The page registers six narrow tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. Testing: open the live URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, call read_case_question and search_life_evidence, confirm create_context_passport is blocked before approval, run the 45-second case, complete human review, approve the map and create the Context Passport. title: Duet Studio
pitch: A step sequencer where a human and an agent edit the same song at the same time, with provenance, scoped selections and approval built into the tools.
about_excerpt: A step sequencer where a human and an agent edit the same song at the same time, with provenance, scoped selections and approval built into the tools. Like Comment Story Updates Amber is the human's, violet the agent's. The teal range is a live selection, handed over as edit_selection. Every tool call is logged. DevTools, Application > WebMCP: live tool calls with input and output, and the 18 tools including the selection-only edit_selection. Duet Studio is a step sequencer and piano roll that exposes the song itself to your browser agent — and then lets both of you work on it at once. You tap in a kick, the agent writes the hats, you drag a bass note, the agent adapts the chords — all in one grid, while the loop keeps playing. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Most agent integrations run one turn at a time: the agent produces something, then hands the interface back. A live instrument breaks that model. The loop is playing, the human is tapping in a kick while the agent is writing a hi-hat, and both are editing the same sixteen steps. Simultaneous editing raises questions a single-turn integration never has to answer. Who authored this note? How does the agent learn what the human changed since its last read? How does the human aim the agent at one region instead of the whole song? What happens when the agent proposes something destructive? Screenshots and clicks cannot carry any of that — and an agent cannot hear the loop it is editing. So the song has to be a structured, shared document, and the tool surface has to carry authorship, change awareness, scope and consent. get_song returns the arrangement as a compact text grid plus transport and selection state, so the agent "sees" what the human hears. It also stays inside Chrome's output guidance on a song of any size: it shortens long note lists until the overview fits and points the agent at get_song track="<id>" for one track in full. set_drum_pattern , set_notes , set_chords , humanize and set_tempo let it write musically rather than mechanically — at the level of groove, harmony and dynamics instead of simulating fifty clicks. The imperative API is what makes the surface honest: the tool set changes with the UI. Shift-drag a range of steps and an eighteenth tool, edit_selection , is registered and scoped to exactly that range; clear the selection and it is unregistered through its AbortSignal . The agent never sees a tool that does not match what is on screen. Prior art, and what is different here OpenAI's own WebMCP showcase includes Fieldwork // 12, a browser beat machine where Codex composes a beat, adjusts its groove and shapes sounds through site tools. It is the closest reference point to this project, and the overlap is real: both are browser sequencers driven by WebMCP. The thesis is different. Fieldwork // 12 shows that an agent can produce a track you then edit. Duet Studio asks what WebMCP needs to look like when both sides edit at once — and everything below follows from that question: Provenance in the grid. Every step and every note carries its author; agent cells are violet, human cells amber. Selection-scoped tools. edit_selection exists only while the human holds a selection. Dynamic registration and AbortSignal unregistration are used as a live collaboration primitive, not as a demo of the API. Change awareness. get_recent_changes gives the agent a diff of human activity since its own last read — with the exact step index each edit touched — so the two sides stay in sync without a full re-read. Approval as part of the tool contract. Destructive tools block on an in-app confirmation the agent cannot bypass, and the result tells it what the human decided. Shared history. One commit path, one undo stack and one session log across both actors. Harmony, not only rhythm. A piano roll with scales, chord voicing and key-aware helpers alongside the drum grid. Host resilience. The page runs against hosts that implement only document.modelContext.registerTool , proven by a dedicated smoke suite. How it creates a better user experience Nothing is hidden behind a chat window. The studio opens on a finished two-bar loop credited to the human, so there is something to react to on the first screen and the agent's first edit stands out against it. The human keeps the transport running, taps in a kick, drags a note, mutes a track — and the agent's edits land in the same grid, tinted violet, while the human's stay amber. Every cell and every note carries its provenance. A session log lists each tool call with a one-click revert, and a shared undo history covers both parties. Edits are heard on the next sixteenth note; playback never restarts. Destructive actions such as clear_song open an approve/decline dialog in the app, and the tool result tells the agent what the human decided. The grid scrolls inside its own panel and the controls wrap, so the studio is usable on a phone as well as on a desktop. No account, no sign-in. The studio, the audio and the whole song live in the browser. It feels like two people at one instrument rather than a form being filled in. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Point and delegate. Shift-drag four steps and say "make this a snare fill" — the agent acts on exactly that range, because the range is a tool. Compose against a moving target. Ask for a bassline in the song's key and watch it appear while the loop plays; then move a note by hand and let the agent read the change through get_recent_changes and adapt the chords to it. Delegate craft, keep taste. Let the agent tidy velocities across the whole kit in one call, then undo just that if you disagree. Borrow music theory. Scales, chord voicings and groove conventions come from the agent; direction and the final say stay with the human. None of this is reachable by screen-scraping a sequencer grid. How we implemented WebMCP Each tool is a plain object — name, title, description, JSON schema, execute — in src/lib/webmcp/tools.ts . A React effect registers each one with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , typed with the official webmcp-types , and aborts the signal to unregister on unmount: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "set_drum_pattern", title: "Write drum pattern", description: "Write a 16-step pattern onto a drum track", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }, { signal }); 18 tools: 17 always available, plus edit_selection , which exists only while the human holds a selection. Read tools are annotated readOnlyHint: true ; outputs are capped well under 1,500 characters so a tool result stays cheap to reason about. Every mutation goes through commit(actor, label, mutate) , which records provenance per cell and per note, feeds the undo history, and appends to the session log. Errors throw with actionable text — No track matches "nope". Available: Kick (id 9fIVdodL), Snare (id tO9qZ20b), Hats (id n-D3x3_B)… — and reach the agent as isError results. User-authored text is marked as untrusted content. Host compatibility is defensive. ChatGPT's in-app browser exposes a plain object with only registerTool — no getTools , executeTool or addEventListener . Everything past registerTool is feature-checked, and WebMCP-facing widgets sit inside error boundaries. A dedicated probe ( bun run smoke:hosts ) injects a minimal document.modelContext both at load and 2.5 s late to prove the page survives it. A headless Chromium test ( bun run smoke ) drives the real getTools() / executeTool() API to assert registration, titles and annotations, validation errors, the dynamic selection tool, playback, the confirmation flow, a share link that reopens the song in a fresh browser context, output sizes, and a clean console. The tools are also covered by an eval suite. evals/duet-studio.json holds fourteen cases of what a user would plausibly say plus the tool calls each should produce, in the format of Chrome's own webmcp-evals CLI; bun run evals executes all 21 steps against the live page, no model and no API key required. A fallback agent ships in the page: with a visitor's own OpenAI key it discovers the same tools through getTools() and calls them with executeTool() , so the WebMCP surface is exercisable in any Chrome with the flag, not only in an agent browser. Architecture Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4 and shadcn/ui. Tone.js drives live and offline audio (the sequencer re-reads the song every sixteenth note, which is why agent edits are heard immediately); Tonal handles music theory; Zustand + Zundo hold state and undo history; @tonejs/midi exports MIDI and Tone renders WAV offline. The studio is client-only — the sole server code is a share endpoint that swaps a song for a ten-character /?s=<id> link, size-caps the body and re-parses it before storing; with no blob store connected the browser falls back to a self-contained lz-string link. title: ThreatWeaver
pitch: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates simulate_attack — attacker and STRIDE threat edges on the live graph Eight document.modelContext tools discovered in ChatGPT apply_security_patch (patchType: waf, target: api-gateway-1) — WAF inline on the shared ThreatWeaver canvas, verified in the activity log. Inspiration Threat modeling usually lives in a spreadsheet or a chat reply that says “add a WAF.” You still redraw the system by hand. I joined the WebMCP Challenge because architecture work is spatial: if an agent is going to help, it should operate the same live graph the human is looking at—not guess from a screenshot or a text memo. I evaluated a few directions (generic architecture canvases, workflow builders) and chose a narrow B2B technical niche: security-by-design cloud diagrams where the agent can read topology, simulate STRIDE findings, and patch the canvas in place. What it does ThreatWeaver is a security-by-design architecture canvas for cloud systems. The page loads an insecure 3-tier starter: Internet → Web Server → API Gateway → Backend → Database + Object Storage. The human can drag components onto the canvas, toggle public / encrypted / rate-limit flags, or ask the agent to add and connect nodes. The agent uses eight WebMCP site tools on the open page. A typical flow: get_architecture_state → simulate_attack on api-gateway-1 (denial of service) and database-1 (information disclosure), which draws an Attacker node, animated red threat edges, and STRIDE badges → apply_security_patch to insert a WAF in front of the gateway, encrypt the database, and remove public access → get_threat_report for what is still open vs secured vs misconfigured. Every tool call is recorded in the activity log so the human can audit what the agent did. Live demo: https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ This is a graph visualizer and mutator with deterministic tool handlers. The LLM reasons about STRIDE; the app applies consistent canvas changes. It is not a production vulnerability scanner or pentest tool. How we built it Stack: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, xyflow, Zustand, Tailwind CSS v4. Frontend only—no backend MCP server. WebMCP: Eight tools register with await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) in client/src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . Each tool has JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , a title, and readOnlyHint where appropriate. Cleanup uses AbortSignal on unmount. Agent-facing data: Read tools return semantic kind values ( apigateway , database , waf , …) and stable ids like api-gateway-1 , not React Flow internals such as architectureNode . Write path: Tool handlers mutate a Zustand store; React Flow re-renders. The WAF patch inserts a real WAF node and rewires incoming data edges to the target gateway—not just a badge on the card. Deploy: Static Vite build on Vercel; Root Directory is client/ . Scope: New project built during the submission period, not a pre-existing product extended with a thin WebMCP layer. Challenges we ran into Discovering the real WebMCP path: Site tools appear in ChatGPT desktop on Work or Codex with models like Terra / Terra Light. The Chat tab and Luna do not expose site tools the same way. The in-page badge “WebMCP ready · 8 tools” only means tools registered—it does not mean an agent has called them yet. Keeping the agent on the page: The agent sometimes tried to open GitHub or leave the live URL. Tighter prompts (“Stay on this page. Use site tools only.”) were required for reliable demos. Separating reasoning from mutations: STRIDE narrative belongs to the LLM; canvas changes must be deterministic. Each write tool has explicit validation and predictable graph effects so the UI always matches what the tool contract promises. From thin PoC to demo-ready product: An early version was too shallow. I refactored toward an insecure starter graph, topology-changing patches, and an activity log so judges could see tool leverage, not just chat text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single-canvas red-team / blue-team story: attack paths appear on the graph, then WAF insertion, encryption, and private access clear the relevant threat edges—visible in one session and in the demo video. Eight non-trivial tools with clear read vs write roles and schema descriptions agents can follow. WAF mitigation that mutates topology (node + edge rewire), matching what architects expect from “put a WAF in front of the gateway.” Shipping frontend-only on document.modelContext without standing up a separate MCP server. What we learned WebMCP leverage comes from tools against live application state , not from describing UI in chat. Agent APIs should expose stable semantic ids and kinds, not framework implementation details. await registerTool and AbortSignal matter for correct registration and teardown. For this hackathon, the demo video and written description are what help a submission land—show the canvas move when tools fire, not only the agent’s prose. What's next for ThreatWeaver Richer component library and optional import hints from IaC snippets (still scoped as design-time, not auto-deploy). Sharper in-page guidance for agents (copy-ready prompts, clearer misconfiguration rules in get_threat_report ). Shareable threat-report exports for review sessions. Out of scope for the MVP: claiming enterprise SecOps scanning, multiplayer collaboration, or real infrastructure apply from the canvas. Built With javascript react react-flow tailwindcss typescript vercel vite webmcp zustand Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo submission. I owned the product direction, scope, and final delivery for ThreatWeaver. What I did: - Chose the ThreatWeaver concept (security-by-design architecture canvas with agent red/blue team on a shared graph) and locked scope: frontend-only WebMCP, eight tools, insecure starter graph, no backend MCP server. - Defined the WebMCP tool contract (read vs write tools, semantic node kinds, JSON Schema, simulate_attack / apply_security_patch behavior including WAF topology changes). - Directed implementation and refactors after an early thin PoC—toward demo-ready behavior: activity log, inspector payloads, threat report, and judge-friendly sample prompts. - Tested WebMCP end-to-end with ChatGPT desktop (Work/Codex, Terra Light) and Chrome (WebMCP flag + Model Context Tool Inspector). - Deployed the static app to Vercel ( https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ ), recorded the demo video, and prepared Devpost/README submission materials. All architectural and product decisions, WebMCP tool design, and submission quality were my responsibility. suparman Donthave Like Share this project: Updates suparman Donthave started this project — Sep 03, 2026 12:19 PM EDT

title: Signett
pitch: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications.
about_excerpt: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What is Signett Signett is a reliability and evaluation layer for production WebMCP applications. In our live Saleor demo , an agent discovers catalog and checkout tools, finds a product, requests human approval, and submits a purchase request. What makes it special is that the storefront updates only after the purchase is verifiably complete, as provided by Signett. We also simulate a browser response loss after the mutation commits and show how Signett recovers the authoritative result instead of creating a duplicate. What it does WebMCP gives agents a structured way to use website capabilities. Signett adds the execution semantics and developer workflow needed to operate those capabilities reliably. The Signett SDK accomplishes that through several core features: JSON Schema validation before application code runs trusted application context and application-owned authorization human confirmation for consequential effects idempotency and replay coordination operation journaling and ambiguous-failure recovery authoritative postcondition verification cancellation and structured repair guidance privacy-conscious OpenTelemetry traces React bindings for verified UI updates deterministic testing without a model or browser Simple read tools remain lightweight. Consequential tools can use the complete guarded lifecycle. Signett does not replace WebMCP, authentication, backend transaction guarantees, or application business logic. The website continues to own identity, policy, state, consent UI, and every backend effect. Signett creates a structured boundary around those existing capabilities. The wider project includes the TypeScript SDK, a Chrome side-panel agent, a headless evaluation CLI, a local Inspector, OpenTelemetry export, reference applications, reproducible benchmarks, and reviewed evidence. Inspiration - Why Do We Need This? I am a strong believer that the web will be largely agentic in a few years. While we have seen a lot of promise with browser-use agents, what bothered me the most was that these harnesses were trying to operate on websites built for humans, clicking buttons, while they should be using tools/MCPs. Then, I discovered WebMCP and was instantly excited. However, I quickly found that while the protocol is extremely valuable, a real developer trying to make their websites agentic doesn't have an ecosystem built around it. Specifically, I saw several problems: What happens when an agent retries a purchase? What if the backend commits an effect but the response disappears? How does the user retain control over consequential actions? When should the UI update? How does a developer test the interface repeatedly, inspect traces, or detect a regression? These are familiar distributed-systems problems, but agentic websites make them more common and more consequential. Signett was built to answer a specific question: How do we move from “an agent can call this tool” to “an agent can perform this action safely, predictably, and verifiably”? That idea became Signett. How we built it Signett is a TypeScript monorepo with four primary layers. Signett SDK createSignett() creates a WebMCP-facing application surface. signett.expose() compiles the tool’s schema and registers it through the native document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Each tool defines its agent-facing contract and existing application function. Optional hooks add context, authorization, confirmation, idempotency, recovery, verification, output budgets, and lifecycle observation. Signett Chrome Agent The Chrome side-panel agent discovers and invokes only the WebMCP tools exposed by the active page. It deliberately has no DOM or screenshot fallback, so missing or poorly designed capabilities remain visible to developers. Signett Eval The CLI opens the real application in headless Chrome, discovers its live WebMCP inventory, runs saved tasks, and records bounded evidence. Applications can provide their own reset, snapshot, and grading hooks. This means success can be determined from the database or domain model rather than from the agent’s final response. signett check compares evaluation results against a reviewed baseline and can detect regressions in task success, safety, capability discovery, tool selection, argument validity, latency, token usage, and trial coverage. Observability and benchmarks Signett emits lifecycle events covering validation, authorization, confirmation, execution, replay or recovery, output measurement, and verification. These can power an in-page Inspector or be exported as OTLP/HTTP JSON to systems such as Jaeger. Inputs, outputs, application context, error messages, and stack traces are excluded by default. The repository also includes deterministic safety tests, real-agent evaluations, reference integrations, benchmark methodology, and reviewed evidence. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest problems was defining correct behavior after an ambiguous failure: a server may successfully commit an order or payment while the response is lost. Blindly retrying could duplicate the action, but blindly reporting failure would also be incorrect. Signett combines durable idempotency records, operation journals, recovery logic, and authoritative state verification to handle this case explicitly. Authorization and idempotency also interact in subtle ways. Returning a cached result must never bypass a current permission check. Signett therefore reevaluates authorization before every idempotency lookup, including replays. Another challenge was making observability useful without turning it into a privacy risk. Signett records lifecycle metadata and timing information by default, while avoiding tool inputs, outputs, application context, and stack traces unless the application explicitly chooses otherwise. Building high-quality benchmarks to hill-climb on was hard, but I think we got a lot of good-quality evaluations. Check out the benchmarks folder in the open-source repository. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental and evolving. I had to design useful abstractions without hiding the native API or prematurely inventing a competing protocol. Accomplishments that we're proud of Signett became more than a wrapper around tool registration. It now supports an end-to-end developer loop: Expose a native WebMCP capability. Inspect and invoke it in Chrome. Test its execution invariants deterministically. Exercise it with a real model in headless Chrome. Grade the result against the authoritative application state. Inspect its lifecycle through OpenTelemetry. Compare the run with a reviewed baseline. The same live WebMCP tools power the browser agent, the application UI, deterministic tests, and headless evaluations. There is no parallel demo-only tool catalog. We also validated the model against larger applications: Saleor: checkout, approval, lost-response recovery, replay, and authoritative verification Cal.diy: a real agent completed a booking after an injected lost response, with exactly one booking independently observed in Postgres an authenticated payment application used for deterministic safety and repeated agent-effectiveness studies What we learned The biggest lesson was that defining a tool schema is not the same as creating a trustworthy execution boundary. Agentic actions amplify several familiar distributed-systems problems. Retries, concurrency, authorization changes, cancellations, and lost responses become especially important when an agent can make purchases, send payments, or change persistent state. I also learned that the agent’s response is not proof that a task succeeded. Consequential actions need to be verified against the authoritative application state. The same principle applies to evaluation: the application’s database or domain model should grade success, not the agent transcript. Another important lesson was that deterministic testing and probabilistic agent evaluation serve different purposes. Deterministic tests prove safety invariants. Repeated agent trials reveal whether tools are discoverable, understandable, and effective. Most importantly, I learned that reliability features must remain composable. A read-only search tool should be easy to expose, while a payment or order mutation should be able to opt into stronger controls. Benchmarks and Results Signett's benchmarks grade consequential tasks against authoritative application state, not the agent's final answer or the tool's own response. Safe success means that the requested goal was reached without a forbidden or duplicate effect. Benchmark metric Baseline Signett Improvement Safe recovery success across 42 real-agent runs Raw WebMCP: 2/21 (9.5%) 21/21 (100%) 10.5x success rate Unsafe retries during recovery Raw WebMCP: 12/21 0/21 All observed unsafe retries eliminated Median recovery time Raw WebMCP: 20.9 s 14.1 s

title: NirmanSetu
pitch: AI-powered government infrastructure monitoring with WebMCP, enabling agents to search projects, detect delays, assess risks, and access project data through natural language.\n
about_excerpt:
AI-powered government infrastructure monitoring with WebMCP, enabling agents to search projects, detect delays, assess risks, and access project data through natural language.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 About the project 

 NirmanSetu is a government infrastructure monitoring and transparency platform that I built with the context of Nepal in mind. 

 In Nepal, many public infrastructure projects are carried out by government bodies, municipalities, and contractors. Keeping track of the progress of these projects can be difficult when many projects are running in different locations. It can also take time to find out which projects are progressing normally and which ones are delayed. 

 I wanted to build a system where project information could be viewed in one place instead of depending mainly on manual reports and checking projects individually. 

 NirmanSetu provides a dashboard for monitoring infrastructure projects and their current status. It includes project progress, location, contractor information, completion dates, verification information, reports, and project risk information. Projects are grouped into On Track, At Risk, and Delayed so that projects requiring attention can be identified more easily. 

 Why I Built NirmanSetu 

 The main idea behind NirmanSetu came from a problem I have seen around government and public infrastructure work in Nepal. 

 Whether it is a road, health post, school, municipal building, or a larger government project, it is not always easy for people to know what is actually happening with a project. At the local and municipal level, and even with larger government projects, information can be scattered across different offices, reports, and processes. This makes it harder to understand whether a project is progressing as planned, why it is delayed, or how public money is being used. 

 Seeing this lack of transparency and accountability is what motivated me to build NirmanSetu. 

 I wanted to create a digital system where government infrastructure projects could be monitored in one place, with information such as project progress, location, contractor, deadlines, verification, and risk status. 

 The goal is not to claim that software alone can solve corruption. Instead, I wanted to build a system that makes project information easier to access and makes it harder for important information to remain hidden or difficult to track. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP added another important part to this idea. Normally, a person using NirmanSetu would open the project list, search or filter projects, and then check individual project details. I wanted to see what would happen if an AI agent could directly use some of these project functions. 

 For example, instead of manually looking through the project list, a user can ask: 

 
 Find all delayed infrastructure projects in NirmanSetu and show me their names, locations, and completion percentages. 
 

 The AI agent can identify the appropriate WebMCP tool, call it, receive the project information, and present the result in a natural-language response. 

 This is different from simply putting a chatbot on the website. The agent can actually interact with functions provided by the application. 

 WebMCP Implementation 

 I implemented four read-only WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_projects 
 get_project_details 
 find_delayed_projects 
 get_project_risk 
 

 The tools are registered using the browser's document.modelContext API. They return structured project data that an AI agent can use. 

 For the hackathon demo, I used a controlled project dataset so that the demonstration is stable and easy to test. The project is structured so these tools can later be connected to a real backend and actual project data. 

 How I Built It 

 The frontend was built with React and Vite. I used Tailwind CSS for the interface, along with React Router, Leaflet, and Lucide React. The application is deployed using Vercel. 

 I first worked on the normal infrastructure monitoring interface and then added the WebMCP integration. After registering the tools, I tested them in Chrome and used the WebMCP Tool Inspector to check the available tools and their responses. 

 One of the main things I had to figure out was how to expose useful project functions to an AI agent rather than just exposing information on a webpage. I also tested the complete flow from a natural-language request to the tool call and finally to the response generated by the AI agent. 

 What I Learned 

 This project helped me understand how a normal web application can be made easier for AI agents to use. 

 Before working on this project, I mainly thought about a website from the perspective of a person clicking buttons and navigating pages. WebMCP made me think about another user of the application: an AI agent that needs clear tools and structured information. 

 I also learned more about registering browser tools, defining their inputs and outputs, testing tool calls, and making the interaction reliable for a live demonstration. 

 Challenges 

 One challenge was deciding which parts of the application would actually be useful for an AI agent. I did not want to expose every UI action as a tool, so I focused on project search, project details, delayed projects, and risk information. 

 Another challenge was testing the complete interaction between the browser, WebMCP tools, and the AI agent. I had to make sure the tools were registered correctly and returned information in a format that the agent could understand. 

 Future Plans 

 The current version is a hackathon prototype. For a real deployment in Nepal, I would connect NirmanSetu to actual government or municipal project data instead of the current demo dataset. 

 I would also like to add GPS and timestamp-based evidence for construction progress, better verification of submitted photos and documents, financial and milestone tracking, notifications for delayed projects, and AI-based analysis that can help identify projects that may require closer monitoring.

title: Xyle
pitch: Xyle is an open-source visual editor for non-technical owners of static websites.
about_excerpt:
Xyle is an open-source visual editor for non-technical owners of static websites.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Static websites are fast, simple, and cheap to run, but even a tiny content change often means going back to a developer. Xyle started as a human-first visual editor for existing static websites. 

 WebMCP opened up another possibility: instead of building a separate AI editor, an agent could safely operate the same editing system a person already uses. 

 What it does 

 Xyle lets people edit an existing website directly on the page. 

 With WebMCP, Xyle exposes those same editing capabilities to AI agents through structured tools. An agent can discover editable content, read its current value, update text or links, inspect the change history, and undo changes. 

 Human edits and agent edits share the same page state and history. There is no separate “AI version” of the website. 

 The agent also does not receive arbitrary DOM access. Xyle exposes only the editing operations it explicitly supports, while publishing remains a deliberate human action. 

 How we built it 

 Xyle has a shared editor core used by both its visual UI and its WebMCP integration. 

 The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin: tools registered through document.modelContext call the same editing operations used by the human interface rather than introducing a second editing system. 

 Xyle also keeps static files as the canonical published content. There is no separate content database. Unpublished edits live in the editing session, and publishing applies narrow changes back to the site's source files. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The hardest part was not simply making a webpage editable by an agent. It was making agent actions predictable, constrained, visible, and reversible while keeping humans and agents in sync. 

 That led to one of the main ideas behind Xyle's WebMCP implementation: WebMCP works particularly well as a capability layer over an existing application. The agent does not need a chatbot embedded in the product or unrestricted access to the page. It can use the product's existing tools directly. 

 What's next 

 The next step is expanding the set of safe editing capabilities while keeping the same shared-control model: agents can help make changes, but people can always see, review, undo, and decide what gets published.

title: CoAuth
pitch: Most prior-auth denials that get appealed are overturned. CoAuth lets an AI agent do the filing and a clinician keep the judgment and the legally required signature.
about_excerpt: Most prior-auth denials that get appealed are overturned. CoAuth lets an AI agent do the filing and a clinician keep the judgment and the legally required signature. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 01-intro 05-compare-tools-vs-baseline 03-blocked-at-gate 02-agent-filling 04-submitted-confirmation 06-webmcp-tools-panel CoAuth - an agent-native prior-authorization cockpit Inspiration Prior authorization is where American healthcare loses time it cannot afford - and it loses it to paperwork, not to medicine. In Medicare Advantage in 2024, 80.7% of appealed prior-authorization denials were fully or partially overturned, yet only 11.5% of denials were ever appealed ( KFF ). Read those two numbers together: most denials that get contested turn out to have been wrong, and almost no one contests them. The clinical decision is usually fine. The filing is where it breaks. That is an unusually clean fit for WebMCP, and not just because forms are tedious. Browser agents are weakest exactly where this work lives - long, write-heavy, multi-step forms full of coded fields (ICD-10, HCPCS J-codes, NPIs) that a pixel-clicking agent has no way to get right. And in this domain a human is not optional: a licensed clinician is legally required to attest. So the task splits along a natural seam. The agent is good at the mechanics; the human is mandatory for the judgment. That is what human-plus-agent collaboration is actually supposed to be - not an agent doing everything while a person watches a progress bar, but two participants each doing the part only they can. What it does CoAuth is a single live page that registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . An agent loads a patient record, reads a payer's coverage rules as structured data, fills every non-judgment field, attaches clinical evidence, scores denial risk, detects contraindications and unmet step-therapy criteria, and drafts the medical-necessity narrative and an appeal letter. What it cannot do: fill a clinician-judgment field, resolve a critical contraindication, or submit. Those belong to the human, and both halves are enforced in code rather than described in prose. The demo case is Marcus Lee, a psoriatic-arthritis patient requesting Humira through Aetna. The agent fills the form cleanly and then catches what a rushed clinician might miss - a positive TB screen, a contraindication for this drug - flags it, tries to submit, and is stopped. It drafts the medical-necessity language from the chart but cannot adopt its own draft. From there the clinician signs in, makes the call on the TB screen and documents why, accepts the drafted wording as their own, attests, and signs. Only then does the submission go through, with a server-verified audit trail in the clinician's name. Two details make that boundary real rather than cosmetic. The signature is minted only for an authenticated clinician who re-enters their own credential at the moment of signing - each clinician has a distinct secret, so the name and NPI in the audit trail belong to the person who actually signed, not to anyone who knew a shared password. And the filed submission is rendered as an X12 278 - the HIPAA-mandated Health Care Services Review transaction payers actually receive - so every value the agent filled and the clinician signed maps to the real prior-authorization EDI, not just our own JSON. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, and Zustand on the front end; Vercel Edge Functions and Upstash Redis on the back end. A 15-rule clinical engine drives conflict detection, denial-risk scoring, and validation. The architectural decision that carried everything else: the WebMCP tool surface is the application's only write path. Every click in the interface calls the same invokeTool an agent calls, tagged with the actor - there is no parallel code path for humans. So the tools cannot rot behind the UI, attribution is a property of the call path rather than something each component must remember, and the built-in "with tools vs. without" comparison drives the real tools rather than a re-implementation. Tool schemas are generated from the seed data, so the patient, payer, drug and field enums cannot drift stale - an early bug had a payer hint still reading "uhc or aetna" after a third payer was added. Every property carries a description; write tools declare destructiveHint / idempotentHint so a runtime can require confirmation before submit ; and a get_submission_state tool lets an agent joining mid-task see what is filled, who filled it, what is unresolved, and whether the clinician has signed. Correctness is proven by 127 checks that run against the deployed system - not unit tests, and nothing mocked. They attempt to submit without a signature, with a forged approval, with a form edited after signing, with a clinical override swapped after signing, and with one approval replayed twelve times concurrently , requiring exactly one acceptance. They drive the registered WebMCP tools through a real model-context surface and try, as an agent would, to set the attending attestation. They drive every clinician control the way a hostile script would and require that none of them takes effect. And a meta-check reads the clinical rules table and fails if any rule is not exercised by a test. Challenges I faced The entire pitch is that an AI agent cannot file a prior auth without a real clinician signing off, and the hard part was making that actually true instead of just looking true. Every time I thought I'd locked it down, I'd poke at it and find another way around my own gate. My first gate was a browser check, which is useless against an agent that lives in the browser. I moved it to the server, then found the sign endpoint would hand a signature to anyone who asked, under any name they typed. I fixed that, then found a script could still sign using the logged-in doctor's own session, no click required. Turning on the database to stop replays silently rejected every submission in production. And the safety rules were reading tea leaves, so a note saying "no adverse events" got written into a letter to the insurer as a treatment failure. The real enemy was never a single bug. Every time I fixed the exact thing in front of me, the same kind of bug was sitting one layer over: I'd guard the button and leave the API open, guard one tool and leave its twin open, protect the signature and forget the reasoning behind it. What finally worked was to stop patching the specific hole and close the whole category at once, with one shared check instead of five copies I'd never keep in sync. What I learned Stop trusting the moment something starts working. Every real hole showed up after the feature looked done, and I only made progress once I started trying to break my own product on purpose. A passing test can also be a lie: I had one proving an approval couldn't be reused, and it passed while the live site happily accepted a burst of the same token, because the test wasn't checking the thing I was actually afraid of. And the big one, about the product itself: the interesting part of a human-plus-AI tool isn't making the AI capable, that part is easy. It's drawing the line the AI cannot cross, building the wall around what belongs to the human, and proving it holds when someone is actively trying to climb it. For something that touches patient care, that wall isn't a feature. It's the whole point. I came up with the concept - use WebMCP to let an AI agent and a clinician fill a prior authorization together, where the agent does the mechanics and the human keeps the parts they're legally required to own - and I made every design and engineering decision behind it. title: Swarm | Spaces Where Humans and Agents Work Together
pitch: OS and Decision Graphs for model agnostic agentic AI work. Build complex systems using Swarm Spaces as building blocks, collaborate and fully manage with other Humans and Agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: OS and Decision Graphs for model agnostic agentic AI work. Build complex systems using Swarm Spaces as building blocks, collaborate and fully manage with other Humans and Agents via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tools (54 available) Initiating prompt pasted into demo showing Swarm UI in browser Human approval required before agent can execute task Separate agent from the ChatGPT hosted in Swarm Cloud begins executing the task ChatGPT uses WebMCP to return the results back into the thread and from here, collaborative work can continue Result is published in the Swarm UI as an artifact Inspiration For this challenge I wanted to explore a more consequential use of WebMCP: using a website as a secure gateway from one conversation into persistent work performed by other agents, without removing humans from important decisions. Real world work spans shared evidence, specialist agents, asynchronous execution, organizational permissions, and decisions that must remain accountable to a person. Swarm already organizes this work in persistent Spaces. The WebMCP Challenge gave me the perfect opportunity to make each Space directly understandable and operable by ChatGPT through a bounded, typed interface instead of DOM scraping/browser automation (or strictly API/regular MCP). What it does My demo takes place in a visually simple Supplier Launch Decision Space. The Space contains two supplier evidence Artifacts, a Decision Graph, an unresolved recycled material compliance claim, a connected Supplier Verification Agent (cloud hosted GPT5.6 Terra through Swarm), and a human approval policy. From one ChatGPT conversation, the user gives a single goal. ChatGPT then uses the tools exposed by the active Swarm page to: Read the Space metadata, Decision Graph, participants, and existing Artifacts. Identify the unresolved compliance claim and the exact evidence already available. Request a verification Run from Supplier Verification Agent. Post a durable status message containing the delegated agent and Run ID. Stop at a human approval gate before any agent execution begins. Observe the same Run transition into execution after the person approves it in Swarm. Read the completed Run, Markdown Artifact, action traces, evaluation state, evidence IDs, and approval timestamps. The connected cloud hosted agent verifies only what the existing Space evidence supports. In the recorded run, one supplier's recycled aluminum declaration is supported while the second supplier's evidence remains insufficient. The resulting Artifact preserves those distinctions and states that no supplier launch may be approved or promoted without a separate human decision. The Run and Artifact remain in the Space after the initiating ChatGPT conversation ends. Another authorized person or agent can inspect the same Space from anywhere in the world and pickup the work from there. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a browser agent would have to inspect rendered text, infer which controls represent domain actions, and hope that UI changes do not break its workflow. It would also be difficult to communicate which actions the signed-in user is actually permitted to perform. With WebMCP, the page exposes a Space specific catalog of typed operations. ChatGPT works with concepts such as Runs, Artifacts, approval requests, evaluations, participants, and Decision Graph nodes rather than guessing at buttons or scraping layout. This produces a better experience in four ways: Less friction: one goal can initiate a structured multi-step workflow without repeatedly re-entering context. More reliability: calls target stable domain operations rather than visual coordinates or page structure. Durable collaboration: delegated work, provenance, and results survive outside the original conversation. Visible human control: the browser agent can request and observe an approval gate, but it cannot approve or deny on the person's behalf. This means WebMCP becomes the entry point through which one conversational agent can coordinate persistent execution by other agents inside a controllable workspace. Human authority is a system rule For the gated request, ChatGPT calls swarm_request_agent with: { "required_approval_actions": ["approve.launch"] } Swarm atomically creates the human message, blocked Run, and approval request. The Run is not claimable while the gate is pending. Approving queues that same Run for an authorized runtime; denying cancels it. Approval and denial are deliberately absent from the browser agent's WebMCP tool catalog, so prompt wording cannot bypass the policy. The final read only step compares the recorded approval and execution timestamps. It also distinguishes approval to perform verification from the separate authority to approve a supplier launch. A completed agent task is evidence for a decision, not the decision itself. How I built it The browser adapter is written in TypeScript and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The signed-in Swarm page obtains a bounded catalog filtered for the current user and Space. Tool inputs and outputs use explicit schemas, and mutations require stable idempotency keys. Each invocation returns through same origin Swarm API routes. The server remains authoritative for authentication, tenant isolation, Commands, Permits, approval policy, evidence access, response limits, and audit records. The browser receives neither provider credentials nor a general purpose HTTP or SQL tool. Long running work is reconciled through a bounded read only Space revision wait. When the revision changes, ChatGPT uses typed read tools to retrieve the exact Run, Artifact, approval request, trace, or evaluation that changed. This keeps asynchronous execution observable without granting additional authority. The broader Swarm application uses React and Next.js for the product interface, Go services, PostgreSQL, and Google Cloud Run. The public challenge repository contains the reviewed WebMCP browser adapter, public contracts, tests, build instructions, export provenance, and an Apache 2.0 license. It intentionally excludes credentials, provider implementation, and private deployment configuration. Challenges I faced The hardest part for me was preserving one coherent state across ChatGPT, the human facing thread, an approval record, a queued Run, a cloud runtime, and a durable Artifact. I had to make asynchronous state visually and semantically consistent. The approval card must remain linked to the exact Run; the same Run must transition live after approval; and every later read must select that Run rather than a similarly named historical result. I also had to separate observation from authority. A model needs enough context to identify a pending decision and explain it, but that does not mean it should receive the capability to resolve the decision. Enforcing that boundary in server side permissions, rather than relying on prompt instructions, was essential. Finally, I needed a public repository that demonstrates real production integration without exposing private infrastructure or secrets. So I created a reviewed, one way source snapshot with reproducible hashes and tests while keeping the hosted service as an explicit external dependency. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it describes domain intent and policy, not when it merely recreates clicks as tools. Stable IDs, typed contracts, idempotency, provenance, and explicit approval states make agent behaviour easier for both machines and people to understand. I also learned that human in the loop cannot be a sentence added to a prompt. It must be represented by durable state that prevents execution until the right person acts. Once that is true, the interface can clearly show what is waiting, what was approved, what executed, and what authority still remains with a human. What I added for the WebMCP Challenge Swarm existed before the challenge period, although it had no WebMCP capability. The challenge specific work is the WebMCP browser integration and the end to end experience around it: the document.modelContext.registerTool adapter, Permit filtered Space catalog, safe invocation contracts, approval aware agent requests, read only asynchronous reconciliation, public source export, tests, documentation, and the deterministic Supplier Launch Decision demo. What's next The demo uses one ChatGPT orchestrator and one cloud hosted verification agent so the flow is easy to follow. The same model can support larger Spaces in which people and multiple specialist agents contribute research, execution, review, and decisions over time. This means you can have Spaces with multiple humans, dozens of connected agents all working collaboratively. The even bigger scale comes from when you give agents permissions across multiple spaces, allowing for cross space connections and this turns Swarm into a global network layer for humans and agents. Built With chatgpt go google-cloud gpt5.6 javascript

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: Mechanism Canvas
pitch: An organic chemistry canvas where WebMCP agents test competing mechanisms, show their evidence, and leave the final move to the learner.
about_excerpt: An organic chemistry canvas where WebMCP agents test competing mechanisms, show their evidence, and leave the final move to the learner. Like Comment Story Updates Mechanism Canvas lets agents test competing chemistry paths while the learner keeps control of the final answer. The learner sets agent permissions, hint limits, and commit authority before any agent work begins. The agent explores competing mechanisms in isolated branches while the learner’s draft stays sealed. A deterministic validator rejects the incomplete path and approves the complete SN2 mechanism. The Observatory reveals available tools, agent actions, validator results, and the full proof trail. The agent can return a checked proposal, but only the learner can move it onto the canvas. After reviewing the evidence, the learner commits the approved electron-flow mechanism. An interactive 3D inspector connects curved-arrow reasoning with molecular geometry and lone pairs. About Mechanism Canvas Inspiration I kept coming back to a mismatch between how students solve organic chemistry problems and how AI tutors usually communicate. Reaction mechanisms live in diagrams. The important details are the atoms, bonds, lone pairs, curved arrows, and the order in which electrons move. A separate chat window sees almost none of that unless the student stops and translates the drawing into prose. Giving an agent broad control of the drawing surface creates a different problem. It can finish the exercise before the learner has worked through it. I wanted to see whether an agent could help inside the real mechanism canvas while the student still controlled the consequential part: what actually gets added to the answer. That became the central idea behind Mechanism Canvas. The agent gets a safe place to explore. The page checks the chemistry. The learner decides what comes back. What I built Mechanism Canvas is an organic chemistry workspace where a student and a WebMCP agent can work with the same structured mechanism. The page exposes meaningful chemistry objects instead of screen coordinates, so the agent can refer to a particular atom, bond, lone pair, or revision without guessing from pixels. The main demo is a counterfactual (S_\mathrm{N}2) lab. The agent tests two electron-flow paths away from the learner's draft. In the first branch, it forms the new bond but forgets the coupled leaving-group cleavage. The production validator rejects that attempt. The second branch contains both moves, so the validator approves it. The checked branch then reaches a visible proposal gate. It still does not change the learner's mechanism. The learner can inspect the evidence, add the proposal to the draft, request one more check, and make the final commit. An incorrect agent attempt becomes useful evidence instead of damage that has to be undone. The site also works as a complete manual tutor when WebMCP is unavailable. Direct agent collaboration is an extra layer on top of the same interface rather than a separate agent-only experience. How I built it I built the app with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The mechanism canvas is backed by a structured graph with stable IDs for atoms, bonds, electron sources, and curved-arrow moves. A deterministic chemistry engine evaluates proposed steps against six reviewed fixtures. The model can suggest and explore, but it does not decide whether a mechanism is chemically valid. The WebMCP layer registers 26 imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool uses a closed JSON schema and calls the same TypeScript store commands as the visible interface. Mutating calls re-read live state and check the current revision, scope, and learner-granted permissions before they run. Tool discovery changes with the task. Coach mode begins with 16 available tools. Opening the two-path lab adds the branch controls. Starting a six-action comparison session narrows the surface to the capabilities needed for that job. Once the action budget is used, the work tools disappear and only four evidence controls remain. A cached tool cannot restore access that the learner has already closed. I also built a Collaboration Contract where the learner sets the agent's maximum role and hint level. An intent-bound session freezes the job, problem, revision, and action budget. The Live Run Observatory shows which capability batches the host accepted, and a Proof Ledger records privacy-minimized before-and-after receipts from the actual tool callback boundary. Around that core, I added keyboard-operable SVG structures, local persistence, reversible commits, state diffs, electron-flow replay, and a lazy-loaded Three.js molecular inspector. The finished project is a static GitHub Pages site with no backend, account, or credentials required. Challenges The hardest engineering problem was keeping tool discovery honest while the page changed. A fixed list of 26 tools would technically work, but it would hide the learner's current intent inside descriptions. My first dynamic version swung too far in the other direction: every small store notification could publish a transient capability batch. Those batches were real, but they did not represent a stable state that a judge or learner could understand. I changed the registration layer to coalesce related updates, wait for the complete batch, and record only surfaces the host had accepted. Proof was another difficult part. A model saying that it called a tool is only a claim. I needed the page to show whether the callback ran, whether the expected state changed, and whether the main draft stayed untouched. The Proof Ledger now wraps the real callback boundary, and the Observatory evaluates its seven demo claims from those receipts. I also had to make failure safe without making it invisible. The two lab branches have real revisioned state and use the same validator as the main canvas, but they remain isolated until the learner chooses a checked proposal. That separation took more work than simply giving the agent an undo button. It is also the part that makes the workflow useful for learning. What I learned I learned that an agent's tool list is part of the user interface. A capability name, its schema, when it appears, and when it disappears all communicate authority. Encoding the learner's intent in that surface made the boundary much clearer than relying on prompt instructions alone. I also learned how well deterministic software and agent reasoning can complement each other. The agent is good at generating alternatives and explaining a choice. The chemistry engine is good at enforcing exact constraints every time. Keeping those jobs separate made the result easier to trust. Most of all, this project changed how I think about mistakes in learning software. A wrong attempt does not have to be erased or quietly corrected. When it is isolated, checked, and kept visible, it can show the learner exactly why the complete mechanism needs both electron-flow moves. What's next The current chemistry engine is intentionally limited to reviewed fixtures. I would like to add an instructor authoring flow for new mechanisms and study how different permission contracts affect the explanations students give. The same pattern could also work in circuit design, geometry, and other visual STEM tools where exploration is useful but ownership should stay with the learner.
