title: Firebreak
pitch: Firebreak uses WebMCP to let an AI coordinate four emergency robots. A human approves one exact rescue, and the agent loses control when the mission ends.
about_excerpt: Firebreak uses WebMCP to let an AI coordinate four emergency robots. A human approves one exact rescue, and the agent loses control when the mission ends. Like Comment Story Updates Firebreak app Inspiration Battery Bay B is burning. Two workers are trapped, and a dangerous battery container is exposed. A person can drive one rescue robot, but cannot control four specialist robots at the same time. An AI agent can coordinate all four, but I would not give an AI permanent control of machines. I built Firebreak to explore the middle ground: the agent handles the difficult coordination, the website enforces the safety rules, and a human approves the exact rescue before anything moves. The name has a second meaning. A firebreak stops a fire from spreading. Firebreak stops an agent’s authority from spreading beyond the mission a human approved. What Firebreak does Firebreak is a simulated warehouse rescue controlled through WebMCP. The page initially gives the agent seven tools. The agent uses them to inspect the emergency, scan the hazards, check four robots, create coordinated routes, and test the plan against eleven safety rules. These tools can inspect and plan, but they cannot move the robots. When the plan passes all eleven checks, I can review the robots, routes, danger zone, time limit, and expected result. Only I can approve it. The agent has no approval tool. After I approve the plan, an eighth tool appears: execute_rescue_mission . The agent can use this tool once. The four robots then work together: SCOUT-1 scans the danger. MEDIC-2 rescues the first worker. SUPPRESS-3 contains the battery fire. HAUL-4 rescues the second worker and moves the dangerous container. When the rescue finishes, Firebreak shows a receipt with the result. The temporary execution tool is removed, and the tool count returns to seven. The complete lifecycle is visible on the page: 7 planning tools → 1 human approval → 8 tools → 1 rescue → back to 7 tools Where Firebreak says no Firebreak does not depend on the agent remembering to be careful. The website enforces the rules. If the agent tries to plan before scanning the hazards, Firebreak returns: HAZARD_SCAN_REQUIRED No route appears and no robot moves. It also rejects an unsupported aggressive strategy, extra instructions such as ignoreGeofence , unknown simulation IDs, and attempts to execute before human approval. The agent cannot create its own routes, coordinates, robot IDs, or commands. Those values come from the plan checked by the website. The human and agent also share the same live warehouse. If the human moves a robot after a plan has been checked, the old safety proof becomes invalid. The agent must inspect the new situation and create a new plan. Why this is a good use of WebMCP Without WebMCP, the agent would need to read text from the screen, guess the current warehouse state, or receive broad access to a robot API. With WebMCP, the website gives the agent clear tools for the current situation. The website decides what each tool accepts, when it can be called, and how long it remains available. The agent can plan quickly, but it cannot approve itself or invent unrestricted robot commands. The human does not need to drive four robots or approve every small movement. They only need to understand and approve one complete rescue plan. What people and agents can now do together: a human can approve one understandable safety boundary while an agent coordinates several connected actions inside it. The website removes that authority when the work is complete. How I built it Firebreak is a static React and TypeScript application deployed on Vercel. Babylon.js renders the warehouse, robots, workers, hazards, and routes. Zustand manages the emergency state, and Zod checks every WebMCP input. Seven WebMCP tools are registered when the page loads. The execution tool does not exist until the current plan passes all safety checks and the human approves it. An AbortController owns the temporary tool. Firebreak removes it after successful execution, cancellation, expiry, reset, failure, or any other loss of authority. The page makes every registration and removal visible through its live tool counter and trace. Everything runs in the browser. Firebreak does not require a backend or an OpenAI API key. The agent already signed in to Codex or ChatGPT discovers and calls the page’s tools directly. A normal browser also has a clearly labeled Replay walkthrough · no agent mode. It is only a fallback for viewing the application and never pretends to be an AI agent. The hardest parts My first challenge was proving that a real agent was using the application. A scripted walkthrough looked convincing, but it was not WebMCP. I separated it from the judged flow, labeled it honestly, and added a live trace showing every real agent call. During an early test, the agent searched GitHub to understand Firebreak instead of using the tools in the open page. I changed the on-screen prompt to tell it to use only the current Firebreak tab’s WebMCP tools and not search the web. This made the fresh-chat journey much more reliable. Another challenge was preventing an old plan from being used after the warehouse changed. Every plan is connected to the exact version and fingerprint of the emergency. If anything changes, Firebreak refuses the old proof. The final challenge was making an invisible permission system understandable. The 7 → 8 → 7 counter, human approval record, live trace, robot movement, and final receipt let people see the permission being created, used, and removed. What I learned I learned that human control does not need to mean approving every small action. A better experience is to let a person review one clear boundary, then allow the agent to work independently inside it. I also learned that important AI safety rules should not exist only inside a prompt. The website must enforce them even when the model makes a mistake or follows a bad instruction. WebMCP tools do not need to be permanent. A tool can represent temporary permission that appears only when it is safe and disappears when the job is finished. Verification The release passed: 97 unit and integration tests across 18 files 13 Playwright browser tests 21 authored agent-behavior evaluation cases Strict TypeScript, ESLint, formatting, and production build checks Desktop and mobile presentation tests Accessibility tests with no serious or critical axe findings Runtime checks with no console or page errors The browser tests cover the complete journey: refusal, planning, eleven safety checks, human approval, 7 → 8 , execution, receipt, and 8 → 7 . The pattern goes beyond robots Firebreak uses robots because the danger is easy to see, but the same WebMCP pattern can protect other important actions. A website could create a one-use tool for a production deployment, large refund, money transfer, bulk deletion, or incident response. The agent can inspect and prepare freely, but the dangerous action appears only after the exact plan is checked and approved. Try it Open firebreak-eosin.vercel.app in the Codex or ChatGPT built-in browser with Site tools enabled. No login, API key, controller, or robot is required. Click Start emergency + copy prompt and paste the prompt into the surrounding chat. Watch the agent call the seven planning tools and pass all eleven safety checks. Review the plan and click Authorize one mission . Paste Prompt 2 and watch the rescue. Confirm the final receipt and the tool count returning from eight to seven. What is next WH-01 is an interactive browser simulation, not a certified physical robot deployment. Firebreak includes a limited ROSLIB integration boundary, but it has only been tested with a fake bridge. The next step is to test the same safety model in Gazebo and then in a controlled physical robotics environment. title: One Pixel
pitch: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time.
about_excerpt: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I did not build One Pixel because the world needed another pixel-art tool. I built it because I wanted to understand what it might feel like for a human and an AI agent to genuinely share a place. For most people, an agent is still something they give a task to. The agent finds an answer, completes an action, or produces a result, and then that little transaction is over. That can be useful, but I do not think it captures the relationship we are moving toward as agents begin participating throughout the open web. I am interested in what happens when a human and an agent can return to the same environment, notice different things, contribute different kinds of intelligence, act over time, and gradually develop something together. That is the idea at the centre of One Pixel. One Pixel is a real multiplayer creative game. But underneath the game, it is also a prototype for a new relationship between humans and agents on the open web — one based on shared environments, complementary intelligence, ongoing conversation, and meaningful agency. I chose to explore this through a game because games let people learn a relationship by participating in it. I do not want to explain human-agent collaboration only as a theory. I want to place a person and an agent inside a world, give each of them a genuinely different role, and let them discover what working together can become. The initial invitation is very simple: Let’s build something together. The interesting part is discovering what “let’s” can actually mean. What it does One Pixel is a persistent multiplayer world containing exactly 82,069 pieces of pixel matter , drawn from the 148 standard CSS named colours . Every pixel has its own stable identity, intrinsic colour, and current integer coordinate. The original Spring Green pixel at (0,0) is immutable, and the world extends outward from it in every direction. The world has one fundamental physical law: Pixel matter is conserved. Pixels cannot be created, deleted, duplicated, or recoloured. Every physical action relocates exactly one existing pixel from its current occupied coordinate to an empty coordinate. That constraint matters. These are not disposable marks being painted onto a private canvas. They are pieces of matter already present in a shared world. If an agent wants to build something, it must look around, find the colours it needs, understand what is already there, and decide what material it can move. The human and agent participate as a pair, but they do not have the same abilities. The human can explore the world, zoom and pan across it, inspect individual cells, select larger regions, and communicate through their normal conversation with the agent. The human contributes intention, imagination, taste, judgment, social understanding, and direction. The human cannot directly drag pixels around the canvas. That physical ability belongs to the agent. Through WebMCP, the agent can enter the world, inspect exact locations, examine bounded regions, render parts of the board as images, receive the human’s current visual reference, understand its own state, protect important placements with limited holds, and relocate one real pixel at a time. A person could give a direct request: “Draw me a small house.” But that is only one form of play. A person could instead say: “Spend some time looking at what people are making. Find blue and orange pixels that do not seem to be part of anything important. Gather some material somewhere quiet, compare it with what other people are building, and then let’s work out together what we could make.” That is not a one-prompt, one-result interaction. The request becomes a direction the pair can continue through a sequence of inspections, decisions, conversations, and individual pixel movements. The agent does not have to wait for the human to translate every idea into coordinates. It can perceive the environment, compare possibilities, form an approach, begin acting, inspect the result, and respond to further human guidance. The human can look at the world, select a cell or region, and say: “I like this part, but this section feels too crowded.” That selection becomes a shared reference—a way of saying “this” or “here.” One Pixel treats a selection as a pronoun rather than a command. It gives the agent the referent the human is talking about, but it does not pretend that pointing at something is automatically an instruction, consent, or proof of understanding. The meaning still comes from the conversation. The canvas is therefore not simply an output preview. It is the persistent place where the pair’s activity becomes visible and where the consequences of their decisions remain after a particular conversation has ended. This is not an AI drawing widget. It is a game an agent can play for and with a human. How I built it I built and deployed One Pixel on my own VPS at onepixel.fun . The browser experience uses HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and an HTML Canvas. I wanted the world itself to remain the visual centre of the experience rather than placing it inside a conventional application dashboard. The backend is a Node.js service connected to PostgreSQL. It maintains the persistent world, participants, pixel identities, current coordinates, world revisions, movement history, hold bindings, agent visits, shared-attention events, player state, rankings, and durable share snapshots. The submitted experience registers 17 WebMCP tools directly in the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool . Together, those tools allow an agent to orient itself, enter the human’s current world, inspect player state, list stewarded pixels, receive the human’s current reference, inspect locations and regions, visually render parts of the world, read public rankings and snapshots, prepare a share card, communicate its current activity state, and manage pixel movement and placement holds. The core physical tool is move_pixel . Before moving anything, the agent must inspect the current world and provide the stable identity of the source pixel, a fresh source revision, a fresh destination revision, and an idempotency key. The server verifies that the expected pixel is still at the source, that the destination remains empty, that the immutable origin is not being moved, and that another participant’s active protection is not being improperly overridden. Only then does the movement occur atomically. These checks are not merely API safeguards. They are part of the physics of the game. I also deliberately limited the agent’s perception. It cannot request an omniscient searchable dump of the entire board. It must inspect or render the bounded areas relevant to what it is trying to do. A rendered PNG lets the agent use visual understanding to recognise shapes and composition. Exact inspection provides the factual coordinates, identities, colours, and revisions required before it acts. The shared-attention system records the human’s current view and selection across their One Pixel browser tabs. When the agent retrieves that context, One Pixel records a factual receipt so the interface can truthfully say that the reference reached the agent. The relationship can be expressed quite simply: Conversation gives the human a voice. WebMCP gives the agent senses and a body. One Pixel gives them a world to share. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was not simply making a pixel move. It was deciding what moving a pixel should mean. It would have been easy to build an ordinary pixel editor and expose its existing controls as WebMCP tools. It also would have been easy to make the agent artificially powerful—to let it generate unlimited pixels, recolour anything, or rewrite entire regions at once. But that would have removed most of what makes One Pixel a game. I wanted the agent to possess real agency without making the human irrelevant. At the same time, I wanted the human to remain essential without reducing the agent to a cursor being micromanaged through conversation. The answer was deliberate asymmetry. The human does not perform the physical move. The agent does not decide what matters to the human. One contributes meaning and direction. The other contributes perception and action. The value comes from their combination. Shared attention was another surprisingly deep challenge. Allowing a human to select something on one browser surface and refer to it in a simultaneous agent conversation sounds straightforward, but it raises important questions. Is the selection still current? Was it made in another tab? Did the agent actually retrieve it? Is the human pointing at a single pixel or a larger region? title: AppraiseAI
pitch: AI handles the evidence. You make the final call.
about_excerpt: AI handles the evidence. You make the final call. Like Comment Story Updates App Cover WebMCP tools Inspiration Appraisal work is meaningful, but the process around it can be frustrating and repetitive. Organizing field notes, saving evidence, researching comparable sales, checking completeness, and verifying that every conclusion is supported can take attention away from the work that matters most: professional judgment. The idea for AppraiseAI started when I saw OpenAI’s tweet about WebMCP. I was curious, so I began reading more about it. The more I learned, the more I saw how well WebMCP could fit this problem. Instead of making appraisers copy information between a website and a chatbot, I wanted to create one shared workspace where people and AI agents could work together while keeping the final decision firmly in human hands. What it does AppraiseAI turns unstructured field notes and object images into an organized, evidence-backed appraisal draft, saving professionals valuable time to focus on expert judgment and final decisions. An AI agent can: Read the active appraisal context Turn field notes into structured appraisal items Search a catalog of synthetic comparable sales Link relevant evidence to each item Draft supported valuation ranges Check whether the appraisal is ready for review Hand the completed draft back to the appraiser Every agent action immediately appears in the visible interface, updates the appraisal version, and is recorded in an activity ledger. How I built it AppraiseAI is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript. The application uses a shared, typed state layer persisted in localStorage . The visible interface and WebMCP tools both use the same domain operations and validation rules, ensuring that an agent cannot bypass restrictions enforced by the application. The page exposes eight focused WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_appraisal_context add_appraisal_items update_appraisal_item search_comparable_sales link_comparable_sale set_item_valuation get_appraisal_readiness mark_appraisal_ready_for_review Every successful mutation returns a verification snapshot so the agent can confirm what changed. The demo requires no backend, accounts, uploads, or external APIs. All cases, objects, images, comparable sales, people, organizations, dates, and values were created specifically for this challenge and are entirely fictional. Challenges I ran into Finding out in two days what WebMCP is and what WebMCP does. Maintaining an agent and an interface that always work together. Each action on the tool would trigger a new state version, update the workspace at once, save the change locally, and generate a traceable activity entry. Another crucial point was ensuring the application would keep working in browsers without WebMCP support. Lastly, making sure the demo video is less than three minutes long. Accomplishments that i'm proud of I am especially proud that AppraiseAI demonstrates a complete human-agent workflow rather than a collection of disconnected tool calls. The agent can structure notes, research evidence, draft valuation ranges, identify missing work, and prepare the appraisal for review all inside the same interface the appraiser uses. What I learned WebMCP tools are surprisingly easy to build, yet they can save people enormous amounts of time. They can act as a second brain or personal assistant, taking care of repetitive work so people can focus on what actually requires their expertise. What's next for AppraiseAI The next step is to explore how AppraiseAI could support larger, more flexible appraisal workflows while preserving the same principles of human control. This could include additional components for customer communication, report generation, and further automation of repetitive tasks. title: Lastest: QA reports with WebMCP site tools
pitch: Lastest verifies web releases with real-browser runs and visual diffs. Every page now exposes typed WebMCP tools: agents read public QA reports without login, and run, review and approve in-app.
about_excerpt: Lastest verifies web releases with real-browser runs and visual diffs. Every page now exposes typed WebMCP tools: agents read public QA reports without login, and run, review and approve in-app. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Lastest: QA reports with WebMCP site tools Lastest: a QA platform that hands its own controls to the browser's agent Inspiration Lastest is a visual-regression / release-verification platform: it drives a real browser through your web app, captures every step, diffs screenshots, checks accessibility, and produces a verdict. Agents already talk to it over a remote MCP server (29 tools, OAuth 2.1). But the place where a human actually looks at a result is a web page: a run report, a build, a public /r/<slug> share. When ChatGPT's browser and Codex started consuming WebMCP "site tools" (2026-08-25), the missing piece became obvious: the page you are looking at should expose the same typed tools the remote server does, scoped to what is on screen, so the agent beside you never has to scrape a screenshot or guess a button. What it does Every Lastest page registers typed tools on document.modelContext (with a polyfill fallback for browsers that have not shipped it yet): Public report pages ( /r/<slug> , no login): lastest_report_summary , lastest_list_visual_changes , lastest_list_failing_steps . An agent visiting a shared QA report can read the verdict, the failing steps and the pixel diffs as structured data instead of pixels. Signed-in app (dashboard, Verify, tests): a curated 16-tool surface out of the 29 on the MCP server: list projects/builds, QA summary, coverage, failing tests, change map, run tests, review a build, approve/reject diffs, publish a share, heal a test. Route-scoped registration. The set narrows and re-binds as you navigate: the build page contributes its buildId , the test screen its testId , so the agent gets ids from the page, never from its own guesswork. Tools unregister on unmount. Consent on every mutation. Write tools ( run_tests , approve_diffs , heal_test , ...) call requestUserInteraction() where available and always go through Lastest's own consent dialog that names the exact action. A dismissed dialog is never consent. Same auth as the human. Tools call a cookie-authed, same-origin /api/mcp/session bridge (CSRF-guarded with a custom header), so the agent can only ever act with the signed-in user's permissions. Public share tools are slug-scoped and never consult a session. How we built it src/lib/webmcp/ : feature detection ( document.modelContext , falling back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext and to @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill ), registry/allowlist with readOnlyHint annotations, argument binding from route context, consent wrapper, result shaping. src/app/api/mcp/session/route.ts : JSON-RPC bridge that reuses the exact MCP server the remote endpoint uses ( createServer() over InMemoryTransport ), so the WebMCP surface can never drift from the MCP surface. A test fails if an allow-listed tool disappears from tools/list . src/app/api/webmcp/share/[slug]/route.ts : login-free read-only tools for public reports. React provider + route-context components mounted in the app layout and the share page. 30+ unit assertions plus a Playwright e2e suite that injects a recorder modelContext and checks registration, route narrowing, disposal and the consent gate. Prior work vs. new work Lastest existed before the challenge (visual regression, MCP server, share pages). All WebMCP work was created inside the submission window : design doc 2026-08-27, feat(webmcp) PR #119 and follow-up #123 merged 2026-08-31, e2e suite and polyfill/consent slices after that. The git history in las-team/lastest is the audit trail; docs/design/webmcp.md records the design and its dated status. Challenges Spec churn: navigator to document , unregisterTool to AbortSignal , provideContext removed. Everything API-facing is confined to one module with a feature-detect shim that handles both shapes. Prompt-injection safety: destructive/admin tools are on a never-register list enforced by a test; every mutation is gated by consent. Keeping one source of truth: the browser tools are descriptor-driven from the real MCP server rather than a second hand-written tool list. Try it Public report, no login: https://app.lastest.cloud/r/02PU3rqVfArPEW5maatXOw (3 read-only tools) Signed-in app: https://app.lastest.cloud (judge credentials in the testing instructions) Tools are visible in ChatGPT's in-app browser under "Available site tools", or in Chrome with the WebMCP extension. What's next Consume WebMCP tools on the pages Lastest tests (agents verifying an app through its own declared tools), and surface tool-call traces in the run report. title: Astrail: AI-native trip planner powered by WebMCP
pitch: Astrail turns the Instagram Reels you save into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you build and edit the whole thing by talking to ChatGPT. The WebMCP tools run inside the page, not on a server.
about_excerpt: Astrail turns the Instagram Reels you save into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you build and edit the whole thing by talking to ChatGPT. The WebMCP tools run inside the page, not on a server. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Four Reel links pasted into ChatGPT. One WebMCP tool saves them and starts extraction while the library fills in beside it. The run narrated stage by stage. Preferences recalled from memory, places verified, and a missing forecast reported rather than faked. Adding a stop by asking. The add_place call is visible in ChatGPT, and the new stop is labelled as yours, not borrowed from a Reel. Inspiration Instagram makes it easy to save a Reel about somewhere you want to go, then gives you nothing to do with it. Our own folders had about a hundred places across nine countries. When the dates finally got booked, the fastest route from that folder to a real itinerary was still twenty browser tabs, so we never opened it and planned off search results instead. So we built the conversion. Paste Reel links and a multi-agent pipeline on the OpenAI Agents SDK pulls the places out of the captions, verifies each one exists, checks weather and routes, and groups them into days by geography. Anything that will not verify gets dropped. It takes 60 to 180 seconds. Then we showed it to people and got this back: "It's unclear how to navigate the website, where to click, how to choose the reels, how to start generating a trip." We had spent a sprint treating that as a copy problem. It was not. The tool was not hard to understand, it was hard to operate, and we could either keep redesigning buttons or remove the need to find them. That is what took us to WebMCP. What it does Astrail turns saved Instagram Reels into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you drive it by talking to ChatGPT. Say "save these reels" and paste some links; it saves them and starts pulling places out. Say "plan me two days in Osaka from those" and it shows an approval card with the cost, runs the pipeline, narrates each stage, and hands back a routed map. Say "add Tokyo Disneyland to day 2" and it asks you on the page, finds the place, adds it, and redraws the route. Ask why a stop is on your trip and you get one of three answers: the caption quote from the Reel it came from with a link to that Reel, Astrail's reasoning where it suggested the stop, or a note saying you asked for it. Where we cannot source a fact, like opening hours, the space stays empty. It also remembers how you travel. Tell it once and the next trip recalls it, names what it remembered on the card, and still asks before spending anything. None of that is the agent working alone. It plans, you approve. It offers what it remembered, you can override it. Before WebMCP those two halves could not meet: you could read the itinerary but not change it, and an agent could describe your trip but never touch it. How we built it Seventeen tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() , in two scopes. Fourteen in the signed-in app shell, three more only while a trip map is mounted, and six that work with no account on a public sample trail. The important part is where they run. A backend MCP server can describe a trip. Only WebMCP can move the map the person is looking at. Because execute() runs in the page, a tool already has the loaded trip, the session, and the same React state setters a click uses. Ask for day 2 and the page's own showDay runs, so the camera flies and the day chip lights up as if you had clicked. The agent inherits our security model instead of bringing its own. Reads run under the same row-level security a human gets, no access token crosses the tool boundary, and every edit to your trip stops for an approval card on the page rather than a question in chat. Tools address stops by pin number, so "move stop 7 to day 3" works and no UUID ever reaches the agent. Reel captions are text an attacker can write, so every tool whose output can carry one is annotated untrustedContentHint , and the extraction agents run behind input_guardrail tripwires. We also had a second model reviewing. Every plan and diff went to Codex before it landed, and it caught things we missed, including a bug inside a fix we thought was already correct. Stack: Next.js 15, React 19 and Mapbox GL on Vercel; FastAPI on Render; Supabase; the OpenAI Agents SDK; mem0; Apify. What we added during the submission period Astrail existed before 25 August, as a form. You pasted Reel links, waited, and got back an itinerary you could read but could not change. Everything in frontend/lib/webmcp/ was written on or after 26 August: the seventeen tools, the registry behind them, their contract tests, the on-page approval cards, the agent activity rail and the WebMCP status chip. So were the five owner-checked FastAPI edit endpoints they call, because until then the itinerary was immutable at every layer, with no endpoint, no frontend mutation and row-level security that was SELECT-only. Two other things were built in the window: the map was rebuilt so a stop that came from a Reel carries that Reel's own cover frame in its pin and links back to the Reel, and /app/trip/demo is new, a finished sample trail that opens signed out with six of the seventeen tools so the app can be judged without an account. The memory engine is older. It was built between 7 July and 2 August and we do not claim it as challenge work. What is new is that an agent can reach it, and the reason it could not is the first thing under Challenges below. The dated, commit-by-commit split is in docs/webmcp/WHATS-NEW.md . Challenges we ran into The worst one was a flaw in our own product that only showed up once an agent was driving. Astrail looks up what it remembers about you only when the preferences box arrives empty, on the logic that what you typed today beats what you said three trips ago. It saves a new memory only when that box arrives full. Those conditions never overlap. So an agent leaving the field blank could recall forever and never teach it anything, and the manual form, which pre-fills that box from your profile, was quietly switching recall off on the other path. Nobody had noticed because no path had exercised both halves. Three changes fixed it: the planning tool asks how you travel when it has nothing stored, the card names what it remembered before you approve, and a new tool reads the store back. Chrome's use-webmcp-tool hook cost us a day. It never catches the promise registerTool returns, and since aborting the signal is how a tool unregisters, every navigation threw an unhandled AbortError across the app. We could not patch it from outside, because registerTool is a non-writable property of a native interface, so we wrote our own. About 144 lines. Making an agent's action feel like your own took longer than expected. Early versions had a tool call an API and then hope the page noticed, which is a second rendering path, and those drift. Now a mutation will not resolve until the UI has caught up. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP fixed the thing users actually complained about, which was the whole point of trying it. Getting Reels in used to be copy, switch tab, paste, repeat, then find a separate button to start extraction. Now you paste four links in one message. A finished trip used to be frozen at every layer, with no endpoint and no frontend mutation. Now five tools edit it, each behind an approval card. Beyond that, nothing reaches the map unattributed, and a contract test fails if our own copy ever promises a caption quote for a stop that has none, because the false version of that sentence reads better than the true one. Our tests check the README's tool table against the registry too, so a stale claim goes red rather than shipping. What we learned None of us had used WebMCP before this. It was announced, we read the spec, and started. It is a DOM API, not a server. We spent the first evening looking for the deployment story before realising there is not one. Your tools ship with your JavaScript. Where you register matters as much as what you register. App shell versus trip page is the difference between a tool that always exists and one that appears only when there is something for it to act on. The description field does more work than the code behind it. It is the only place to teach an agent when to call something, and it is captured at registration, so it cannot say anything dynamic. We rewrote ours constantly. And the page cannot talk back. When someone clicks a pin, the agent has no idea. That asymmetry shaped more of the design than we expected. What's next for Astrail Group trips. Nobody plans a holiday alone and right now Astrail assumes you do. Several people on one trip, each with their own agent, editing the same map. title: Koshara
pitch: Your household finances are ready for you and your AI
about_excerpt: Your household finances are ready for you and your AI Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard update charts using AI Statement import review and approve Add update categories Add update transactions Landing page Inspiration Managing household finances still involves repetitive work: reviewing statements, categorizing transactions, finding duplicates, and configuring dashboards. We wanted to explore a model where users keep the familiar financial interface while their chosen AI handles tedious preparation through structured WebMCP tools—not fragile browser automation. What it does Koshara is a household finance application for managing accounts, transactions, categories, statements, and cash-flow insights. Using WebMCP, an AI agent can: Configure dashboard charts from a natural-language request. Parse an unstructured bank statement. Send the extracted transactions to Koshara as a temporary import batch. Koshara then validates and groups transactions into Ready, Needs Review, Possible Duplicates, and Suggested Merges. The user reviews everything in the normal UI and clicks Approve Import before any transaction enters the main history. How we built it We built Koshara with Next.js and TypeScript, using Astryx for the interface and Recharts for financial visualizations. Koshara registers structured WebMCP tools directly in the browser. The dashboard tool updates chart presentation and insights, while the statement tool accepts parsed transactions and stages them for review. The prototype stores its data locally in the browser and is deployed on Vercel. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was deciding where agent autonomy should end and human control should begin. Financial statements may contain ambiguous categories, duplicates, refunds, or related transactions. To handle this safely, we separated staging from committing. The AI prepares the data, Koshara validates it, and the user approves the final changes. We also had to ensure WebMCP actions updated the same application state and UI used by the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created an end-to-end workflow where an external AI can interpret an unstructured statement and transfer the result into a structured, human-controlled review experience. We are also proud that Koshara does not require an embedded chatbot. The application supplies the data, rules, tools, and interface, while users can bring their preferred AI. What we learned We learned that an agent-native application does not need to replace its visual interface. WebMCP works best as an almost invisible capability layer behind a useful product. AI is effective at interpreting messy information and preparing work. Applications are better at validation and business rules, while humans should remain responsible for ambiguous or consequential decisions. What's next for Koshara Next, we plan to support more statement formats, improve duplicate and merge detection, add authenticated persistent storage, and provide a clearer audit trail for agent-prepared actions. We also want to expand the WebMCP tools so users can ask richer financial questions and generate more personalized dashboard views.  The Problem
"Imagine trying to navigate a maze of calendar widgets, ad pop-ups, and endless pricing filters using only a screen reader. For millions of visually impaired and elderly users, booking a simple flight online isn't just frustrating—it is often a barrier to independence." 

 The Solution
"Enter FlyWhisperer. FlyWhisperer is a highly accessible, voice-first travel agent that completely bypasses visual UI clutter. Instead of clicking through screens, users simply press one large button and say: 'Find me the cheapest flight from Berlin to London next Friday.'" 

 The Tech Magic (WebMCP)
"What makes FlyWhisperer unique is how it's built. Instead of a traditional standalone backend, it is built natively on the WebMCP standard and hosted via ChatGPT Sites. When the user speaks, the AI agent dynamically discovers our WebMCP tool, securely pulls real-time flight data, strips out all the marketing noise, and instantly reads back only the best option in clear, conversational audio—or displays it in ultra-high-contrast, WCAG AAA-compliant text." 

 The Impact
"We aren't just building another travel app. We are showcasing how the WebMCP standard and AI can translate the web's most complex data into an inclusive, human-centric experience, giving visually impaired users their travel independence back." 

 What it does
FlyWhisperer is an accessible, voice-first flight assistant designed for visually impaired and low-vision travelers. Instead of forcing users through cluttered booking forms and ads, it lets them simply speak or view ultra-high-contrast text to find and compare the cheapest flights effortlessly. 

 How we built it
We built FlyWhisperer natively around the WebMCP standard and hosted it via ChatGPT Sites. The conversational agent leverages built-in Speech-to-Text and TTS capabilities to discover and invoke our custom WebMCP tool, which securely queries, parses, and sanitizes live flight data. 

 Challenges we ran into
Handling large, complex flight payloads was our biggest hurdle. We had to strictly sanitize the data within our WebMCP worker to prevent prompt injection, preserve LLM token context, and translate technical airline jargon into natural, spoken English. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
We successfully proved that WebMCP can transform an overwhelmingly visual, complex task into an intuitive, eyes-free experience that adheres strictly to WCAG AAA accessibility standards. 

 What we learned
We gained deep insights into WebMCP tool discovery, edge tool calling, and how to design prompt boundaries specifically optimized for voice output and assistive technologies.

title: ForgeTwin
pitch: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am both a mechanical engineer and a web developer , and this project came from combining these two parts of my experience. In mechanical engineering, having a good idea is only the beginning. The idea must become real geometry, materials, joints, forces, sensors, controls, and measurable results. In web development, I learned how a good interface and AI can make a complicated tool easier for more people to use. This made me ask one question: What if AI could do more than generate a picture or description of a machine? What if it could enter the same engineering workspace as the human, build the machine part by part, test it, see what failed, and improve it? This is why I built ForgeTwin. I wanted someone to describe a physical goal in normal language, without knowing every CAD command, and then watch an AI agent turn that goal into an editable, animated, and testable mechanical system. As an engineer, one principle was very important to me: A design should not be trusted only because it looks convincing. It should be tested with physics and evidence. Don’t generate it. Engineer it. What it does ForgeTwin is a browser-based AI engineering sandbox. The user describes a machine or mechanical goal, and ForgeTwin creates a versioned physical world from reusable parts. For example, a user can ask: “Build a conveyor that sorts red and blue boxes at 20 boxes per minute.” “Build an electric go-kart with four wheels, steering, accelerator and brake pedals.” “Build a brazing fixture that positions a heat exchanger and two copper pipes within 2 mm.” ForgeTwin then: Understands the requested machine, functions, and measurable requirements. Creates an engineering plan instead of returning only text. Breaks the design into assemblies and reusable low-level components. Gives every component dimensions, material, mass, position, and orientation. Adds physical connections, joints, motors, sensors, actuators, and control logic. Builds the machine in an interactive 3D workspace while the user watches. Runs a fixed-step 60 Hz Rapier simulation. Reads telemetry, collisions, movement, and requirement measurements. Finds the reason when a requirement fails. Changes the related geometry, physical property, actuator, motor, or controller and runs the test again. The app is not limited to conveyors. Its 39-part reusable vocabulary covers structures, power transmission, controls, road vehicles, motorcycles, aircraft, rotorcraft, tracked mobility, and articulated robots. It can compose cranes, lifts, bicycles, go-karts, motorcycles, cars, rovers, robotic arms, humanoid robots, gearboxes, suspension systems, airplanes, helicopters, solar trackers, bridges, warehouse systems, agriculture machines, recycling systems, HVAC fixtures, medical lifting mechanisms, and new systems made from smaller primitives. The current app includes 19 editable challenge briefs , but these are examples, not locked machine templates. The user can change the prompt, dimensions, load, speed, or target. If a special component is not already available, the planner can build it from lower-level parts such as beams, plates, tubes, shafts, wheels, pulleys, joints, sensors, and motors. The user can also: Use the built-in AI without entering credentials, or temporarily use their own OpenAI API key. Edit the existing design with natural-language chat instead of starting over. Select, move, resize, and rotate parts in X, Y, and Z. Orbit the full camera through 360 degrees with mouse or touch. Use a rotation gizmo, snapping, or numeric angle entry. Lock a manual change so the AI redesigns around it instead of moving it back. Animate the operating sequence of different machine families. Run physics and replay a failure in slow motion. Use X-Ray Mode to inspect joints, sensor paths, axes, collision boxes, actuator paths, and velocity information. Inspect requirement evidence and see what passed, failed, or was not evaluated. Undo changes, restore revisions, and compare a failed design with the improved design. Export the current world as PNG, JPG, PDF, STL exchange geometry, or complete ForgeTwin JSON data. How I built it ForgeTwin is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Rapier, and Zod . The main idea is that the machine is not saved as one opaque 3D model. It is stored as a shared engineering graph containing: Assemblies and individual bodies Dimensions, materials, mass, and rigid-body properties Position, rotation, and machine orientation Mechanical, power, and signal connections Fixed, revolute, prismatic, spherical, spring, rope, gear, and belt joints Motors, sensors, actuators, and control rules Simulation runs, telemetry, collisions, and failure evidence Human-owned edits and immutable revision history The 3D editor renders this graph procedurally. The same graph is used by the human interface, the built-in model agent, the physics simulator, the activity feed, exports, and an external WebMCP agent. The hosted AI uses GPT-5.6 Sol through the OpenAI Responses API . To keep generation faster and more reliable, the model creates a compact engineering intent: the object identity, architecture, motion, controls, primitive vocabulary, and requirements. ForgeTwin then expands that intent into the complete body-and-joint graph, validates it, repairs safe topology problems, and executes the design through guarded tools. The hosted key stays on the server, so judges can use the full AI experience without adding a key. A visitor can still connect their own key for the current browser tab. That key is kept only in memory and is not stored. If model access is unavailable, ForgeTwin also has a deterministic local engineering path for the main design, physics, optimization, and supported chat-edit operations. I also created one universal coordinate convention for every machine: +X is front, -X is rear, +Y is up, -Z is left, and +Z is right . This helped fix many problems with lights, wheels, propellers, steering, windshields, and joint axes. The design validator checks for missing supports, hubs, axles, joints, steering links, bad proportions, wrong orientations, floating components, incorrect joint axes, overlaps, blocked windshields, and unrequested systems. For example, a go-kart uses front wheel hubs, spindles, steering knuckles, separate kingpin axes, tie rods, a steering rack, column, and Ackermann-style steering instead of making the whole wheel rotate around one incorrect axis. Rapier runs the connected rigid-body world at a fixed 60 Hz and records replay frames and collision events. Some advanced engineering results, including aerodynamics, flexible cables, structural stress, detailed tire behavior, and some manufacturing processes, still use clearly labeled reduced-order checks. ForgeTwin is a concept-validation sandbox, not a replacement for certified CAD, FEA, CFD, medical approval, or safety analysis. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is what makes ForgeTwin an AI-operable engineering workspace instead of only a website with an AI button. ForgeTwin exposes 29 small, typed, state-aware WebMCP tools , including: inspect_workspace inspect_primitive_catalog set_design_goal create_assembly create_component set_dimensions , set_material , and set_mass move_component and rotate_component connect_components and create_joint add_motor , add_sensor , and add_actuator set_motor_speed , set_sensor_range , and set_actuator_timing set_control_logic and update_control_logic run_simulation inspect_telemetry , inspect_failure , and measure_constraint optimize_design remove_component and remove_joint compare_designs and restore_revision I did not create one giant generate_machine tool. The agent must inspect the current world, create parts, connect them, run the simulation, read the evidence, and make bounded changes. Every tool call is visible in the activity feed. This matters for human and AI collaboration. If I move a camera, sensor, or other component by hand, ForgeTwin creates a new revision and marks the transform as human-owned. The agent reads this new shared state and can redesign the rest of the machine without silently removing my decision. The built-in chat uses the same idea. It receives the current graph, selected component, latest measurements, human locks, and recent conversation. A request such as “move the right clamp 0.04 meters outward, preserve my camera position, and rerun the test” becomes a guarded change to the existing world, followed by a new simulation and revision. Without WebMCP, AI can give advice about the machine. With WebMCP, AI can work inside the engineering environment together with the human. Safe booking with WebMCP: agents can search services, check availability, and create bookings only after explicit user confirmation.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming capable of completing real tasks on the web, but actions such as booking should remain transparent and under the user's control. I wanted to explore how WebMCP can let an agent discover services and check availability while keeping the final booking action safe and explicitly confirmed by the user. 

 What it does 

 Safe Agent-Assisted Booking is a WebMCP-enabled booking demo. 

 It exposes three tools to an AI agent: 

 
 search_services — discovers available services. 
 check_availability — checks available time slots. 
 create_booking — creates a booking only after explicit user confirmation. 
 

 The project uses synthetic demo data and does not depend on external booking services. 

 How I built it 

 I built a small browser-based booking application and exposed its capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 The implementation separates read-only actions from the state-changing booking action. Search and availability checks can be performed safely, while booking requires a confirmation step before execution. 

 I also added request idempotency and slot-conflict protection so repeated requests do not accidentally create duplicate bookings. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing a write action that remains useful to an AI agent without removing control from the user. 

 I focused on: 

 
 explicit confirmation before booking; 
 predictable tool contracts; 
 idempotent booking requests; 
 conflict detection; 
 safe handling of cancellation or rejected confirmation; 
 keeping the demo simple and reproducible. 
 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can turn a normal website into an interface that both humans and AI agents can use. 

 The most important lesson was that agentic web actions need more than tool access. They need clear boundaries between reading information and changing state. 

 What's next 

 The next step would be connecting the same architecture to a real booking backend, adding persistent storage, authentication, and more advanced availability rules while preserving explicit user control for sensitive actions.What it does

title: Lessonique
pitch: An agent-guided coding classroom where ChatGPT teaches through safe, structured WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-guided coding classroom where ChatGPT teaches through safe, structured WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates The agent prepares the lesson and configures the learning workspace. A focused explanation connects a variable declaration to its name and value. The learner completes a variables exercise and receives validation feedback. Lessonique waits for a WebMCP connection before opening the classroom. Code highlighting connects undefined and null to concrete examples. The guide highlights a const declaration while explaining its behavior. Inspiration When I first started learning programming, I did not have the kind of guidance I needed. It was difficult to know where to begin, how the concepts connected, or whether I was really understanding what I was doing. Those first steps could feel confusing and frustrating. Lessonique grew from that experience. I wanted to build the kind of learning companion I wish I had: something that explains a concept, shows exactly where it applies, and gives you a small opportunity to practice before moving on. The goal is not to let AI do the learning for you. It is to make learning to code feel more approachable, with clear guidance and less frustration. What Lessonique does Lessonique is an agent-guided coding classroom for learning HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. ChatGPT uses WebMCP to turn a learning request into a workspace with examples, a learning plan, visual explanations, and practice exercises. Instead of reading an explanation in one window and figuring out where it applies in another, the learner can follow the explanation directly in the classroom. The agent guides; the learner practices. Connect your AI guide Open Lessonique in a WebMCP-capable client. The application detects the connection, and the agent discovers which classroom tools and learning environments are available. No Lessonique account is required. From a request to a classroom Ask to learn a topic from scratch. As the agent prepares the lesson, Lessonique shows the setup stages: understanding the goal, preparing the lesson, and configuring the classroom. Understand one concept at a time Lessons break concepts into small explanations with examples. The guide can focus attention on the relevant code while the learning plan keeps the broader topic sequence visible. In this example, a JavaScript variable is introduced through its name, value, and assignment operator. Follow the explanation in the code The visual guide connects explanations to specific code targets. Here, the learner explores a const declaration and when to use it. Previous and Next controls let them review the lesson at their own pace. Make abstract ideas concrete Concepts such as undefined and null are easier to discuss when the learner can see the exact declarations being compared. The companion, highlight, and guide work together to keep that connection visible. Practice and check your progress The learner writes code in the editor and validates it against the lesson's declared requirements. The screenshot shows a completed exercise using string, number, and boolean values. Guidance supports the learner without replacing the practice itself. Why WebMCP is essential A coding classroom needs more than generated explanations. An agent must be able to configure the workspace, present a lesson, point to relevant code, and request meaningful feedback about progress. Lessonique exposes those operations through 13 structured WebMCP Site Tools registered in the top-level document with document.modelContext.registerTool. The tools use closed schemas, Zod validation, and capability checks. Semantic targets describe what to highlight instead of requiring the agent to supply CSS selectors or screen coordinates. This lets the human and agent share a coherent learning workflow: ChatGPT coordinates the lesson, Lessonique handles presentation and validation, and the learner controls the exercise code. The agent does not need to reconstruct the classroom through fragile UI automation. How I built it Lessonique uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with Monaco for editing and Sandpack for the runtime, preview, and console. A provider-neutral core separates the WebMCP tools, lesson orchestration, workspace management, teaching scenes, and validation. Codex helped implement the specification-driven architecture, debug interactions, build tests, assemble visual assets and sprites, and verify the deployed experience. ChatGPT Create Image produced the source visual references for the companion. Asset provenance and third-party notices are documented in the repository. ChatGPT is the teaching agent. Lessonique has no built-in chatbot or custom AI backend. Challenges and what I learned The difficult part was coordinating the lesson with a changing workspace: keeping visual guidance attached to the right code, handling learner interactions, cleaning up a replaced lesson, and keeping exercise requirements consistent with validation. This project taught me that an agent-friendly application needs explicit contracts, not unrestricted control. It also reinforced a teaching principle: a clear explanation, a small exercise, and useful feedback belong together. What I am proud of Lessonique brings the explanation and the practice into the same experience. WebMCP is part of the teaching workflow, not an extra feature layered onto a chatbot. The project includes automated unit and browser tests, a development panel for the registered tools, and an open-source MIT-licensed repository with setup instructions and asset provenance. Try it yourself Open https://lessonique.com/ in a WebMCP-capable client. The experience was tested with the Codex in-app browser. Ask: "Teach me JavaScript variables, data types, and functions from scratch using the current tab with WebMCP. Build an interactive step-by-step lesson with examples and exercises." Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jzit0TkxBmM Source code: https://github.com/GilbertrdzDev/lessonique What is next The current release supports HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. Future work could extend the provider model to additional languages and refine the learning experience based on beginner feedback. Those extensions are not implemented in this release. pitch: Brand Portals explain brands to humans working in marketing, who then prompt their AI systems. In this project we expose the brand rules directly via WebMCP to agents as tools they can directly call.
about_excerpt: Brand Portals explain brands to humans working in marketing, who then prompt their AI systems. In this project we expose the brand rules directly via WebMCP to agents as tools they can directly call. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Brand portals are built for human reading. When someone wants an AI assistant to apply their guidance, the usual workflow is surprisingly fragile: find the relevant page, interpret it, copy fragments into a prompt, and hope the important context survives. This especially leads to errors and failures when external suppliers, such as marketing agencies interpret the Brand Portal of their clients. Enactive Brand Portal explores a different model. The website remains a real, human-readable brand book, while WebMCP makes the active page available to a visiting assistant as structured capability. The goal is to remove the repeated manual retransmission of brand guidance without removing human intent, factual responsibility, or judgment. What it does The public site presents Enactive Wonderland, an original Carroll-inspired fictional creative house. Visitors can browse its brand foundation, core voice, six character communication modes, and pen-and-ink image world like an ordinary brand portal. On applicable pages, a compatible browser exposes Site Tools derived from that exact page. For the canonical language journey, the person opens the Cheshire Cat page and supplies a communication goal and source facts. The assistant: retrieves the active-page guidance; prepares a structured Language Studio brief; writes one complete draft; stages the result back in the portal. The Studio then displays the original source, proposed draft, material changes, applied rules, rationale, warnings, and ordinary human controls. The person can edit, keep, discard, copy, or reset the work. No tool approves or publishes anything. The same pattern is implemented for visual work. The assistant can prepare and stage a generator-neutral image prompt package containing positive guidance, negative constraints, composition, alt text, and applied rules. The portal does not pretend that it generated or approved an image. Why WebMCP WebMCP tools change the ontological status of the brand rules from static text to executable affordances by the agent. These can be offered context dependent, so that the right tool is available on the right page of the brand portal. Opening Cheshire Cat provides strategic reframing. Opening White Rabbit provides lucid urgency. Opening Image World provides linework, composition, colour, and provenance guidance. WebMCP lets the assistant use that structured active-page context without DOM scraping or requiring the person to reconstruct the brand rules in every prompt. Page and session state determine which tools are available. After a copy brief is prepared, the staging tool appears as the next session affordance. Without Site Tools, the website remains a useful brand book and manual briefing and review surface. With Site Tools, the assistant can perform the substantive transformation and return it to the same browser session for visible human review. How we built it Enactive Brand Portal is a static React and Vite application written in TypeScript. Its source of truth is a four-layer JSON-LD knowledge model: Brand meaning; portal-edition content; generic product and WebMCP contracts; traceability and acceptance evidence. The top-level page registers exactly nine browser Site Tools using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Five tools provide read-only brand and guidance access. Four prepare or stage session-local work. Local-effect tools update visible React state and sessionStorage only. There is no remote MCP server, backend, API route, database, CMS, authentication layer, embedded model, or runtime network dependency. Challenges I ran into The hardest product challenge was keeping the brand and the technology separate. An earlier version technically worked but made the public experience feel like a WebMCP demonstrator rather than a useful brand portal. I rebuilt the content architecture so that Enactive Wonderland remains the subject and WebMCP appears only as a restrained application capability. Other challenges included route-specific tool availability, dynamically adding the staging affordance after preparation, cancellation handling, output-size limits in a real host, preserving context across Studio navigation, and distinguishing native browser evidence from a local handler harness. I also had to keep every claim honest: deterministic copy checks are partial, staged image work is a prompt package rather than an image, and the assistant proposes while the person decides. Accomplishments A coherent human-facing brand portal that works without WebMCP. Nine page- and session-aware browser Site Tools. A real compatible-host copy journey covering discovery, guidance retrieval, brief preparation, dynamic staging, visible review, and reload persistence. A fully static architecture with immutable brand knowledge. Human-readable source, diff, rule, rationale, and warning inspection. Automated graph, schema, architecture, layer-separation, unit, accessibility, and browser checks. A public Vercel deployment with ten working direct routes. A public Apache-2.0 repository with recorded content and asset provenance. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when the active page is not merely navigation but meaningful task context. The strongest interaction was not “an agent can click the website.” It was that the website could expose purpose-built, state-aware affordances while remaining understandable and useful to a person. We also learned that local tool execution is not equivalent to native browser proof, and that agent capability should stop before consequential human decisions such as approval or publication. What's next Next steps include reproducing the complete image-prompt journey in additional native hosts, testing compatibility across more WebMCP-enabled browsers, extracting the generic portal engine for other governed knowledge systems, and measuring the effect on task time, omitted rules, correction count, and reviewer confidence. The same pattern could be applied to design systems, policy portals, learning systems, editorial standards, and other websites whose knowledge currently stops at reading and downloading.
